f: SIPRI data show Russia as India's largest arms supplier for 2020-24, with about 36 percent of India's imports. France is second.
r: Russia's share of Indian imports has fallen sharply from about 72 percent in 2010-14.

q: Choose the correct form of the sentence: Amna will have repair her bike by next week.
o: Amna will have repaired her bike by next week.
Amna will has repaired her bike by next week.
Amna will have repairing her bike by next week.
Amna will had repair her bike by next week.
f: The future perfect tense is formed with will have plus the past participle, so repair must become repaired.
r: The future perfect tense shows an action that will be completed before a stated time in the future.

q: If 10 men can dig a well in 5 days, how many days will 5 men take to dig it? (2)
f: Total work = 10 x 5 = 50 man-days. With 5 men, days = 50 / 5 = 10 days.
r: Fewer workers need proportionally more time, which is called inverse proportion.

q: In which country is the White House located?
f: The White House stands at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., United States.
r: Construction of the White House began in 1792 and it was first occupied by President John Adams in 1800.

q: Which country is traditionally called the Land of the White Elephant? (5)
f: Thailand (formerly Siam) is known by this name because white elephants were sacred and symbols of royal power there.
r: Sources differ slightly, as Myanmar and Laos have also been linked to white elephants, but Thailand is the textbook answer.

q: Who won the seventh edition of the Pakistan Super League (PSL 7) in 2022?
f: Lahore Qalandars beat Multan Sultans by 42 runs in the final at Gaddafi Stadium, Lahore, on 27 February 2022.
r: It was the first PSL title for Lahore Qalandars, who also won PSL 8 in 2023.

q: Which team won the 2021 ICC Men's T20 World Cup?
f: Australia beat New Zealand by 8 wickets in the final in Dubai in November 2021 to win their first T20 World Cup.
r: Pakistan won the 2009 ICC T20 World Cup, and it reached the 2021 semi-final.

q: When are the articles a and an used? (2)
f: A and an are indefinite articles used before singular countable nouns; a is used before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound.
r: The article the is the definite article and can be used with singular, plural and uncountable nouns.

q: What is the work of the angels Munkar and Nakir, according to Islamic belief?
o: Blowing the trumpet on the Day of Judgement
Questioning a person in the grave
f: Munkar and Nakir are the two angels who question a person in the grave about his Lord, his religion and his Prophet.
r: The angels who record deeds are Kiraman Katibin, who sit on each person's shoulders.

q: In which year did the Holy Prophet Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH) pass away?
f: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) passed away on 12 Rabi-ul-Awwal, 11 AH, which corresponds to June 632 CE, in Madina.
r: He was about 63 years old, and he was buried in the room of Hazrat Ayesha (RA).

q: If one man writes one paper in 5 minutes, how long does one man take to write one paper? (2)
f: The question already states that he takes 5 minutes for one paper, so the answer is 5 minutes.
r: At this rate, he would write 12 papers in one hour.

q: Which famous book was written by Data Ganj Bakhsh (Hazrat Ali Hujwiri)?
f: Data Ganj Bakhsh wrote Kashf-ul-Mahjoob, one of the oldest Persian works on Sufism.
r: His shrine is in Lahore.

q: In which Hijri year was the Battle of Yamama fought? (2)
f: The Battle of Yamama was fought against the false prophet Musaylima in 11 AH (632 CE) in the caliphate of Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA).
r: After heavy losses of Quran memorisers in this battle, the Quran was first compiled in book form.

q: What was the relation of Hazrat Yaqoob (AS) to Hazrat Ismail (AS)? (3)
f: Yaqoob (AS) was the son of Ishaq (AS), who was the younger brother of Ismail (AS), so Yaqoob was Ismail's nephew.
r: Both Ishaq and Ismail were sons of Hazrat Ibrahim (AS).

q: On which date (day) of Ramadan is Youm-e-Furqan observed?
f: Youm-e-Furqan marks the Battle of Badr, which was fought on 17 Ramadan 2 AH.
r: Badr is called the day of distinction between truth and falsehood.

q: Which is the oldest of these heavenly books?
f: The Taurat was revealed to Hazrat Musa (AS), before the Zabur (Dawood AS), the Injeel (Isa AS) and the Quran (Muhammad PBUH).
r: The Quran is the last of the heavenly books.

q: What is the well-known title of Hazrat Zaid bin Haritha (RA)?
f: Hazrat Zaid (RA) was so dear to the Holy Prophet (PBUH) that he was called Hibb Rasulullah.
r: He is the only Companion whose name is mentioned in the Quran (Surah Al-Ahzab).

q: What is the antonym of 'zenith'? (2)
f: Zenith means the highest point, so its opposite is nadir, the lowest point.
r: Apex, summit and peak are synonyms of zenith.

q: Which Indian mathematician is credited with formalising the rules of arithmetic with zero in 628 CE?
f: Brahmagupta, in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta, gave the first clear rules for using zero in calculations.
r: Sources differ on who first invented the zero symbol; some credit Aryabhata and earlier Indian scholars.

q: 3x - 5x + 2 is an example of what?
f: It has variables and constants joined by operations but no equals or inequality sign, so it is an algebraic expression (it simplifies to -2x + 2).
r: An equation needs an equals sign, such as 3x - 5x + 2 = 0.

f: A - B contains the elements of A that are not in B. Only 3 is in A but not in B.
r: B - A would be {5}.

q: If Y = 4X and X = 2, what is Y?
r: Here 4 is the coefficient of X.

q: In the expression 7X + 4, what is 7 called? (5)
f: The number multiplying the variable X is its coefficient; 4 is the constant term.
r: X is the variable of the expression.

q: What is -10 - 10?
f: Subtracting 10 from -10 moves further down the number line to -20.
r: Two negative numbers added give a larger negative number.

q: What is 1/3 of 10% of 99?
r: 99 is divisible by 3, so 1/3 of 99 = 33.

q: What is 2/2 + 1? (6)
r: Any non-zero number divided by itself is 1.

q: What is 20% of 50?
r: 20% equals one fifth.

q: What is 2x + 3x + 1?
f: Add the like terms: 2x + 3x = 5x, so the result is 5x + 1.
r: Only like terms can be combined.

q: What is 2 x 3 - 2 x 2?
f: Multiply first: 6 - 4 = 2.
r: This equals 2(3 - 2) = 2.

q: What is 4x - 1 if x = 2?
r: Substitute first, then multiply, then subtract.

q: What is 54% of 90?
What is 60% of 70? (2)
r: 10% of 70 is 7, so 60% is 6 x 7.

q: What is 80% of 40?
r: 80% equals 4/5.

q: What is 80% of 75?
r: 80% equals 4/5 and 75 x 4 / 5 = 60.

q: What is 9% of 9?
What is 90% of 91? (2)
f: 90% of 91 = 0.9 x 91 = 81.9. Equivalently, 10% of 91 is 9.1, and 91 minus 9.1 = 81.9.
r: Taking 90% of a number is the same as subtracting 10% of it.

q: What is 90% of 99? (2)
f: 90% of 99 = 0.9 x 99 = 89.1. Equivalently, 10% of 99 is 9.9, and 99 minus 9.9 = 89.1.
r: 90% of 100 is 90, so 90% of 99 is 0.9 less than 90.

q: In set theory, what is n(A-B) equal to?
f: A-B contains the elements of A that are not in B. These are all elements of A except those common to both, so n(A-B) = n(A) - n(A intersection B).
r: The union formula is n(A union B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A intersection B).

q: What is the capital of Somalia? (154)
f: Mogadishu is the capital and largest city of Somalia on the Indian Ocean coast.
r: Hargeisa is the capital of the self-declared Somaliland.

q: What is the capital of Malta? (39)
f: Valletta is the capital of Malta and a UNESCO World Heritage city.
r: Mdina was the old capital of Malta before Valletta.

q: What is the capital of Kazakhstan? (117)
f: Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan; it replaced Almaty as capital in 1997.
r: Astana was renamed Nur-Sultan in 2019 and returned to the name Astana in 2022.

q: The Khyber Pass connects Peshawar with which town of Pakistan? (21)
f: The Khyber Pass runs from near Peshawar through Jamrud and Landi Kotal to the Torkham border with Afghanistan.
r: Landi Kotal is the highest point of the pass and lies close to the Afghan border.

q: In which year was the first Cricket World Cup held? (104)
f: The first Cricket World Cup (the Prudential Cup) was played in England and began on 7 June 1975.
r: West Indies won the first two tournaments, in 1975 and 1979.

q: Who discovered X-rays in 1895? (43)
f: Wilhelm Conrad Rontgen, a German physicist, discovered X-rays in 1895 while experimenting with cathode ray tubes.
r: Rontgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for this discovery.

q: Which person led the launch of the iPhone, which Apple introduced in 2007? (19)
f: Steve Jobs, co-founder and then CEO of Apple, unveiled the first iPhone in January 2007. Apple is the company that made it.
r: Steve Jobs died in 2011 and Tim Cook became Apple's CEO.

q: Where and in which year were the first Asian Games held? (39)
f: The first Asian Games were held in New Delhi, India, in 1951. Eleven countries took part.
r: The Asian Games are held every four years under the Olympic Council of Asia.

q: What does the green colour in the national flag of Pakistan represent? (60)
f: The dark green field of the flag stands for the Muslim majority of Pakistan, while the white stripe stands for religious minorities.
r: The crescent symbolises progress and the star symbolises light and knowledge; the flag was adopted on 11 August 1947.

q: Which of the following countries does NOT share a border with Pakistan? (30)
f: Pakistan borders India, China, Afghanistan and Iran. Tajikistan is separated from Pakistan by the narrow Wakhan Corridor of Afghanistan.
r: The Wakhan Corridor is only about 14 to 15 km wide at its narrowest point.

q: Reykjavik is the capital of which country? (17)
f: Reykjavik is the capital and largest city of Iceland.
r: Reykjavik is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state in the world.

q: What is the capital of Ghana? (16)
f: Accra is the capital and largest city of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea coast.
r: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from Britain, in 1957.

q: What is the capital of Latvia? (24)
f: Riga is the capital and largest city of Latvia.
r: Latvia is one of the three Baltic states.

q: Which country won the 2018 FIFA World Cup? (17)
f: France beat Croatia 4-2 in the final in Moscow in July 2018.
r: Russia hosted the 2018 tournament, and Argentina won the next one in 2022.

q: Who discovered bacteria? (35)
f: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first observed bacteria through his handmade microscope in the 1670s. He called them animalcules.
r: Louis Pasteur proved the germ theory of disease and Robert Koch identified the bacteria causing anthrax and tuberculosis.

q: Who was the first woman Speaker of the United States House of Representatives? (14)
f: Nancy Pelosi of California became the first woman Speaker of the US House in January 2007. She held the post again from 2019 to 2023.
r: Pelosi was succeeded as Speaker by Kevin McCarthy in 2023, and later by Mike Johnson.

q: Moroni is the capital of which country? (12)
f: Moroni is the capital of the Union of the Comoros, an island nation in the Indian Ocean.
r: Comoros lies between Mozambique and Madagascar.

q: Which country has won the most Cricket World Cup titles? (29)
f: Australia has won the men's Cricket World Cup six times (1987, 1999, 2003, 2007, 2015 and 2023).
r: India has won it twice and Pakistan once, in 1992.

q: Which is the highest peak of the Salt Range? (17)
f: Sakesar, in district Khushab, is the highest peak of the Salt Range at about 1522 m.
r: The Salt Range lies between the Jhelum and Indus rivers in Punjab.

q: Who is credited with discovering the proton? (30)
f: Ernest Rutherford identified the proton as a particle in 1917-1919.
r: Thomson discovered the electron and Chadwick discovered the neutron.

q: Whose slave was Hazrat Bilal (RA) before he accepted freedom through Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA)? (12)
f: Hazrat Bilal (RA) was the slave of Umayyah ibn Khalaf, who tortured him for accepting Islam. Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) bought and freed him.
r: Hazrat Bilal (RA) became the first muezzin of Islam.

q: How many atmospheric layers does the Moon have? (11)
o: None, it has practically no atmosphere
f: The Moon is too small and its gravity too weak to hold an atmosphere. It has only an extremely thin exosphere that is almost a vacuum.
r: Because there is no air, sound cannot travel on the Moon and the sky looks black even in daytime.

q: Who discovered the neutron? (34)
f: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.
r: Chadwick received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1935 for this discovery.

q: Which is the smallest ocean in the world? (21)
f: The Arctic Ocean has an area of about 14 million square kilometres and is the smallest and shallowest ocean.
r: The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean.

q: Which team won the Asia Cup cricket tournament in 2022? (10)
f: Sri Lanka beat Pakistan by 23 runs in the final in Dubai in September 2022 to win the T20 format Asia Cup.
r: The 2022 Asia Cup was played in the United Arab Emirates after being moved from Sri Lanka.

q: In which year was the Suez Canal completed and opened? (23)
f: The Suez Canal was opened to traffic on 17 November 1869 after about ten years of construction.
r: It was built under the French engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps and links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea.

q: In which surah of the Holy Quran are the faraiz (obligatory acts) of wudu mentioned? (11)
f: The faraiz of wudu are described in verse 6 of Surah Al-Maidah, which orders washing the face and arms, wiping the head and washing the feet.
r: The same verse also gives the command for tayammum when water is not available; Surah An-Nisa (4:43) also mentions tayammum.

q: Ghani Khan, the famous poet and philosopher, wrote mainly in which language? (10)
f: Ghani Khan (1914-1996) was a well known Pashto poet, painter and philosopher from Charsadda.
r: He was the son of Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan and wrote the book The Pathans.

q: Which prophet (AS) was given the ability by Allah to soften and melt iron? (15)
f: The Quran says Allah made iron soft for Hazrat Dawood (AS), so he could make armour from it. He is the prophet who received the Zabur.
r: Hazrat Sulaiman (AS) was the son of Hazrat Dawood (AS).

q: What is the currency of Japan? (65)
f: Japan's currency is the yen. Its code is JPY.
r: The Bank of Japan issues the yen.

q: During which months of 1999 was the Kargil conflict between Pakistan and India fought? (11)
f: The Kargil conflict began in early May 1999 and ended in late July 1999, after a ceasefire request following talks in Washington.
r: Kargil lies in the Ladakh region along the Line of Control.

q: Who is known by the title Quaid-e-Millat? (41)
f: Liaquat Ali Khan, the first Prime Minister of Pakistan, is known as Quaid-e-Millat (Leader of the Nation).
r: He was assassinated in Rawalpindi on 16 October 1951.

q: With which neighbouring country does Pakistan share a border of about 2,400 km? (20)
f: The Pakistan-Afghanistan border, the Durand Line, is about 2,430 km long and is commonly quoted as about 2,400 km.
r: Pakistan's border with India is about 3,300 km, with Iran about 900 km and with China about 520 km.

q: Napoleon Bonaparte belonged to which country? (18)
f: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French general who became Emperor of the French. He was born on the island of Corsica, which was a French territory.
r: Napoleon was finally defeated at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

q: In the x,y coordinate system, what is the y-coordinate also called? (14)
f: In a point (x, y), the x-value is called the abscissa and the y-value is called the ordinate.
r: The point where both coordinates are zero is called the origin.

q: Where is the shrine of the famous Pashto poet Rehman Baba located? (9)
f: The mausoleum of Abdur Rehman Mohmand, known as Rehman Baba, is at Hazar Khwani near Peshawar.
r: Rehman Baba is called the Nightingale of Pashto poetry and lived in the 17th century.

q: What is the average height of the Potohar Plateau above sea level according to most Pakistani textbooks? (9)
f: The Potohar Plateau lies between the Indus and Jhelum rivers and has an average height of about 300 to 600 metres.
r: Sources differ slightly, with some giving the height in feet as about 1000 to 2000 feet.

q: In which year did Pakistan launch its first satellite, Badr-1? (14)
f: Pakistan's first satellite, Badr-1, was launched on 16 July 1990 from China by SUPARCO. It was a low-earth-orbit experimental satellite.
r: Pakistan later launched Badr-B in 2001 and PakSat-1R in 2011.

q: What is the capital of Zambia? (10)
f: Lusaka is the capital and largest city of Zambia.
r: Zambia is a landlocked country in southern Africa that was formerly Northern Rhodesia.

q: Which is the second highest mountain of Pakistan? (30)
f: K2 is the highest peak in Pakistan and Nanga Parbat, at about 8,126 m, is the second highest.
r: Nanga Parbat is nicknamed the Killer Mountain and is in Gilgit-Baltistan.

q: What does CPEC stand for? (11)
f: CPEC stands for China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, a package of infrastructure and energy projects linking Gwadar port with western China.
r: CPEC was formally launched in 2015 and its flagship port is Gwadar in Balochistan.

q: In which city is the Air Headquarters of the Pakistan Air Force located? (8)
f: The Air Headquarters of the Pakistan Air Force is in Islamabad. The PAF Air Command and Staff College is at Karachi.
r: The Pakistan Air Force Academy is at Risalpur.

q: In which year was the 18th Amendment to the 1973 Constitution of Pakistan passed? (8)
f: The 18th Amendment was passed by Parliament in April 2010 and signed by President Zardari. It transferred many powers from the centre to the provinces.
r: It renamed the North-West Frontier Province as Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and removed the President's power to dissolve the National Assembly under 58(2)(b).

q: What is the antonym of superiority? (8)
f: Superiority means being higher in quality or rank; the opposite is inferiority.
r: The terms inferiority complex and superiority complex were popularised by the psychologist Alfred Adler.

q: Into which sea does the Indus River flow? (8)
f: The Indus River flows through Pakistan and falls into the Arabian Sea near Karachi in Sindh.
r: The Indus delta is near Thatta.

q: What is the approximate maximum height of the Kirthar range (its highest point, Zardak Peak)? (9)
f: The highest point of the Kirthar range is Zardak Peak at roughly 2,260 metres, or about 7,400 feet.
r: Sources give slightly different figures, from about 2,260 to 2,267 metres.

q: What was the Regional Cooperation for Development (RCD) of Pakistan, Iran and Turkey renamed as in 1985? (8)
f: The RCD was revived and renamed the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO) in 1985 by its three founding members.
r: ECO later expanded in 1992 to include Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

q: Which is the busiest sea (ocean) trade route of the world according to standard textbooks? (11)
f: The North Atlantic sea route links eastern North America with north-western Europe and carries the heaviest volume of ocean trade in most textbooks.
r: Modern shipping statistics sometimes rank Asian routes through the Strait of Malacca very high, so sources can differ.

q: Who is traditionally credited in Pakistani textbooks with inventing the telescope? (30)
f: Galileo Galilei built and used an improved telescope in 1609 to observe the Moon, Jupiter's moons and the planets. Textbooks therefore credit him with the telescope.
r: Sources differ: the Dutch spectacle maker Hans Lippershey filed the first known patent for a telescope in 1608.

q: Which is the largest temple in the world? (8)
f: Angkor Wat in Cambodia covers about 162 hectares and is the largest religious monument in the world.
r: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century by King Suryavarman II, first as a Hindu and later a Buddhist temple.

q: Which is regarded as the first women's university in Pakistan, and in which city is it located? (9)
o: Kinnaird College for Women University, Lahore
Sardar Bahadur Khan Women's University, Quetta
f: Fatima Jinnah Women University was founded in 1998 in Rawalpindi and is generally regarded as Pakistan's first women's university. It is named after Fatima Jinnah, the sister of the Quaid-e-Azam.
r: Some sources call it the first public sector women's university, because Kinnaird College in Lahore was a much older women's college.

q: What was the code name of Pakistan's nuclear tests conducted in May 1998? (7)
f: Pakistan's tests at Chagai in Balochistan were named Chagai-I (28 May 1998, five tests) and Chagai-II (30 May 1998, one test).
r: Pakistan observes 28 May as Youm-e-Takbeer; Smiling Buddha was the code name of India's 1974 test.

q: In which city is the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations located? (8)
f: The FAO has its headquarters in Rome, Italy. It leads international efforts against hunger and works on food and agriculture.
r: The FAO was founded in 1945 and its World Food Day is observed on 16 October.

q: Who was the first ambassador of Pakistan to the United States? (7)
f: Mirza Abol Hassan Ispahani, a close associate of Jinnah, was the first Pakistani ambassador to the USA. He served until 1952.
r: Sources differ on whether he took up the post in 1947 or 1948; he later served as High Commissioner to Britain.

q: Tallinn is the capital of which country? (7)
f: Tallinn is the capital and largest city of Estonia, on the Gulf of Finland.
r: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are the three Baltic states.

q: What do the five rings of the Olympic flag represent? (22)
o: Five inhabited continents of the world
f: The five interlocked rings stand for the five inhabited continents joined by Olympism: Africa, the Americas, Asia, Europe and Oceania.
r: The rings are blue, yellow, black, green and red on a white background, designed in 1913 and first flown in 1920.

q: The Karakoram mountain range lies between Pakistan and which country? (9)
f: The Karakoram range runs along the northern border of Pakistan and separates Gilgit-Baltistan from the Xinjiang region of China.
r: The Karakoram Highway crosses this range through the Khunjerab Pass and links Pakistan with China.

q: According to the commonly given number in Pakistani textbooks, how many Companions served as Katib-e-Wahi (scribes of revelation) for the Holy Prophet (PBUH)? (9)
f: Many Pakistani books state that about 40 Companions wrote down the revelation, including Hazrat Ali, Hazrat Usman and Hazrat Zaid bin Thabit (RA).
r: Sources differ on the exact number, and Hazrat Zaid bin Thabit (RA) is the best known of the scribes.

q: In which country did noodles originate? (7)
f: The oldest known noodles, about 4000 years old, were found at the Lajia site in China, and China is generally credited with their origin.
r: Italy and China have long argued about the origin of pasta and noodles.

q: The Olympic Games take their name from Olympia and Mount Olympus. In which country did the Olympic Games originate? (19)
f: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece, and Mount Olympus is also in Greece. The modern Olympics are named after these ancient games.
r: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in 1896.

q: On which date was the Battle of Plassey fought? (28)
f: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the British East India Company under Robert Clive and Nawab Siraj ud Daula of Bengal.
r: The Battle of Plassey is seen as the start of British political rule in India.

q: The word 'terrorism' was first used in connection with which historical event? (7)
f: The term came into use in the 1790s for the Reign of Terror of the Jacobins in revolutionary France.
r: Sources differ on the exact year, with 1794 and 1795 both quoted.

q: Who wrote the poems Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa? (54)
f: Allama Muhammad Iqbal wrote Shikwa in 1909 and Jawab-e-Shikwa in 1913.
r: Both poems were later included in his Urdu collection Bang-e-Dra.

q: What is the antonym of friendly? (6)
f: Friendly means kind and welcoming; the opposite is hostile, meaning unfriendly or aggressive.
r: Hostile comes from the Latin hostis, meaning enemy.

q: To which country did Winston Churchill, the famous leader of World War II, belong? (16)
f: Winston Churchill was British and served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and again from 1951 to 1955.
r: Churchill won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

q: Who conquered Sindh in 711-712 AD? (9)
f: The young Arab general Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh during the Umayyad caliphate. He defeated Raja Dahir.
r: Sindh is therefore called Bab-ul-Islam, the gateway of Islam, in the subcontinent.

q: The determinant of the transpose of a square matrix A is equal to what? (7)
o: Negative of the determinant of A
The inverse of the determinant of A
f: Interchanging rows and columns does not change the determinant, so det(A transpose) = det(A).
r: Also det(AB) = det(A) x det(B) for square matrices of the same order.

q: The speed of a train is double that of a car. If the car's speed is 60 km/h, what is the speed of the train? (6)
f: Double of 60 km/h is 2 x 60 = 120 km/h.
r: Speed = distance divided by time.

q: In which year did the Muslims of the subcontinent get the right of separate electorates? (8)
f: Separate electorates were granted to the Muslims by the Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909.
r: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 later made the Congress accept separate electorates.

q: What is the average gestation period of a cow? (6)
f: A cow carries her calf for about 283 days, which is roughly nine months. This is close to the human pregnancy length.
r: The gestation period of a buffalo is longer, about 310 to 315 days.

q: Kalimullah (the one who spoke with Allah) is the title of which prophet? (7)
f: Hazrat Musa (AS) spoke directly with Allah on Mount Tur, so he is called Kalimullah.
r: Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) is called Khalilullah and Hazrat Isa (AS) is called Ruhullah.

q: Who has scored the most Test runs for Pakistan? (45)
f: Younis Khan scored 10,099 runs in Tests and is Pakistan's leading Test run scorer. He was the first Pakistani to pass 10,000 Test runs.
r: Javed Miandad (8,832) and Inzamam-ul-Haq (8,829) come next.

q: What does the name Moen jo Daro (Mohenjo-daro) mean? (20)
f: Mohenjo-daro is a Sindhi name meaning Mound of the Dead. It was a major city of the Indus Valley Civilization.
r: It is located in Larkana district of Sindh and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

q: Which Islamic Summit of the OIC was held in Pakistan (Lahore) in 1974? (17)
f: The Second Islamic Summit Conference of the OIC was hosted in Lahore in February 1974. The first summit was held in Rabat in 1969.
r: The Lahore summit was attended by many Muslim heads of state and led to Bangladesh being recognised by Pakistan.

q: What is the antonym of the word plentiful? (15)
f: Plentiful means more than enough, and its opposite is scarce, meaning in short supply.
r: Other antonyms of plentiful are rare, sparse and insufficient.

q: On which date was the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) established? (12)
f: The SCO was formally established in Shanghai on 15 June 2001 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
r: Pakistan and India became full SCO members in 2017.

q: What does SCO stand for? (23)
f: SCO stands for Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, a Eurasian political, economic and security grouping.
r: Its permanent bodies are the Secretariat in Beijing and the Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure in Tashkent.

q: According to the 1973 Constitution, how many seats does Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KPK) have in the Senate of Pakistan? (16)
f: After the 2018 merger of FATA and the 2024 changes, KPK has 23 Senate seats: 14 general, 4 women, 4 technocrat and 1 non-Muslim.
r: Before the merger of FATA, KPK had 22 seats and the Senate had 104 members.

q: What is the closest meaning (synonym) of the word 'utility'? (6)
f: Utility means the quality of being useful or serving a practical purpose. Usefulness is therefore its closest synonym.
r: The word 'utilize' means to make practical use of something.

q: According to the 2017 census, what was the population of Pakistan? (7)
f: The 6th Population and Housing Census of 2017 counted 207,684,626 people in Pakistan.
r: The next census, held in 2023, counted about 241.5 million people.

q: Who made the first solo non-stop flight across the Atlantic Ocean in 1927? (5)
f: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis alone from New York to Paris in May 1927.
r: Alcock and Brown made the first non-stop transatlantic flight (not solo) in 1919, and Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly it solo in 1932.

q: What is the antonym of the word advance? (5)
f: To advance means to move forward, and its opposite is to retreat or move backward.
r: Advance can also mean to lend money beforehand, in which case it is a noun meaning a loan paid early.

q: Who described Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah as the Ambassador of Hindu-Muslim Unity? (19)
f: Sarojini Naidu gave Jinnah this title, praising his work for unity at the time of the 1916 Lucknow Pact. Her 1918 book on him is titled Mohomed Ali Jinnah: An Ambassador of Unity.
r: Gopal Krishna Gokhale had earlier made a similar remark about Jinnah, so some sources trace the phrase to him.

q: What is the antonym of fertile? (12)
f: Fertile land or a fertile mind produces plenty; the opposite is barren, which produces nothing.
r: Sterile is also accepted as an antonym of fertile, so sources may give either word.

q: What is the antonym of protect? (8)
f: To protect is to keep safe from harm; the opposite is to endanger, to put in harm's way.
r: Defend, guard and shield are synonyms of protect.

q: What is the baby (young one) of a frog called? (5)
f: A young frog hatches from an egg as a tadpole, which lives in water and breathes with gills. It later grows legs and lungs and becomes an adult frog.
r: The change from tadpole to frog is called metamorphosis.

q: Bani Israel (Children of Israel) are the descendants of which prophet, whose title was Israel? (8)
f: Israel was the title of Hazrat Yaqub (AS), and his twelve sons formed the twelve tribes of Bani Israel. Hence the people are called Bani Israel.
r: Hazrat Musa (AS) is the most prominent prophet sent to Bani Israel.

q: Maputo is the capital of which country? (5)
f: Maputo, formerly Lourenco Marques, is the capital of Mozambique.
r: Mozambique gained independence from Portugal in 1975.

q: There are 24 members in a committee and 5 are men. What is the percentage of women? (5)
f: Women = 24 - 5 = 19. Percentage = 19 / 24 x 100 = 79.17 percent.
r: The men are 5/24 x 100 = 20.83 percent, and the two percentages add up to 100.

q: How many nations and territories belong to the Commonwealth Games Federation, which takes part in the Commonwealth Games? (5)
f: The Commonwealth Games Federation has 74 members (nations and territories), including dependent territories that compete under their own flags.
r: The Commonwealth of Nations has only 56 member states, and about 72 teams took part in the Glasgow 2026 Games according to some reports.

q: Who introduced the system of Basic Democracies in Pakistan? (18)
f: Ayub Khan introduced Basic Democracies through the Basic Democracies Order of 1959. Ordinary citizens elected Basic Democrats from local union councils, who then acted as the electoral college.
r: The system was ended by General Yahya Khan's government and replaced under the 1973 Constitution.

q: Diamond is an allotrope of which element? (29)
f: Diamond is made of carbon atoms joined in a rigid tetrahedral crystal structure.
r: Graphite is another allotrope of carbon, and diamond is the hardest natural substance.

q: What is the antonym of "embrace" in the sense of accepting an idea? (6)
f: To embrace an idea is to accept it eagerly, so its opposite is to reject it.
r: Embrace also means to hold someone in the arms, and in that sense a synonym is hug.

q: For what is Sadequain famous? (5)
f: Sadequain (1930-1987) was a famous Pakistani painter and calligrapher, known for his Quranic calligraphy and murals.
r: He painted the ceiling mural at the Mangla Dam power house and the Frere Hall murals in Karachi.

q: What was the relation of Hazrat Fatima (RA) to Hazrat Muhammad (PBUH)? (6)
f: Hazrat Fatima (RA) was the youngest daughter of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) and Hazrat Khadija (RA).
r: She is known as Zahra and Sayyidat Nisa al-Alamin.

q: The Flemish people are found mainly in which country? (8)
f: The Flemish are the Dutch-speaking people of Flanders, the northern region of Belgium.
r: The French-speaking people of southern Belgium are called Walloons.

q: What is the width (length between the posts) of a standard football goal? (5)
f: The two posts of a standard football goal are 24 feet (7.32 m) apart.
r: The goal height is 8 feet (2.44 m).

q: What is the capital of Iceland? (5)
f: Reykjavik is the capital and largest city of Iceland. It is the northernmost capital of a sovereign state.
r: Iceland is a Nordic island country in the North Atlantic Ocean.

q: In which city is the National Library of Pakistan located? (28)
f: The National Library of Pakistan is located in Islamabad on Constitution Avenue in the same complex as other national institutions.
r: It was established in 1951 in Karachi and later moved to Islamabad.

q: In which year was the construction of Pakistan Steel Mills at Karachi started (established)? (10)
f: The foundation of Pakistan Steel Mills was laid in 1973 by Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto with Soviet help.
r: The mill began production in 1981.

q: What is the length of the Panama Canal in nautical miles, approximately? (5)
f: The Panama Canal is about 82 km (51 miles) long. Since 1 nautical mile is 1.852 km, this is about 44 nautical miles.
r: The canal connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans and opened in 1914.

q: Which is generally regarded as the oldest sea port of Pakistan? (14)
f: Karachi Port is the oldest and busiest port of Pakistan; modern port development there began in the 19th century.
r: Port Qasim is the second major port and Gwadar is the newest deep-sea port.

q: How many provinces does Pakistan have? (6)
f: Pakistan has four provinces: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.
r: Islamabad Capital Territory, Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir are not provinces.

q: Which angel is in charge of rain and provision according to Islamic belief? (5)
f: Hazrat Mikail (AS) is the angel entrusted with rain, vegetation and sustenance. Jibrail brings revelation, Israfil blows the Trumpet and Izrail takes souls.
r: Mikail is also spelled Mika'il and is mentioned by name in Surah Al-Baqarah.

q: Who first suggested the name Pakistan? (11)
f: Chaudhry Rehmat Ali, a Cambridge student, proposed the name Pakistan in his 1933 pamphlet Now or Never.
r: The name is made from the letters of Punjab, Afghania, Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan.

q: How many main blood groups are there in the ABO system? (5)
f: The main blood groups are A, B, AB and O, which makes four.
r: Each group can be Rh positive or Rh negative, giving eight common types.

q: Who presented the famous Poor Man's (labourer's) Budget in the interim government of British India just before independence? (4)
f: Liaqat Ali Khan, as Finance Member of the interim government, presented a budget that taxed big business and industrialists to relieve the poor. It was called the Poor Man's Budget.
r: The budget was presented on 28 February 1947; the interim government itself was formed in September 1946.

q: To which city did Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) migrate in 622 AD? (8)
f: In 622 AD the Prophet (PBUH) migrated from Makkah to Madinah, which was then called Yathrib.
r: This migration, the Hijrah, marks the start of the Islamic Hijri calendar.

q: Ahmed is 3 years old and his sister is 4 times his age. What will be the age of his sister after 12 years? (4)
f: Sister's age now is 3 x 4 = 12 years. After 12 years she will be 12 + 12 = 24 years old.
r: The age difference between two people always stays the same over time.

q: What is the antonym of appropriate? (7)
f: Appropriate means suitable for the situation; the opposite is inappropriate or unsuitable.
r: Suitable, fitting and proper are synonyms of appropriate.

q: In which region of Pakistan is Attabad Lake located? (15)
f: Attabad Lake lies in the Hunza valley of Gilgit-Baltistan near Karimabad. It was formed by a landslide that blocked the Hunza River.
r: The landslide happened in January 2010 and the lake submerged part of the Karakoram Highway.

q: The line y = 7 is parallel to which axis? (4)
o: It is parallel to neither axis
f: The line y = 7 is horizontal, because every point on it has y equal to 7. A horizontal line is parallel to the x-axis.
r: The line x = 7 would be vertical and parallel to the y-axis.

q: What is the antonym of the word breach? (4)
f: To breach means to break a rule or agreement. Its opposite is compliance or observance, meaning keeping the rule.
r: Violation, rupture and gap are synonyms or near synonyms of breach, not opposites.

q: What is the capital of Zimbabwe? (5)
f: Harare is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe.
r: Harare was formerly called Salisbury.

q: In a circle, what is the distance from the center to any point on the circle called? (5)
f: The distance from the center to a point on the circle is the radius.
r: The diameter is twice the radius.

q: What is the antonym of the word 'comic'? (4)
f: Comic means funny or amusing, while tragic means sad and causing sorrow, so tragic is the opposite.
r: Comedy and tragedy are the two classic types of drama.

q: In which year was the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) institution founded by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan at Aligarh? (10)
f: Sir Syed founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental School at Aligarh on 24 May 1875, which later became MAO College.
r: The school was raised to MAO College in 1877 and became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920; some sources date the college itself to 1877.

q: How many member countries does the Commonwealth of Nations have? (22)
f: The Commonwealth of Nations has 56 member states, the latest being Gabon and Togo who joined in June 2022.
r: Before 2022 the Commonwealth had 54 members.

q: In which year was the Communal Award announced by the British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald? (4)
f: The Communal Award was announced on 16 August 1932 and gave separate electorates to Muslims and other minorities.
r: Gandhi fasted against the grant of separate electorates to the Depressed Classes, which led to the Poona Pact.

q: In which city and country is the headquarters of the Asian Development Bank located? (52)
f: The Asian Development Bank was founded in 1966 and has its headquarters in Mandaluyong City, Metro Manila, in the Philippines.
r: Japan and the United States are its largest shareholders, and Pakistan is a founding member.

q: In which direction is China located with respect to Pakistan? (7)
f: China lies to the north-east of Pakistan and borders Gilgit-Baltistan through the Khunjerab Pass.
r: The Karakoram Highway links Pakistan and China across the Khunjerab Pass.

q: Change into indirect speech: Ali said, "I was doing work." (4)
o: Ali said that he was doing work.
Ali said that he had been doing work.
Ali said that I had been doing work.
Ali said that he has been doing work.
f: The reporting verb is in the past, so past continuous 'was doing' changes to past perfect continuous 'had been doing', and 'I' becomes 'he'.
r: Backshift moves each tense one step into the past in indirect speech.

q: A car moves at 60 km/h and a train is twice as fast. How far will the train travel in 30 minutes? (15)
f: Train speed = 2 x 60 = 120 km/h. In 30 minutes (half an hour) it covers 120 x 0.5 = 60 km.
r: Distance = speed x time.

q: How many vowels are there in the string EAVNJEGFDUI? (4)
f: The letters are E, A, V, N, J, E, G, F, D, U, I. The vowels are E, A, E, U and I, which makes 5.
r: The English vowels are A, E, I, O and U.

q: What does Radd-ul-Fasaad, the name of the Pakistan Army operation launched in 2017, mean? (17)
f: Radd-ul-Fasaad is Arabic and means rejecting or eliminating discord and mischief. The operation was launched in February 2017 to remove the remaining terrorism and strengthen border security.
r: Operation Zarb-e-Azb (2014) was the earlier major operation in North Waziristan.

q: Which of the following is a prime number: 7, 9, 18, 21? (5)
f: 7 has only two factors, 1 and 7. 9 = 3 x 3, 18 = 2 x 9 and 21 = 3 x 7 are composite.
r: 2 is the only even prime number.

q: Electric current is due to the flow of what? (21)
f: In a metallic conductor, the free electrons drift under a potential difference, and this flow of charge is the electric current.
r: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere.

q: What is the closest meaning (synonym) of genuine? (5)
f: Genuine means real and not imitation. Authentic has the same meaning.
r: Sincere is also used as a synonym of genuine when talking about feelings.

q: The Kirthar Hills (Kirthar Range) lie along the border of which two provinces of Pakistan? (7)
f: The Kirthar Range runs north to south and forms the boundary between Sindh and Balochistan. It is the southern part of the Sulaiman-Kirthar system.
r: Zardak Peak (about 2,260 m) is generally named as its highest point, though sources differ slightly.

q: Who was the mother of Hazrat Ishaq (AS)? (10)
f: Hazrat Ishaq (AS) was the son of Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) and his wife Hazrat Sarah. He was born when Sarah was very old.
r: Hazrat Yaqoob (AS) was the son of Hazrat Ishaq (AS).

q: On which date is Labour Day (International Workers' Day) observed? (7)
f: Labour Day is observed every year on 1 May, including in Pakistan, where it is a public holiday.
r: The day commemorates the Haymarket affair of Chicago in 1886.

q: What is the antonym of the word lethal? (4)
f: Lethal means able to cause death, so its opposite is harmless. Deadly, fatal and poisonous are synonyms or close in meaning.
r: The word lethal comes from the Latin word letum, meaning death.

q: Which letter comes next in the series: Z, X, U, Q, ? (4)
f: The positions are 26, 24, 21, 17 and the differences are 2, 3, 4, so the next difference is 5. 17 minus 5 is 12, which is L.
r: The differences in this series increase by 1 each time.

q: The Kirthar Range is regarded as the southern extension of which mountain range? (4)
f: The Kirthar Range runs north to south along the border of Sindh and Balochistan and is usually described as the southern extension of the Sulaiman Range.
r: Some sources treat the Kirthar Range as a separate range; its highest point is Kutte Ji Kabar.

q: What is the approximate length of the River Nile? (10)
f: The Nile is about 6,650 km (4,130 miles) long. It is traditionally given as the longest river in the world.
r: Sources differ, and some textbooks give figures near 6,400 to 6,700 km; the Amazon is also claimed as longer by some measurements.

q: What is the antonym of the word obsolete? (4)
f: Obsolete means no longer in use or out of date, so its opposite is current or modern.
r: Outdated and archaic are synonyms of obsolete.

q: Porto-Novo is the capital of which country? (4)
f: Porto-Novo is the official capital of Benin in West Africa.
r: Cotonou is the largest city and seat of government of Benin.

q: By which process do green plants prepare their food? (33)
f: Plants use sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make glucose in photosynthesis.
r: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photosynthesis.

q: Who founded the political party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)? (5)
f: PTI was founded by Imran Khan in April 1996 in Lahore. He has remained its founder and leader since.
r: Imran Khan became Prime Minister of Pakistan in August 2018 and was removed through a no-confidence vote in April 2022.

q: Who said that the character of the Holy Prophet (PBUH) was the Quran, that is, he was the embodiment of the Quran? (5)
f: When asked about the character of the Prophet (PBUH), Hazrat Aisha (RA) replied that his character was the Quran.
r: This narration is recorded in Sahih Muslim and the Musnad of Imam Ahmad.

q: Which is the oldest seaport of Pakistan, as given in Pakistani textbooks? (10)
f: Karachi Port is generally given as the oldest and main seaport of Pakistan, with the modern port working from the 19th century. Gwadar and Port Qasim are much newer.
r: Karachi Port Trust was established in 1887; some sources name the ancient port of Banbhore as older.

q: Which tennis Grand Slam tournament is still played on grass courts? (5)
f: Wimbledon in London is the only Grand Slam still played on grass.
r: The French Open is played on clay, while the US Open and Australian Open use hard courts.

q: What is the synonym of afraid? (4)
f: Afraid means feeling fear, which is the same as frightened.
r: Fearless and courageous are antonyms of afraid.

q: What is the SI unit of temperature? (21)
f: The kelvin (K) is the base SI unit of temperature. Celsius and Fahrenheit are not SI units.
r: 0 K is called absolute zero, equal to minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.

q: What is the antonym of 'transparent'? (5)
f: Transparent means see-through, so its opposite is opaque, which does not let light through.
r: Wood and metal are opaque materials.

q: Which type of engine is used in jet aircraft? (5)
f: Jet aircraft are powered by gas turbine engines such as the turbojet and turbofan. They produce thrust by expelling a fast stream of hot gas backwards.
r: Frank Whittle of Britain patented the turbojet engine in 1930.

q: Which major event took place in the 10th year of Hijrah (10 AH)? (4)
o: Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat-ul-Wida) of the Holy Prophet (PBUH)
f: In 10 AH the Holy Prophet (PBUH) performed his only and last Hajj and delivered the Last Sermon at Arafat. The other events took place in earlier years (Badr 2 AH, Hudaibiya 6 AH, Makkah conquest 8 AH).
r: The Holy Prophet (PBUH) passed away in 11 AH, a few months after the Farewell Pilgrimage.

q: Which is the second highest mountain in the world? (8)
f: K2, at about 8,611 m, is the second highest mountain in the world after Mount Everest.
r: K2 is the highest mountain of Pakistan and lies in the Karakoram range.

q: Out of 500 students, 380 are present. What is the percentage of present students? (3)
f: Percentage present = 380 / 500 x 100 = 76%.
r: The absent percentage is 24%.

q: Find the next number in the series: 55, 579, 65, 580, ? (3)
f: The series is two interleaved series. The 1st, 3rd and 5th terms go 55, 65, 75 (add 10) and the 2nd and 4th terms go 579, 580, 581 (add 1). The 5th term is 75.
r: Interleaved series are solved by reading odd and even positions separately.

q: In which surah of the Holy Quran is Ruh-ul-Amin (the Trustworthy Spirit, Hazrat Jibreel AS) mentioned? (3)
f: Surah Ash-Shu'ara (26:193) says that the Trustworthy Spirit brought down the Quran upon the heart of the Prophet (PBUH). The Trustworthy Spirit is Hazrat Jibreel (AS).
r: Jibreel is also called Ruh-ul-Qudus in other verses, for example in Surah Al-Baqarah.

q: In what amount was the valley of Kashmir sold to Gulab Singh under the Treaty of Amritsar (1846)? (10)
f: By the Treaty of Amritsar the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh Dogra for 75 lakh Nanakshahi rupees. This began Dogra rule in Kashmir.
r: The treaty was signed on 16 March 1846 after the First Anglo-Sikh War.

q: What is the antonym of the word amalgamate? (3)
f: To amalgamate means to merge or combine into one. The opposite is to separate.
r: Amalgam is also the name of an alloy of mercury with another metal.

q: What is the antonym of competent? (3)
f: Competent means having the ability to do something well; the opposite is incompetent, meaning lacking ability.
r: Competent and capable are synonyms, so they cannot be the antonym.

q: What is the antonym of foremost? (4)
f: Foremost means first in position or importance; the opposite is last (hindmost).
r: Foremost, leading and chief are all synonyms.

q: What is the antonym of glory? (4)
f: Glory means high honour and fame; the opposite is disgrace or shame.
r: Glory and honour are synonyms.

q: What is the antonym of modern? (4)
f: Modern means belonging to the present or recent time; the opposite is ancient, meaning belonging to the distant past.
r: Old-fashioned is another antonym of modern.

q: In which year was the first Asia Cup cricket tournament held? (3)
f: The first Asia Cup was played in Sharjah, UAE, in 1984. India won it.
r: The Asia Cup was started by the Asian Cricket Council founders including Pakistan, India and Sri Lanka.

q: Who was the father of Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddiq (RA)? (3)
f: Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) was the son of Uthman, who was known as Abu Quhafa. He accepted Islam at the conquest of Makkah.
r: Abu Bakr's mother was Salma bint Sakhr, known as Umm-ul-Khair.

q: What is the base of the common logarithm? (6)
f: The common logarithm uses base 10, so log 100 = 2 because 10 squared is 100.
r: The natural logarithm uses base e, which is about 2.718.

q: In which part of the world do the Bushmen (San people) live? (3)
f: The Bushmen or San are indigenous hunter-gatherers of southern Africa, living mainly in the Kalahari Desert in Botswana, Namibia and South Africa.
r: Their languages are known for click sounds.

q: Accra is the capital of which country? (3)
f: Accra is the capital and largest city of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea.
r: Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from Britain, in 1957.

q: Saint John's is the capital of which country? (26)
f: Saint John's is the capital of Antigua and Barbuda, on the island of Antigua.
r: Antigua and Barbuda became independent from Britain in 1981.

q: What is the capital of Greenland? (3)
f: Nuuk is the capital and largest city of Greenland.
r: Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark.

q: What is the capital of Norway? (5)
f: Oslo is the capital and largest city of Norway.
r: Norway is not a member of the European Union.

q: In which years were the Olympic Games cancelled because of World War II? (5)
f: The 1940 Games (Tokyo/Helsinki) and the 1944 Games (London) were cancelled due to the war.
r: The Olympics were also cancelled in 1916 because of World War I.

q: What is the closest meaning of the word 'clumsy'? (3)
f: A clumsy person moves or handles things in an awkward way and often drops or breaks them.
r: The opposite of clumsy is graceful or deft.

q: Change the voice: Were clothes dried by the mother? (3)
o: Did the mother dry the clothes?
Was the mother drying the clothes?
Had the mother dried the clothes?
Does the mother dry the clothes?
f: The sentence is passive in the past simple tense, so the active form is 'Did the mother dry the clothes?' with the agent as the subject and the verb in base form after did.
r: In the past simple, the passive uses was or were plus the past participle.

q: Which of the following is the synonym of 'contain'? (4)
f: To contain something means to have it inside or to hold it. 'Hold' is the closest in meaning.
r: 'Contain' can also mean to keep something under control, as in contain a fire.

q: Which country owes the largest amount of unpaid dues (arrears) to the United Nations? (3)
f: The United States is the biggest contributor to the UN budget and also has the largest unpaid arrears, over 2 billion US dollars on the regular budget in 2026 plus peacekeeping dues.
r: China is usually the second largest debtor, often paying its dues late in the year.

q: In which year and at which city was the Lahore Declaration signed between Pakistan and India? (6)
f: The Lahore Declaration was signed on 21 February 1999 in Lahore by Nawaz Sharif and Atal Bihari Vajpayee.
r: It was signed a few months before the Kargil conflict of 1999.

q: What is the antonym of the word development? (3)
f: Development means growth or advancement, while retrogression means moving backward or declining.
r: Other opposites of development include decline, regression and deterioration.

q: What is the antonym of 'difference'? (3)
f: Difference means the quality of being unlike. Its opposite is similarity, meaning likeness.
r: Distinction, variety and contrast are synonyms or near synonyms of difference.

q: What is the antonym of 'divided'? (3)
f: Divided means split apart. Its opposite is united.
r: Separated, split and broken are synonyms of divided.

q: What is the closest meaning of 'disgust'? (3)
f: Disgust is a strong feeling of dislike and sickness at something. Revulsion has the same meaning.
r: Loathing and repugnance are also synonyms of disgust.

q: What large sea wave is usually caused by an earthquake under the ocean floor? (4)
f: A strong undersea earthquake suddenly moves the sea floor and displaces a huge volume of water, which travels as a tsunami.
r: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami was caused by a magnitude 9 earthquake near Sumatra.

q: Who was the first woman elected to the United States Congress? (3)
f: Jeannette Rankin of Montana was elected to the US House of Representatives in 1916 and took her seat in 1917.
r: Nancy Pelosi became the first woman Speaker of the US House in 2007.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to "essential"? (3)
f: Essential means absolutely needed, which is the meaning of necessary.
r: Other synonyms are vital and indispensable.

q: What is the antonym (opposite) of the word 'excuse' used as a verb meaning to forgive? (9)
f: To excuse means to forgive or let go without blame. Its opposite is to accuse or blame someone.
r: 'Condemn' and 'blame' are also opposites of excuse in this sense.

q: What is the antonym (opposite) of the word 'exhibit'? (3)
f: To exhibit means to show openly. Its opposite is to conceal or hide.
r: An exhibition is a public show of things.

q: What is the closest meaning (synonym) of the word 'exhibit'? (3)
f: To exhibit means to show something publicly. 'Display' has the same meaning.
r: 'Exhibit' can also be a noun meaning an object shown in a museum or court.

q: What is the closest meaning of the word 'exponent'? (3)
f: An exponent is a person who explains or promotes an idea or cause, so an advocate is the closest meaning. An opponent is the opposite.
r: In mathematics, an exponent is the small raised number that shows the power of a base.

q: What is the antonym of futility? (3)
f: Futility means uselessness or having no result. Fruitfulness, meaning being productive and useful, is the opposite.
r: Uselessness and vanity are synonyms of futility.

q: Ali is going in the direction of west. He turns left and then turns right. In which direction is Ali going now? (3)
f: Facing west, a left turn points him south. Then a right turn from south points him west again.
r: Facing west, his left is south and his right is north.

q: One hectare is equal to how many square metres? (3)
f: One hectare is a square of 100 m by 100 m, which is 10,000 square metres.
r: One hectare is about 2.47 acres.

q: What is the approximate length of the Himalaya mountain range? (3)
f: The Himalayas stretch for roughly 2,400 km (about 1,500 miles) from the Indus gorge in the west to the Brahmaputra gorge in the east.
r: Some sources give 2,400 to 2,500 km; Pakistani textbooks use about 2,400 km.

q: Which country was the world's largest arms importer in the latest SIPRI data (2021-25)? (12)
f: SIPRI's March 2026 data for 2021-25 ranks Ukraine first, with about 9.7 percent of global arms imports, followed by India. The USA is a major exporter, not the top importer.
r: In the 2015-19 and earlier periods India or Saudi Arabia led, and India was second after Ukraine in 2020-24 data as well.

q: At how many points can two distinct lines in a plane intersect each other? (3)
f: Two distinct lines meet in at most one point. If they are parallel they do not meet at all.
r: Two coincident lines share all their points, so they are not distinct.

q: The followers of Hazrat Isa (AS) are called what? (6)
f: The followers of Hazrat Isa (Jesus) are called Christians. Christianity is the largest religion in the world by followers.
r: The Quran calls them Nasara (Nazarenes).

q: Which animal did the people of Thamud kill, despite the warning of Prophet Salih (AS)? (3)
f: The nation of Thamud killed the she-camel sent by Allah as a miracle for Prophet Salih (AS), and was then destroyed.
r: The people of Thamud lived at Al-Hijr in northern Arabia.

q: What is the meaning of the word 'kith' (as in 'kith and kin')? (5)
f: Kith means one's friends, neighbours and acquaintances, while kin means blood relatives.
r: Candidates often answered relatives, but that is the meaning of kin.

q: What is the antonym of 'kith'? (3)
f: Kith means friends and acquaintances, so its opposite is a stranger.
r: The phrase 'kith and kin' means friends and relatives.

q: The word 'Pakistan' means the land of what? (3)
f: Pakistan means 'Land of the Pure' (Pak means pure and stan means land).
r: The name was coined by Choudhry Rahmat Ali in 1933.

q: Complete the sentence: The standard of living ____ since his son joined service. (3)
f: The subject standard is singular and since needs the present perfect tense, so has risen is correct.
r: Since is followed by a point in time and goes with the present perfect tense.

q: Change into passive voice: How did you manage it? (4)
o: How was it managed by you?
How it was managed by you?
How did it managed by you?
How is it managed by you?
f: A simple past question becomes was or were plus the past participle, so the passive is How was it managed by you?
r: In the passive voice the object of the active sentence becomes the subject.

q: On which date was the first martial law imposed in Pakistan? (92)
f: President Iskander Mirza imposed martial law on 7 October 1958 and General Ayub Khan became the Chief Martial Law Administrator. Ayub Khan then removed Mirza on 27 October 1958.
r: The second martial law came in 1969 under Yahya Khan and the third in 1977 under Zia-ul-Haq.

q: Near which city is Mina, the valley where pilgrims stay during Hajj, located? (7)
f: Mina is a valley about 5 km east of Makkah in Saudi Arabia. Pilgrims stay there and perform the stoning of the Jamarat.
r: Arafat and Muzdalifah are the other nearby sites of the Hajj rites.

q: Mogadishu is the capital of which country? (5)
f: Mogadishu is the capital and largest city of Somalia, on the Indian Ocean coast.
r: Somalia is located in the Horn of Africa.

q: Monrovia is the capital city of which country? (3)
f: Monrovia is the capital and largest city of Liberia in West Africa.
r: Monrovia is named after the US President James Monroe.

q: Choose the correct word: When morning ___, the murderer was caught. (3)
f: The natural phrase is 'when morning came', meaning when daylight arrived.
r: 'Arrive' and 'reach' usually need a place or destination, while 'come' suits time and seasons.

q: What is the height of Nanga Parbat, the ninth highest mountain in the world? (7)
f: Nanga Parbat rises to 8,126 metres (26,660 feet) above sea level. It is the ninth highest mountain in the world.
r: Nanga Parbat is also called Diamer, meaning huge mountain, and is the second highest peak in Pakistan after K2.

q: What is the antonym of the word obscure? (3)
f: Obscure means unclear or not well known, so its opposite is clear (or evident).
r: Synonyms of obscure include vague, unclear and dim.

q: What was the old name of Thailand? (3)
f: Thailand was officially known as Siam until 1939, and again briefly from 1945 to 1949. The name was changed to Thailand, meaning land of the free.
r: The Gulf of Siam is now called the Gulf of Thailand.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to optional? (3)
f: Optional means left to choice and not required. Voluntary has the same sense, while the other options mean required.
r: Compulsory is the antonym of optional.

q: From which region does the Indus River originate? (3)
f: The Indus rises in the Tibetan plateau near Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar. It then flows through Ladakh and Pakistan into the Arabian Sea.
r: The Indus enters Pakistan through Gilgit-Baltistan.

q: The girls are 33 and the boys outnumber the girls by 7. How many boys are there? (14)
f: Boys = girls + 7 = 33 + 7 = 40.
r: The total number of boys and girls here is 73.

q: 6 is what percentage of 20? (5)
f: Percentage = 6 / 20 x 100 = 30 percent.
r: Percentage = part divided by whole, multiplied by 100.

q: According to the 1973 Constitution, what is the term of office of the President of Pakistan? (4)
f: Article 44 gives the President a term of five years from the day he enters office.
r: A person cannot hold the office of President for more than two consecutive terms.

q: What is the synonym of the word plentiful? (3)
f: Plentiful means existing in large quantities, which is the same as abundant.
r: Other synonyms of plentiful are ample, copious and bountiful.

q: In which province of Pakistan is Gwadar Port located? (12)
f: Gwadar is a coastal city on the Arabian Sea in southwestern Balochistan, and its deep-sea port is there.
r: Gwadar Port is a key part of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC).

q: Who invented the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440? (7)
f: Johannes Gutenberg of Germany developed the movable-type printing press in the mid-1400s.
r: Movable type had earlier been used in China and Korea, but Gutenberg's press is the textbook answer.

q: Rearrange the letters RAPIS to form the name of a famous capital city. Which city is it, and of which country is it the capital? (8)
f: The letters R, A, P, I, S rearrange to make PARIS. Paris is the capital of France.
r: Paris stands on the River Seine and is the capital of France.

q: What does RCD stand for in the context of Pakistan, Iran and Turkey? (3)
f: RCD stands for Regional Cooperation for Development, a 1964 economic cooperation body of Pakistan, Iran and Turkey.
r: It later became the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO).

q: Which country joined the United Nations in 2002 after its people approved membership in a referendum? (6)
f: Swiss voters approved UN membership in a referendum in March 2002, and Switzerland became the 190th member in September 2002.
r: Switzerland had earlier rejected UN membership in a 1986 referendum.

q: Which Muslim League leader responded to the Nehru Report (1928) with his famous Fourteen Points in 1929? (11)
f: The Nehru Report rejected separate electorates and Muslim demands, so Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points in March 1929 as the Muslim reply.
r: Jinnah had earlier put forward his Delhi Muslim Proposals in 1927.

q: Which word is closest in meaning to seize? (3)
f: To seize means to take hold of something suddenly and by force, which is to grab.
r: Capture and snatch are also synonyms of seize.

q: Who founded the Scientific Society in the subcontinent in 1864? (3)
f: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan founded the Scientific Society at Ghazipur in 1864 to translate Western scientific works into Urdu. It later moved to Aligarh.
r: The society published the Aligarh Institute Gazette.

q: For how many years did the Holy Prophet Muhammad (PBUH) live in Madina after the Hijrat? (3)
f: The Prophet (PBUH) migrated to Madina in 622 CE and stayed there until his death in 632 CE, about ten years. He migrated at age 53 and passed away at 63.
r: The first mosque he built in Madina was Masjid Quba, followed by Masjid-e-Nabawi.

q: Approximately how many princely states existed in British India at the time of the partition in 1947? (3)
f: At partition about 562 princely states were ruled by local rulers under British paramountcy, and each was to join India or Pakistan.
r: Sources differ slightly (562 to 565), and some candidates quote 530 or 565.

q: The Holy Quran as revealed by Allah consists of which of the following? (3)
f: The Quran itself is the Arabic text revealed by Allah. Translations and tafseer are human explanations and are not part of the Quran.
r: The Quran was revealed over about 23 years.

q: Choose the correct direct speech of: The teacher said that he could not meet all of his students. (3)
o: The teacher said, "I cannot meet all of my students."
The teacher said, "He could not meet all of his students."
The teacher said, "I could not meet all of your students."
The teacher said, "I did not meet all of my students."
f: In direct speech the past form could changes back to can and he and his change to I and my.
r: Reporting words said that is dropped and quotation marks are added in direct speech.

q: The Dragon's Mouth (Bocas del Dragon) strait lies between Trinidad and which country? (3)
f: The Dragon's Mouth is a strait between the north-west tip of Trinidad and the Paria Peninsula of Venezuela. It links the Gulf of Paria with the Atlantic Ocean.
r: Trinidad and Tobago is an island nation in the southern Caribbean.

q: Which of the following are the three types of blood cells? (12)
o: Red cells, white cells and platelets
Red cells, white cells and haemoglobin
f: Blood contains red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Plasma is the liquid part, not a cell.
r: Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin.

q: Which of the following is a fard (obligatory) act of wudu according to the Hanafi school? (7)
o: Washing the hands up to the wrists
f: The four faraiz of wudu are washing the face, washing both arms up to the elbows, wiping a quarter of the head, and washing both feet up to the ankles. Gargling and rinsing the nose are sunnah.
r: The four faraiz of wudu are taken from verse 6 of Surah Al-Ma'idah.

q: Who is the author of the book 'Jinnah of Pakistan'? (5)
f: Stanley Wolpert, an American historian, wrote 'Jinnah of Pakistan' (1984).
r: Hector Bolitho wrote another well-known biography titled 'Jinnah: Creator of Pakistan'.

q: What is 2 + 2? (3)
f: Adding 2 and 2 gives 4.
r: Addition is commutative, so the order of the numbers does not matter.

q: Out of 1500 students, 1200 are present. How many students are absent? (4)
f: Absent students = 1500 - 1200 = 300.
r: The percentage of absent students here is 300 / 1500 x 100 = 20%.

q: Who was the first President under the 1973 Constitution of Pakistan, taking office in August 1973? (2)
f: Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto became Prime Minister when the 1973 Constitution came into force on 14 August 1973. Fazal Ilahi Chaudhry became the President at that time.
r: Bhutto had been President before this, and he became Prime Minister under the new parliamentary system.

q: Which country became independent in 1994, ending the last United Nations trusteeship? (3)
f: Palau gained independence on 1 October 1994 and became the last UN Trust Territory to end its trusteeship.
r: Palau later joined the United Nations in December 1994.

q: If the 2nd day of a month is Friday, what day will the 24th be? (2)
f: From the 2nd to the 24th is 22 days. 22 = 3 weeks and 1 extra days, so count 1 days forward from Friday to reach Saturday.
r: Dates that are 7 days apart always fall on the same day of the week.

q: Which country hosted the largest number of refugees in 2017? (2)
f: UNHCR reported that Turkey hosted about 3.5 million refugees at the end of 2017, the largest number worldwide.
r: Turkey stayed at the top of the list for several years because of the Syrian refugee crisis.

q: Who was the 7th President of the United States? (2)
f: Andrew Jackson served as the 7th US President from 1829 to 1837, after John Quincy Adams.
r: Martin Van Buren followed Jackson as the 8th President.

q: Which is the 6th most populous country in the world? (2)
f: The ranking is India, China, USA, Indonesia, Pakistan and then Nigeria in sixth place.
r: Brazil is seventh, and Pakistan is fifth.

q: If a helicopter uses 50 litres of fuel to travel 200 km, how many litres will it use to travel 350 km? (2)
f: Fuel per km = 50 / 200 = 0.25 litre. For 350 km: 350 x 0.25 = 87.5 litres.
r: This is a direct proportion: more distance needs proportionally more fuel.

q: Out of 400 students, 360 are present. What is the percentage of present students? (2)
f: Percentage present = 360 / 400 x 100 = 90%. The absent students are 40, which is 10%.
r: Present and absent percentages add up to 100%.

q: A helicopter uses 80 gallons of fuel to fly 320 km. How many gallons will it need to fly 800 km? (2)
f: Fuel per km is 80 / 320 = 0.25 gallon. For 800 km the helicopter needs 800 x 0.25 = 200 gallons.
r: Problems like this are direct proportion: more distance needs proportionally more fuel.

q: In a class of 1500 students, 1350 are present. What is the percentage of absent students? (2)
f: Absent students = 1500 - 1350 = 150. Percentage absent = 150 / 1500 x 100 = 10 percent.
r: Percentage present in the same class is 90 percent, since the two parts add up to 100 percent.

q: In a class of 500 students, 150 are present. What is the percentage of absent students? (2)
f: Absent students = 500 - 150 = 350. Percentage absent = 350 / 500 x 100 = 70 percent.
r: The percentage present here is 150 / 500 x 100 = 30 percent.

q: On which date is Pakistan Air Force Day celebrated? (4)
f: PAF Day is celebrated on 7 September to honour the PAF's performance in the 1965 war. On that day in 1965 PAF pilots, including M. M. Alam, shot down several Indian aircraft.
r: Defence Day is observed on 6 September.

q: In which year did the United States declare its independence? (4)
f: The Declaration of Independence was adopted on 4 July 1776. That is why 4 July is celebrated as American Independence Day.
r: In July 2026 the United States marked 250 years since its Declaration of Independence.

q: What is the closest meaning of the word annihilate? (10)
f: To annihilate is to destroy something utterly so that nothing remains. Its closest meaning is to destroy completely.
r: The word comes from the Latin annihilare, meaning to reduce to nothing.

q: What is the antonym of the word sumptuous? (2)
f: Sumptuous means grand and expensive-looking, so its opposite is meagre or poor. Lavish, splendid and rich are synonyms.
r: Sumptuous is often used for meals, such as a sumptuous feast.

q: What is the antonym of the word Almighty? (2)
f: Almighty means having unlimited power. Its opposite is powerless or weak.
r: Almighty is used for God in Islam and in many other religions.

q: What is the antonym of coma? (2)
f: A coma is a state of deep unconsciousness, so its opposite is consciousness (being awake and aware).
r: The word coma comes from the Greek koma, meaning deep sleep.

q: What is the antonym of contiguous? (2)
f: Contiguous means sharing a common border or touching; the opposite is separate or detached.
r: Pakistan and India are contiguous countries because they share a border.

q: What is the antonym of divide? (2)
f: Divide means to split into parts; the opposite is unite, to join together.
r: Unity is one of the three guiding principles of the Quaid-e-Azam: Unity, Faith and Discipline.

q: What is the antonym of inaccuracy? (2)
f: Inaccuracy means lack of correctness; the opposite is precision or accuracy.
r: Error, mistake and fault are synonyms of inaccuracy.

q: What is the antonym of isolation? (9)
f: Isolation means being alone and apart from others; the opposite is companionship or togetherness.
r: Isolation, seclusion and solitude are close synonyms.

q: What is the antonym of mild? (2)
f: Mild means gentle or not severe; the opposite is harsh, meaning severe or rough.
r: Some candidates remembered tamed here, but tamed is not the standard antonym of mild.

q: What is the antonym of normally? (2)
f: Normally means in the usual way; the opposite is abnormally, meaning in an unusual way.
r: Usually, regularly and commonly are synonyms of normally.

q: What is the antonym of prosperous? (2)
f: Prosperous means rich and successful; the opposite is impoverished, meaning poor.
r: Prosperous, wealthy and thriving are synonyms.

q: What is the antonym of retrieve? (2)
f: To retrieve is to get something back; the opposite is to lose it.
r: Recover and regain are synonyms of retrieve.

q: What is the antonym of timely? (2)
f: Timely means happening at the right moment; the opposite is untimely, happening at the wrong moment.
r: Prompt, punctual and opportune are close synonyms of timely.

q: What is the antonym (opposite) of apposite? (2)
f: Apposite means very appropriate or relevant to the matter; the opposite is irrelevant or inapt.
r: Apposite, apt and pertinent are synonyms.

q: What is the synonym (closest meaning) of appropriate? (2)
f: Appropriate means right for a particular situation, which is the meaning of suitable.
r: Fitting and proper are also synonyms of appropriate.

q: Which Surah of the Holy Quran was revealed immediately after Surah An-Naml (the Ant) in the commonly given order of revelation? (2)
f: In the commonly used (Egyptian) order of revelation, Surah An-Naml is the 48th Surah revealed and Surah Al-Qasas follows it.
r: Sources differ slightly on the exact order of revelation, but both An-Naml and Al-Qasas are Makki Surahs.

q: Who is the custodian of the House in the National Assembly of Pakistan? (6)
f: The Speaker presides over the sessions of the National Assembly and is regarded as the custodian of the House. He maintains order and decides points of procedure.
r: In the Speaker's absence the Deputy Speaker presides over the House.

q: Where is the headquarters of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)? (46)
f: The IAEA has its headquarters in Vienna, Austria. It promotes peaceful use of nuclear energy.
r: The IAEA is an independent organization that reports to the UN General Assembly and Security Council.

q: In which year did Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah pass the matriculation examination of Bombay University? (2)
f: Most sources state that Jinnah passed the Bombay University matriculation examination at the age of 16 in 1892. He then left for England in early 1893.
r: Some sources give 1891 for his matriculation because his birth year is itself disputed.

q: On which date did the Pakistan Army launch Operation Zarb-e-Azb in North Waziristan? (2)
f: Operation Zarb-e-Azb against militants in North Waziristan began on 15 June 2014. It followed the attack on Karachi airport and the failure of peace talks.
r: Operation Radd-ul-Fasaad was launched in February 2017 as its follow-up.

q: How many Muslims were martyred in the Battle of Badr? (83)
f: Fourteen Muslims were martyred at Badr, six from the Muhajirun and eight from the Ansar. About 70 of the Quraish were killed.
r: About 70 Sahaba were martyred later in the Battle of Uhud.

q: Bait-ul-Maqdas (Bait-ul-Muqaddas), the first qibla of the Muslims, is also known by which name? (4)
f: Bait-ul-Maqdas in Jerusalem is the site of Masjid-e-Aqsa (Al-Aqsa Mosque). The city itself is also called Al-Quds.
r: The qibla was changed from Bait-ul-Maqdas to the Kaaba in the second year of Hijra.

q: A barometer is used to measure what? (3)
f: A barometer measures the pressure of the atmosphere. A falling reading usually warns of bad weather.
r: Evangelista Torricelli invented the mercury barometer in 1643.

q: Basic Democracies of Ayub Khan were given constitutional status by which constitution? (3)
f: The 1962 Constitution made the 80,000 Basic Democrats the electoral college that elected the President and the assemblies.
r: The 1962 Constitution was abrogated by Yahya Khan in 1969.

q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built? (3)
f: East Germany began building the Berlin Wall on 13 August 1961 to stop people leaving for West Berlin.
r: The Wall fell on 9 November 1989.

q: How many surahs of the Quran begin with Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim? (2)
f: There are 114 surahs and only Surah At-Tawbah does not begin with Bismillah, so 113 do.
r: Bismillah occurs twice in Surah An-Naml, once at the start and once inside verse 30.

q: Why do we boil water before drinking it? (6)
f: Boiling kills harmful bacteria and other germs that cause waterborne diseases.
r: Boiling for about one to three minutes is generally advised for unsafe water.

q: In which of Quaid-e-Azam's Fourteen Points was the separation of Sindh from the Bombay Presidency demanded? (11)
f: Point 9 of the Quaid's Fourteen Points (1929) demanded that Sindh be separated from the Bombay Presidency.
r: Sindh was finally separated from Bombay and made a separate province in 1936.

q: Change the voice of the sentence: I bought a book. (4)
o: A book was bought by me.
A book is bought by me.
A book has been bought by me.
A book had been bought by me.
f: The sentence is in the simple past tense, so the passive uses was plus the past participle: A book was bought by me. The object becomes the subject.
r: In the passive voice the doer of the action is introduced with the word by.

q: By whom, and for how much money, was Kashmir bought under the Treaty of Amritsar in 1846? (2)
o: Maharaja Gulab Singh for 75 lakh Nanak Shahi rupees
Maharaja Ranjit Singh for 50 lakh rupees
Maharaja Hari Singh for 75 lakh rupees
Maharaja Gulab Singh for 25 lakh rupees
f: After the First Anglo-Sikh War the British sold the valley of Kashmir to Gulab Singh Dogra for 75 lakh Nanak Shahi rupees under the Treaty of Amritsar.
r: Gulab Singh's dynasty ruled Jammu and Kashmir until Hari Singh, the last Maharaja, in 1947.

q: Who was the Prime Minister of Britain at the time of the partition of India in 1947? (2)
f: Clement Attlee of the Labour Party was British Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951 and passed the Indian Independence Act 1947.
r: Lord Mountbatten was the last Viceroy of India, not the Prime Minister.

q: What does BRT stand for? (2)
f: BRT stands for Bus Rapid Transit, a bus system running on dedicated lanes. Peshawar's BRT is called Zu Peshawar.
r: Peshawar's BRT was built by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government and opened in August 2020.

q: Gautama Buddha, the founder of Buddhism, belonged to which country? (5)
f: Gautama Buddha was born at Lumbini, which lies in present-day Nepal. He later attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya in India.
r: In his time his Shakya clan lived near the present Nepal-India border.

q: What is the approximate gestation period of a buffalo? (6)
f: A buffalo carries its calf for about 10 months, which is roughly 305 to 320 days.
r: A cow's gestation is shorter, about 280 days.

q: In which city does the Green Line bus (BRT) service run? (2)
f: The Green Line is a Bus Rapid Transit service in Karachi that runs from Surjani Town toward Numaish.
r: The Orange Line in Lahore is a metro train, and Peshawar's BRT is called Zu Peshawar.

q: San Jose is the capital of which country? (3)
f: San Jose is the capital and largest city of Costa Rica in Central America.
r: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948.

q: What is the capital of Algeria? (3)
f: Algiers is the capital and largest city of Algeria.
r: Algeria is the largest country in Africa by area since the split of Sudan in 2011.

q: What is the capital of Ethiopia? (3)
f: Addis Ababa is the capital of Ethiopia.
r: Addis Ababa hosts the headquarters of the African Union.

q: What is the capital of Fiji? (3)
f: Suva is the capital and largest city of Fiji, on Viti Levu island.
r: Fiji is an island country in the South Pacific.

q: What is the capital of Finland? (3)
f: Helsinki is the capital and largest city of Finland.
r: Finland joined NATO in April 2023.

q: What is the capital of Kenya? (4)
f: Nairobi is the capital and largest city of Kenya.
r: Nairobi hosts a major United Nations office, UNEP headquarters.

q: What are the members of a Cartesian plane called? (2)
f: Every point of a Cartesian plane is written as an ordered pair (x, y) of coordinates.
r: The Cartesian plane is named after the French mathematician Rene Descartes.

q: Change into passive voice: Dogs always chase the cats. (2)
