r: Other antonyms of lenient: harsh, severe, stern, rigid. Other synonyms: merciful, forgiving, permissive.

q: The word "whose" in "The candidate whose file was missing returned" is a:
f: "Whose" joins the clause "whose file was missing" to the noun "candidate" and shows possession (the candidate's file), so it is a relative pronoun/determiner. B) It is not an interjection: it shows no sudden feeling like "Oh!". C) It is not a preposition: it does not show place or time. D) It is not an article: the only articles are a, an and the.
r: Other relative pronouns: who, whom, which, that. Example: "The boy who won the prize is my cousin."

q: ___ the weather was severe, the exercise continued.
f: B is right: severe weather and the exercise continuing are a contrast, so 'Although' fits. A) 'Because' is wrong: bad weather is not a reason to continue. C) 'Unless' is wrong: it means 'if not', which does not fit. D) 'So that' is wrong: it shows purpose, not contrast.
r: Other contrast words: though, even though, despite, in spite of. 'Despite' and 'in spite of' take a noun: 'Despite the severe weather, the exercise continued.'

q: "She ___ in Rawalpindi for five years." (She still lives there.)
f: She started living there in the past and still lives there, so present perfect 'has lived' with 'for five years' is correct. A) 'lived' is wrong: it means she does not live there now. C) 'had lived' is wrong: past perfect needs another past event. D) 'will live' is wrong: it is future.
r: Present perfect joins past and present: I have known him for ten years. 'For' gives the length of time; 'since' gives the starting point.

q: Indirect: Sara said, "I am busy now."
o: Sara said that she was busy then.
Sara said she is busy now yesterday.
Sara told that I was busy.
f: In indirect speech after "said" (past), the present "am" changes to "was", "I" changes to "she", and "now" changes to "then": "Sara said that she was busy then." B) keeps "is" and "now" and adds "yesterday", which makes no sense. C) "told" needs an object (told me), and "I" was not changed to "she". D) "asked if" is for questions, and the verb "was" is missing.
r: Other changes: here becomes there, this becomes that, today becomes that day, tomorrow becomes the next day. Example: He said, "I will come tomorrow" becomes He said that he would come the next day.

q: Passive of "Someone has stolen my bag" is:
f: Present perfect passive is 'has been + past participle'. 'Someone' is an unknown doer, so we drop 'by someone': My bag has been stolen. B) 'had stolen' is past perfect active and has no 'been'. C) 'is stealing' is active continuous, meaning the bag is doing the stealing. D) 'was stole' uses the wrong verb form; the past participle is 'stolen'.
r: Rule: drop the agent when it is someone, people, they, nobody known. Verb forms: steal, stole, stolen; break, broke, broken.

q: She saved money ___ she could buy a laptop.
f: A is right: 'so that' shows purpose: she saved money in order to buy a laptop. B) 'although' shows contrast, which does not fit. C) 'unless' means 'if not' and gives no sense. D) 'whereas' compares two different facts, not purpose.
r: Other purpose forms: in order to, so as to, to (She saved money to buy a laptop). 'So that' is often followed by can, could, will or would.

q: Read the passage: Discipline is often misunderstood as mere obedience to rules. In demanding institutions, however, it has a wider meaning. It includes the ability to control impulses, keep commitments, manage time, and continue working even when motivation is low. A disciplined person does not depend entirely on mood. He or she builds routines that make useful action easier and harmful delay less likely. Discipline therefore supports reliability: teammates can predict that a disciplined person will prepare, arrive on time, and complete assigned duties. Yet discipline without judgment can become mechanical. Mature discipline combines consistency with the ability to adapt when circumstances genuinely change.  QUESTION: According to the passage, a disciplined person does NOT depend entirely on:
f: B is right: the passage clearly says 'A disciplined person does not depend entirely on mood.' A) 'routine' is wrong: disciplined people build routines. C) 'commitment' is wrong: discipline includes keeping commitments. D) 'time management' is wrong: discipline includes managing time.
r: In NOT questions, three options are things the passage supports; pick the one it rejects. Mood is linked to motivation, which can be low.

q: Choose the synonym of LOWER.
f: Lower means to bring down in level or value; its synonym is Debase (lower in quality or worth). B) Elevate, C) Raise and D) Uplift are wrong: they mean to make higher, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: degrade, reduce, diminish. Antonyms: raise, elevate.

q: Choose: "___ army officer entered the hall."
f: "Army" begins with a vowel sound (a), so we use "an": "An army officer". A) "A" is used before consonant sounds only. C) "The always" is not a correct choice; the officer is not already known, and "always" makes no sense here. D) A singular countable noun like "officer" needs an article, so "no article" is wrong.
r: Other "an" words with vowel sounds: an apple, an hour (silent h), an honest man, an MBA (em sound).

q: Synonym of "assist" is:
f: 'Assist' means to help someone do something, so 'help' is the synonym. B) 'oppose' means to be against, the opposite idea. C) 'delay' means to make late. D) 'refuse' means to say no.
r: Other synonyms: aid, support, back. Noun: assistance; person: assistant.

q: The road was blocked; ___, we took another route.
f: A is right: taking another route was the result of the blocked road, so 'consequently' fits. B) 'although' is wrong: it shows contrast and cannot follow a semicolon like this. C) 'unless' is wrong: it means 'if not'. D) 'because of only' is wrong: 'because of' needs a noun after it and shows a reason, not a result.
r: Consequently = as a result = therefore = hence. A semicolon is used before such linking adverbs: 'It rained; therefore, the match was cancelled.'

q: Which phrase normally takes no article?
f: Single mountain peaks do not take an article, so 'Mount Everest' has none. A) 'the United States' and B) 'the Netherlands' are wrong: countries with plural or 'states/kingdom' names take 'the'. D) 'the Arabian Sea' is wrong: seas take 'the'.
r: No article: Mount Everest, K2, Lake Saiful Muluk (single lakes), Pakistan, Asia. With 'the': the United Kingdom, the Red Sea.

q: Active of "The room is cleaned every day" is:
o: Someone cleans the room every day.
f: "Is cleaned" is simple present passive and no doer is given, so in the active we use "someone" with simple present: "Someone cleans the room every day." B) "cleaned" is past and "tomorrow" is future, so the tense is mixed up, and "the" is missing. C) "The room cleans someone" reverses the meaning. D) "is clean" is wrong grammar for an action verb.
r: Same rule: "English is spoken all over the world" becomes "People speak English all over the world." When no doer is named, use someone, people or they.

q: "The decision depends ___ the weather."
f: The fixed phrase is 'depend on' (or 'depend upon'). A) 'depend in' is not used. C) 'depend at' is not used. D) 'depend for' is not correct here; we never say the decision depends for the weather.
r: Similar: rely on, count on, insist on. Noun form: dependent on (adjective), e.g. Children are dependent on their parents.

q: In "The candidates waited outside," "outside" functions as a:
f: 'Outside' tells WHERE they waited, so it modifies the verb 'waited' and is an adverb of place. B) article is wrong: the only articles are a, an, the. C) pronoun is wrong: it does not replace a noun. D) conjunction is wrong: it joins nothing.
r: Words like outside, inside, here, there, upstairs are adverbs when no noun follows. With a noun after them (outside the hall) they become prepositions.

q: In "Running improves stamina," "Running" is a:
f: 'Running' is the -ing form used as the subject of the sentence, so it is a gerund working as a noun. B) finite verb is wrong: the finite verb is 'improves'. C) adjective is wrong: it does not describe a noun here. D) preposition is wrong: it shows no relation.
r: Gerunds as nouns: Swimming is good exercise. I enjoy reading. Compare a participle used as adjective: a running tap.

q: He is not only punctual ___ also reliable.
f: A is right: the fixed pair is 'not only ... but also'. B) 'and only' does not form this pair. C) 'nor' pairs with 'neither' (neither ... nor). D) 'or' pairs with 'either' (either ... or).
r: Other correlative pairs: either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and, whether ... or. Example: Both Ali and Sara passed.

q: Read the passage: Discipline is often misunderstood as mere obedience to rules. In demanding institutions, however, it has a wider meaning. It includes the ability to control impulses, keep commitments, manage time, and continue working even when motivation is low. A disciplined person does not depend entirely on mood. He or she builds routines that make useful action easier and harmful delay less likely. Discipline therefore supports reliability: teammates can predict that a disciplined person will prepare, arrive on time, and complete assigned duties. Yet discipline without judgment can become mechanical. Mature discipline combines consistency with the ability to adapt when circumstances genuinely change.  QUESTION: The central idea of the passage is that discipline:
f: B is right: the passage says discipline is more than obedience; it includes self-control and reliability, and mature discipline combines consistency with judgment. A) is wrong: line 1 says it is 'misunderstood as mere obedience'. C) is wrong: a disciplined person 'does not depend entirely on mood' or motivation. D) is wrong: the last line says it adapts 'when circumstances genuinely change'.
r: A central idea question asks for the whole message, not one detail. 'Mere' means only; 'impulses' are sudden urges to act.

q: Which word is an interjection?
f: 'Alas!' expresses a sudden feeling of sorrow, so it is an interjection; the exclamation mark is a clue. B) 'although' is wrong: it is a conjunction. C) 'their' is wrong: it is a possessive determiner. D) 'smoothly' is wrong: it is an adverb.
r: Other interjections: Hurrah! (joy), Oh! (surprise), Ouch! (pain), Bravo! (praise), Alas! (sorrow).

q: "The sun ___ in the east."
f: The sun rising in the east is a universal truth, so simple present 'rises' is used. A) 'rose' is wrong: facts that are always true are not put in the past. C) 'is rising always' is wrong: continuous form is not used for permanent facts and the word order is odd. D) 'has risen daily' is wrong: present perfect is not used for general truths.
r: Other universal truths in simple present: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius. The earth moves round the sun.

q: "Assert" means:
f: A is right: assert means to state something confidently and strongly. B) 'hide' is wrong: that is conceal. C) 'forget' is wrong: that is to fail to remember. D) 'apologize' is wrong: that is to say sorry.
r: Synonyms of assert: declare, claim, affirm, maintain, insist. Antonym: deny. Related: assertive (confident), assertion (a firm statement).

q: Choose the synonym of EFFICIENCY.
f: Efficiency means power to do work well; Potency (power, effectiveness) is the closest synonym. B) Weakness, C) Waste and D) Laziness are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: effectiveness, competence, capability (see sa-63). Antonym: inefficiency.

q: Choose the synonym of EFFICIENCY.
f: Efficiency means ability to do work well; its synonym is Capability. B) Inability, C) Idleness and D) Weakness are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: competence, effectiveness, potency (see sa-45). Antonym: inefficiency.

q: Active of "The message was sent by Ali" is:
o: Ali sends the message now necessarily.
Ali was sent the message by it.
f: 'Was sent' is simple past passive, so the active is simple past with Ali as subject: Ali sent the message. B) 'sends' is present tense and adds extra words. C) reverses the meaning: the message sent Ali. D) is still passive and adds a new meaning.
r: Rule: the 'by' agent becomes the subject. The cake was baked by Mother becomes Mother baked the cake.

q: Which sentence is in present perfect tense?
f: 'I have finished the work' uses have + past participle, which is present perfect. A) is wrong: 'finish' is simple present. B) is wrong: 'finished' is simple past. D) is wrong: 'had finished' is past perfect.
r: Present perfect = has/have + past participle (has written, have gone). Past perfect = had + past participle (had written).

q: He was exhausted, ___ he continued working.
f: A is right: 'yet' shows contrast here: he was tired, but still he continued working. B) 'because' shows reason; tiredness is not the reason for continuing. C) 'unless' means 'if not' and gives no sense. D) 'therefore because' joins two connectors together, which is wrong.
r: Other contrast words: but, however, still, nevertheless. Example: It was raining, yet we went out.

q: Choose the antonym of RAMBLING.
f: Rambling means talking or writing in a long, wandering, unorganized way; its opposite is Methodical (orderly, organized). A) Disorganized, C) Lengthy and D) Wandering are wrong: they all describe rambling.
r: Other antonyms: concise, organized, systematic, to the point. Synonyms: digressive, long-winded.

q: Which pair consists entirely of prepositions?
f: 'In' and 'on' both show relation of place or time, so both are prepositions. B) 'and, but' are wrong: they are conjunctions. C) 'very, quite' are wrong: they are adverbs (intensifiers). D) 'he, they' are wrong: they are pronouns.
r: More prepositions: at, by, with, from, into, under, over, between, among. A preposition plus its noun makes a prepositional phrase: on the table.

q: Choose the synonym of DILIGENT.
f: Diligent means hard-working and careful; its synonym is Industrious. B) Idle, C) Lazy and D) Careless are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: hard-working, assiduous, sedulous. Do not confuse industrious (hard-working) with industrial (of industry).

q: Choose the synonym of TENDENCY.
f: Tendency means a natural leaning toward something; its synonym is Leaning. A) Dislike, C) Reluctance and D) Aversion are wrong: they mean not wanting, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: inclination, propensity, bent, trend. Antonym: disinclination (see sa-14).

q: The instructions were so clear ___ everyone understood them.
f: B is right: the pattern is 'so + adjective + that' to show a result. A) 'than' is wrong: it is used for comparison. C) 'as' is wrong: it is used in 'as ... as' comparisons. D) 'which' is wrong: it is a relative pronoun, not a result linker.
r: Similar pattern: 'such + noun + that': 'It was such a clear lecture that everyone understood.' Also 'too ... to': 'too difficult to understand'.

q: Which reporting verb is most suitable for a question?
f: Questions are reported with 'asked' (also inquired, wanted to know). B) 'ordered' is for commands. C) 'exclaimed' is for exclamations like Alas or Hurrah. D) 'promised' is for promises, and 'always' makes no sense here.
r: Matching verbs: statements use said/told, requests use requested, advice uses advised, wishes use prayed/wished.

q: "Endeavour" means:
f: A is right: an endeavour is a serious attempt or effort; as a verb it means to try hard. B) 'victory' is wrong: that is the result, not the attempt. C) 'order' is wrong: that is a command. D) 'rest' is wrong: that is the opposite of effort.
r: Synonyms of endeavour: attempt, effort, undertaking, venture, strive. Spelling: British 'endeavour', American 'endeavor'.

q: Passive of "She has completed the task" is:
o: The task has been completed by her.
The task was completed by her.
The task is completing by her.
f: Present perfect active (has completed) becomes 'has/have been + past participle': The task has been completed by her. A) misses 'been', so it sounds like the task did the completing. C) 'was completed' is simple past, wrong tense. D) 'is completing' is active continuous, not passive.
r: Same rule: They have sold the house becomes The house has been sold by them. Past perfect: had been + past participle.

q: "Reluctant" means:
f: B is right: reluctant means unwilling or hesitant to do something. A) 'eager' is wrong: it is the opposite (keen, willing). C) 'certain' is wrong: that means sure. D) 'powerful' is wrong: that means strong.
r: Synonyms of reluctant: unwilling, hesitant, loath, disinclined. Antonyms: eager, willing, keen. Noun: reluctance.

q: Choose the simple past sentence.
f: 'He trained yesterday' uses the past form 'trained' with the finished time 'yesterday', so it is simple past. A) is wrong: 'trains daily' is simple present. C) is wrong: 'has trained' is present perfect. D) is wrong: 'will train' is simple future.
r: Simple past time clues: yesterday, last week, ago, in 2010. Irregular past forms: go - went, see - saw, write - wrote.

q: Read the passage: Discipline is often misunderstood as mere obedience to rules. In demanding institutions, however, it has a wider meaning. It includes the ability to control impulses, keep commitments, manage time, and continue working even when motivation is low. A disciplined person does not depend entirely on mood. He or she builds routines that make useful action easier and harmful delay less likely. Discipline therefore supports reliability: teammates can predict that a disciplined person will prepare, arrive on time, and complete assigned duties. Yet discipline without judgment can become mechanical. Mature discipline combines consistency with the ability to adapt when circumstances genuinely change.  QUESTION: Which quality is linked directly with discipline in the passage?
f: A is right: the passage says 'Discipline therefore supports reliability.' B) 'Humor' is wrong: it is not mentioned. C) 'Popularity' is wrong: it is not mentioned. D) 'Creativity only' is wrong: it is not mentioned.
r: Reliable means dependable; others can predict you will prepare, arrive on time and complete duties. Synonyms: dependable, trustworthy, consistent.

q: Choose the antonym of COMPULSORY.
f: Compulsory means something you must do; its opposite is Optional (you may choose). B) Mandatory, C) Necessary and D) Obligatory are wrong: they all mean must-do, like compulsory.
r: Other antonyms: voluntary, elective, discretionary. Synonyms: required, binding.

q: Choose the synonym of SIN.
f: Sin means a wrong or evil act; Crime (a wrong act) is the closest synonym. B) Goodness, C) Virtue and D) Merit are wrong: they mean good qualities, the opposite of sin.
r: Other synonyms: wrongdoing, evil, offence, misdeed. Antonym: virtue (see sa-37).

q: Choose the synonym of COMPLEX.
f: Complex means having many parts and hard to understand; its synonym is Complicated. A) Easy, B) Plain and C) Simple are wrong: they are opposite in meaning to complex.
r: Other synonyms: intricate, involved, elaborate. Antonym: uncomplicated (see sa-1).

q: "Prudent" means:
f: B is right: prudent means wise and careful, showing good judgment about the future. A) 'careless' is wrong: it is the opposite (imprudent, reckless). C) 'angry' is wrong: that is irate or furious. D) 'rapid' is wrong: that means fast.
r: Synonyms of prudent: judicious, sensible, cautious, wise. Antonyms: rash, reckless, imprudent. Noun: prudence.

q: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: Strong teams should address problems:
f: B is right: the passage says strong teams 'address problems early'. A) 'only at the end' is wrong: the opposite of early. C) 'secretly and never openly' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'after standards are removed' is wrong: strong teams 'make standards clear'.
r: Address a problem means deal with it. Proverb with the same idea: 'A stitch in time saves nine.'

q: "He sat ___ me during the lecture."
f: 'Beside' means next to or by the side of: He sat beside me. A) 'besides' is wrong: it means 'in addition to' (Besides English, he knows Arabic). C) 'among' is wrong: it is for more than two people, and 'me' is one person. D) 'across' is wrong: it means on the other side or from side to side.
r: Commonly confused pairs: beside/besides, principal/principle, stationary/stationery, affect/effect, lose/loose.

q: Choose the synonym of AFFECTION.
f: Affection means a feeling of liking and care; its synonym is Love. A) Anger, B) Dislike and C) Hatred are wrong: they are negative feelings, opposite to affection.
r: Other synonyms: fondness, warmth, tenderness. Do not confuse affection (love) with affectation (showing off).

q: Choose the synonym of CURB.
f: Curb means to control or hold back; its synonym is Restrain. A) Release, B) Encourage and D) Free are wrong: they mean let go or push forward, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: check, control, limit, suppress. Example: curb your anger. Do not confuse with kerb (edge of a road).

q: "She speaks ___ Urdu fluently."
f: Names of languages take no article: 'speaks Urdu'. A) 'a', B) 'an' and C) 'the' are wrong: we do not put an article before a language name.
r: But we say 'the Urdu language' when the word 'language' follows. Similarly: She speaks English. But: the English (meaning the people).

q: Choose the synonym of BLAME.
f: Blame means to say someone is responsible for a wrong; its synonym is Censure (criticize strongly). A) Approve, B) Pardon and C) Praise are wrong: they are opposite in meaning to blame.
r: Other synonyms: condemn, criticize, reproach. Censure is also the antonym of praise (see sa-41).

q: Choose the synonym of NEGLECT.
f: Neglect means not giving proper care; its synonym is Negligence. A) Care, B) Attention and D) Diligence are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: carelessness, disregard. Do not confuse negligent (careless) with negligible (very small).

q: In "The wounded soldier recovered," "wounded" is functioning as a:
f: 'Wounded' describes the noun 'soldier' (which soldier?), so here this past participle works as an adjective. A) noun is wrong: the noun is 'soldier'. C) adverb is wrong: it does not modify the verb 'recovered'. D) conjunction is wrong: it joins nothing.
r: Participles often act as adjectives: a broken chair, a running train, a trained soldier, a falling leaf.

q: Which is grammatically correct?
f: 'Know' is a stative verb (a state of mind), so it is used in simple form: 'I know him'. A) is wrong: stative verbs are not normally used in continuous form. C) is wrong: 'have knowing' is not a correct verb form. D) is wrong: 'was know' mixes 'was' with a base verb.
r: Other stative verbs: believe, understand, like, love, want, own, belong, seem. Say 'I understand', not 'I am understanding'.

q: Choose the synonym of DECIDE.
f: Decide means to make up one's mind; its synonym is Determine. A) Hesitate, B) Waver and C) Doubt are wrong: they all mean being unable to decide.
r: Other synonyms: resolve, settle, conclude. Noun forms: decision, determination.

q: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: Skimming is mainly used to:
o: grasp the main argument or general idea
f: B is right: the passage says readers 'skim an article to grasp its main argument'. A) 'find a single word only' is wrong: that is scanning. C) 'translate every sentence' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'check spelling' is wrong: that is proofreading.
r: Grasp means understand. Skim for gist (general idea), scan for specific details, read intensively for full understanding.

q: "His father went to ___ school to meet the principal."
f: His father did not go to study; he went to the building to meet the principal, so 'the school' is used. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: a specific school (his son's) is meant. D) is wrong: no article is used only when we go for the main purpose (to study).
r: Compare: The patient went to hospital. His wife went to the hospital to see him. The prisoner is in prison. His lawyer went to the prison.

q: Passive of "The manager is reviewing the application" is:
o: The application is being reviewed by the manager.
The manager is being reviewed by the application.
f: A is right: present continuous passive is is/are + being + past participle: 'is being reviewed', and the object 'the application' becomes the subject. B) 'is reviewed yesterday' has the wrong tense and a past time word. C) 'has review' is not a passive and the verb form is wrong. D) it swaps the roles: the manager reviews the application, not the other way.
r: Past continuous passive: was/were being + past participle (The road was being repaired). Present perfect passive: has been reviewed.

q: Read the passage: Pressure narrows attention. This can be useful when a task demands immediate focus, but it can also make a person overlook information that would normally be considered. Good decision makers therefore use simple structures under stress: they identify the objective, separate facts from assumptions, compare the most realistic options, and consider the likely consequences of each. They also know when time is too limited for perfect information. In such cases, the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence. Afterward, reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment.  QUESTION: Good decision makers separate:
f: A is right: the passage says good decision makers 'separate facts from assumptions'. B) 'speed from strength' is wrong: not mentioned. C) 'leaders from teams' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'rules from laws only' is wrong: not mentioned.
r: A fact can be proved; an assumption is something we believe without proof. Other steps in the passage: identify the objective, compare options, consider consequences.

q: "Pakistan is in ___ Asia."
f: Names of continents take no article, so 'in Asia'. A) 'a', B) 'an' and C) 'the' are wrong: continent names like Asia, Africa, Europe are used without any article.
r: No article: most countries (Pakistan, China), cities (Lahore), continents (Asia). But: the Middle East, the USA, the UK.

q: Choose the synonym of MOB.
f: A mob is a large, often disorderly, group of people; its synonym is Crowd. B) Loner, C) Few and D) Individual are wrong: they mean one or a small number of people.
r: Other synonyms: throng, horde, multitude, rabble. Mob rule means rule by crowds, not by law.

q: The task was ___ difficult that many candidates ran out of time.
f: A is right: the pattern is 'so + adjective + that'; 'difficult' is an adjective. B) 'such a' needs a noun: 'such a difficult task that'. C) 'too much' does not go before an adjective with 'that'. D) 'very a' is not correct English.
r: Compare: so + adjective (so hot that), such + a + adjective + noun (such a hot day that). 'Too' is used with 'to': too hot to go out.

q: Which is a correct passive sentence?
f: A passive needs 'be' + past participle; 'is being repaired' is correct present continuous passive. A) 'is repairing' is active, meaning the road repairs something. C) has wrong word order. D) 'has repairing' is not a correct verb form; it should be 'has been repaired'.
r: Similar: The house is being painted. The bridge was being built. The room has been cleaned.

q: Choose: "___ United Kingdom".
f: C is right: names of countries with words like Kingdom, States or Republic take 'the': the United Kingdom. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are for one thing among many, not a unique country name. D) 'no article' is used with most single-word country names like Pakistan, not with this one.
r: Also: the United States, the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, the Netherlands, the Philippines. But: Pakistan, China, France (no 'the').

q: Which word is a pronoun in "They completed the obstacle course"?
f: 'They' is used in place of the names of people, so it is a pronoun. B) 'completed' is wrong: it is the verb (action). C) 'obstacle' is wrong: here it describes 'course' like an adjective (noun used as modifier). D) 'course' is wrong: it is a noun.
r: Subject pronouns: I, we, you, he, she, it, they. Object pronouns: me, us, you, him, her, it, them.

q: Choose the synonym of EQUAL.
f: Equal means the same in amount or level; Uniform (the same throughout) is the synonym. B) Different, C) Unequal and D) Uneven are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: same, identical, even. Antonym: uneven (see sa-36).

q: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: The passage says individual talent alone is:
o: not sufficient for effective team performance
f: B is right: the passage says a team 'is not effective merely because its members are individually talented'; coordination is also needed. A) 'sufficient' is wrong: it is the opposite of 'not merely'. C) 'harmful' is wrong: talent is not called bad. D) 'unrelated to performance' is wrong: talent helps, it is just not enough.
r: 'Not merely' means 'not only'. Sufficient means enough; insufficient means not enough.

q: "The bus ___ before we reached the stop."
f: The bus left before another past action (we reached), so the earlier action takes past perfect 'had left'. A) 'left' is wrong: it does not show which action happened first as clearly. B) 'has left' is wrong: present perfect does not match the past 'reached'. D) 'leaves' is wrong: it is present tense.
r: Rule: earlier past action = past perfect, later past action = simple past. Example: When I reached the hall, the lecture had started.

q: Choose the antonym of MERRY.
f: Merry means happy and cheerful; its opposite is Sad. B) Cheerful, C) Jolly and D) Lively are wrong: they all mean happy or full of fun, so they are synonyms.
r: Other antonyms of merry: gloomy, sorrowful, glum. Synonyms: joyful, gay, jovial.

q: "Impartial" means:
f: B is right: impartial means neutral and fair, not favouring any side. A) 'biased' is wrong: it is the opposite (partial, prejudiced). C) 'hostile' is wrong: that means unfriendly. D) 'uncertain' is wrong: that means not sure.
r: Synonyms of impartial: unbiased, neutral, objective, even-handed. Antonyms: biased, partial, prejudiced. Note: 'partial' can also mean incomplete.

q: The officer asked the men ___ remain calm.
f: B is right: the pattern is 'ask + person + to + verb': asked the men to remain calm. A) 'for' is wrong: 'ask for' is used before a thing, e.g. ask for help. C) 'that they to' is wrong: 'that' needs a full clause, and 'they to' is not one. D) 'of' is wrong: 'ask of' means request something from someone, not this pattern.
r: Same pattern with tell, order, advise, request, warn: 'He told me to wait.' 'She advised us to rest.'

q: You will not improve ___ you practise regularly.
f: B is right: 'unless' means 'if not': you will not improve if you do not practise. A) 'if' is wrong: it gives the opposite meaning (you will not improve if you practise). C) 'because' is wrong: practice is not a reason for not improving. D) 'and' is wrong: it does not make a conditional link.
r: Unless = if ... not. Example: 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus' = 'If you do not hurry...'. Do not add another 'not' after unless.

q: Read the passage: Pressure narrows attention. This can be useful when a task demands immediate focus, but it can also make a person overlook information that would normally be considered. Good decision makers therefore use simple structures under stress: they identify the objective, separate facts from assumptions, compare the most realistic options, and consider the likely consequences of each. They also know when time is too limited for perfect information. In such cases, the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence. Afterward, reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment.  QUESTION: When perfect information is impossible, the goal should be:
f: B is right: the passage says 'the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence'. A) 'total certainty' is wrong: the passage rejects it directly. C) 'no decision at all' is wrong: a decision is still needed. D) 'a random choice' is wrong: the decision must be based on evidence.
r: Pattern 'not X but Y' tells you the answer is Y. Evidence-based means supported by facts.

q: Choose the synonym of AGREEABLE.
f: Agreeable means willing to agree or go along; Conformable (fitting in, in agreement) is the synonym. A) Opposed, B) Hostile and D) Contrary are wrong: they mean against, the opposite.
r: Agreeable also means pleasant (an agreeable person). Other synonyms: compliant, willing, pleasing.

q: "Scrutinize" means:
f: A is right: scrutinize means to examine something very closely and carefully. B) 'avoid looking at' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'destroy' is wrong: that means to ruin. D) 'summarize quickly' is wrong: scrutinizing is slow and detailed.
r: Synonyms of scrutinize: examine, inspect, study, analyse, peruse. Antonyms: glance at, skim, overlook. Noun: scrutiny.

q: In passive voice, the main verb is normally in the:
f: Every passive uses a form of 'be' + the past participle (third form): written, done, built. A) the base form (write) is not used after 'be' in passive. C) the present participle (-ing) is used for active continuous, not passive. D) 'infinitive without be' is not a passive form at all.
r: Examples of past participles: go-gone, eat-eaten, take-taken, make-made. Passive: The food was eaten; The work is done.

q: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: Trust in a team does NOT mean:
f: B is right: the passage says 'trust does not mean the absence of accountability'. A) 'reduced unnecessary checking' is wrong: trust does reduce checking. C) 'confidence in basic duties' is wrong: trust does mean this. D) 'reliable performance' is wrong: trust is linked to members doing their duties.
r: Accountability means being responsible and answerable for your actions. In NOT questions, pick the option the passage rejects.

q: Synonym of "accurate" is:
f: 'Accurate' means exactly correct with no mistakes, so 'precise' is the synonym. B) 'careless' means without care, often causing mistakes. C) 'vague' means not clear. D) 'rough' here means not exact (a rough guess).
r: Other synonyms: exact, correct. Antonyms: inaccurate, wrong. Noun: accuracy.

q: "Credible" means:
f: A is right: credible means believable and worthy of trust. B) 'unrelated' is wrong: that is irrelevant. C) 'illegal' is wrong: that means against the law. D) 'weak' is wrong: that means feeble.
r: Synonyms of credible: believable, plausible, reliable, trustworthy. Antonym: incredible (hard to believe). Do not confuse with 'credulous' (too ready to believe others).

q: Synonym of "vital" is:
f: 'Vital' means very important or necessary, so 'essential' is the synonym. B) 'minor' means small and unimportant, the opposite. C) 'optional' means not required, also the opposite idea. D) 'weak' means lacking strength.
r: Other synonyms: crucial, necessary, indispensable. Vital also means related to life: vital signs (heartbeat, breathing).

q: The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."
o: The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun only.
The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
The teacher told that the earth has revolved.
f: A universal truth (a fact that is always true) does not change its tense: The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun. A) changes to 'revolved' and adds 'only'. C) 'told that' needs an object and 'has revolved' changes the meaning. D) 'earth revolving' is not a complete clause.
r: Other truths keep present tense: He said that water boils at 100 degrees. She said that honesty is the best policy.

q: "By the time you arrive, I ___ the report."
f: The report will be finished before a future moment (you arrive), so future perfect 'will have finished' is correct. A) 'finish' is wrong: it does not show completion before a point. B) 'finished' is wrong: it is past. D) 'am finishing yesterday' is wrong: present continuous cannot go with 'yesterday'.
r: After 'by the time', 'when', 'before' in a future sense we use simple present (you arrive), not 'will arrive'. Example: By the time he comes, we will have left.

q: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: If a key sentence is unclear, skilled readers should:
o: pause, reread, and connect it with context
f: B is right: the passage says they 'pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas'. A) 'guess and move on always' is wrong: they pause and reread. C) 'stop the test' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'ignore the paragraph entirely' is wrong: they work to understand it.
r: Monitoring comprehension means checking your own understanding while reading. Context (surrounding ideas) helps explain hard words and sentences.

q: Choose the antonym of HUMBLE.
f: Humble means modest, not proud; its opposite is Vain (proud of oneself). B) Modest, C) Simple and D) Meek are wrong: they are all close in meaning to humble.
r: Other antonyms of humble: proud, arrogant, haughty. Note that sa-73 uses Meek as a synonym of humble.

q: Which word is a coordinating conjunction?
f: C is right: 'but' is a coordinating conjunction; these are FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so. A) 'although', B) 'because' and D) 'while' are subordinating conjunctions; they start a dependent clause.
r: Coordinating conjunctions join equal parts: I was tired, but I worked. Subordinating ones make one clause depend on another: Although I was tired, I worked.

q: Choose the synonym of "abandon".
f: 'Abandon' means to leave something or someone completely and not come back, so 'leave' is the synonym. B) 'collect' means to gather, which is the opposite idea. C) 'repair' means to fix. D) 'praise' means to say good things about someone.
r: Other synonyms of abandon: desert, quit, give up, forsake. Antonyms: keep, retain, support.

q: I will call you ___ I arrive.
f: A is right: 'when' tells the time: I will call you at the time I arrive. B) 'unless' means 'if not', so the meaning becomes wrong. C) 'despite' must be followed by a noun or -ing, not a clause like 'I arrive'. D) 'during' is followed by a noun (during the trip), not a clause.
r: In time clauses about the future we use present tense: 'when I arrive', not 'when I will arrive'. Same with as soon as, before, after, until.

q: Choose the antonym of ACTIVITY.
f: Activity means being busy or moving and doing things; its opposite is Inactivity (doing nothing). A) Energy, C) Movement and D) Action are wrong: they are all close in meaning to activity, not opposite.
r: Other antonyms: idleness, inertia, rest. The prefix in- makes many opposites: active - inactive, efficient - inefficient.

q: Passive of "They make cars here" is:
f: Simple present active (make) becomes 'am/is/are + past participle': Cars are made here. 'They' is a general subject so it is dropped. B) 'were made yesterday' is past tense and adds new time. C) 'Cars make here' is active and has no 'be'. D) 'are making' is active continuous, meaning cars are making something.
r: Same rule: They grow cotton in Sindh becomes Cotton is grown in Sindh. Make, made, made; grow, grew, grown.

q: He succeeded ___ working consistently.
f: A is right: 'by + -ing' shows the method or means of doing something: succeeded by working consistently. B) 'with' is wrong: 'with' is used with a tool or noun, not with -ing for method. C) 'at' is wrong: 'at' is for skill (good at). D) 'to' is wrong: it does not show method.
r: Note: 'succeed in' + -ing shows what was achieved: 'He succeeded in passing the test.' 'By' shows how: 'He passed by studying daily.'

q: "Here" commonly changes to:
f: In reported speech, 'here' (this place) usually changes to 'there' (that place). B) 'then' is the change for 'now', a time word. C) 'that' is the change for 'this'. D) 'before' is the change for 'ago'.
r: Related: this becomes that, these becomes those, come may change to go when the place changes.

q: Which word is a determiner/article in "An officer entered the room"?
f: 'An' is the indefinite article placed before 'officer', which starts with a vowel sound. A) 'officer' is wrong: it is a noun. B) 'entered' is wrong: it is a verb. D) 'room' is wrong: it is a noun; 'the' before it is also an article, but it is not an option.
r: Articles are determiners: a/an (indefinite) and the (definite). Other determiners: this, that, some, every, my, his.

q: Choose the correct form: "He ___ to the academy every morning."
f: A daily habit (every morning) uses simple present, and the singular subject 'He' takes -es: 'goes'. A) 'go' is wrong: it is for I/we/you/they. C) 'went' is wrong: 'every morning' shows a present habit, not past. D) 'going' is wrong: an -ing form needs 'is' before it.
r: Third person singular adds -s/-es: she watches, he does, it fixes, he studies. Time clues for simple present: every day, always, usually.

q: Choose the synonym of COLLAPSE.
f: Collapse means to fall down suddenly or fail; its synonym is Break down. A) Build up, B) Recover and D) Rise are wrong: they mean getting stronger or higher, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: fall, cave in, crumble, fail. A building or a system can collapse.

q: Read the passage: Pressure narrows attention. This can be useful when a task demands immediate focus, but it can also make a person overlook information that would normally be considered. Good decision makers therefore use simple structures under stress: they identify the objective, separate facts from assumptions, compare the most realistic options, and consider the likely consequences of each. They also know when time is too limited for perfect information. In such cases, the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence. Afterward, reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment.  QUESTION: Why review the outcome afterward?
o: To make the original decision perfect
f: B is right: the passage says 'reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment'. A) 'To assign blame' is wrong: blame is not mentioned. C) 'To avoid evidence' is wrong: the passage values evidence. D) 'To make the original decision perfect' is wrong: a past decision cannot be changed.
r: Outcome means result. Reviewing past results to improve is like analysing errors in learning.

q: Choose the antonym of IMAGINARY.
f: Imaginary means existing only in the mind; its opposite is Real. B) Fanciful, C) Fictional and D) Unreal are wrong: they all mean not real, the same as imaginary.
r: Other antonyms: actual, factual, existing. Do not confuse imaginary (not real) with imaginative (creative).

q: Synonym of "rapid" is:
f: 'Rapid' means very fast, so 'swift' is the synonym. A) 'slow' is the opposite. C) 'late' means after the right time, not speed. D) 'weak' means lacking strength.
r: Other synonyms: quick, speedy, fast, hasty. Antonyms: slow, sluggish.

q: "He waited for ___ hour."
f: The h in 'hour' is silent, so it begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' is for consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: no specific hour is meant. D) is wrong: 'hour' is a singular countable noun and needs an article.
r: Silent h: an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour. Pronounced h: a hospital, a hero, a historic day.

q: Choose the synonym of WICKED.
f: Wicked means very bad; its synonym is Evil. A) Virtuous, C) Kind and D) Noble are wrong: they mean good, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: sinful, vicious, cruel. Antonym: virtuous (see sa-24).

q: "I ___ this book since Monday."
f: 'Since Monday' shows an action that started in the past and is still going on, so present perfect continuous 'have been reading' is correct. A) 'read' is wrong: simple tense does not show continuation till now. B) 'am reading' is wrong: present continuous cannot be used with 'since'. D) 'had read' is wrong: past perfect needs another past event.
r: Present perfect continuous: have/has been + verb-ing, with since (point of time) or for (period). Example: She has been waiting for two hours.

q: "___ Quran is the holy book of Islam."
f: Names of well-known holy books take 'the', so 'The Quran'. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are wrong: there is only one Quran, not any one of many. D) is wrong: the name is used with 'the' by convention.
r: Similarly: the Bible, the Torah, the Gita. Some famous newspapers too: the Times, the Guardian.

q: Complete: "He left early ___ avoid the traffic."
f: A is right: 'in order to' + base verb shows purpose: he left early to avoid traffic. B) 'because' needs a full clause (because he wanted to avoid). C) 'although' shows contrast and needs a clause. D) 'despite' shows contrast and needs a noun or -ing, not 'avoid'.
r: Other purpose forms: to, so as to, so that (He left early so that he could avoid the traffic). Negative: so as not to, in order not to.

q: Choose the antonym of EQUAL.
f: Equal means the same in size, amount or level; its opposite is Uneven (not the same). A) Same, B) Uniform and D) Identical are wrong: they all mean alike, like equal.
r: Other antonyms: unequal, different, unlike. In sa-76, Uniform is a synonym of equal.

q: He said, "May you succeed!"
o: He prayed that I might succeed.
He said that I may succeeded.
f: A wish or prayer (May you...) is reported with 'prayed/wished that' + 'might': He prayed that I might succeed. B) keeps 'may' and uses 'succeeded'; after a modal use the base form. C) 'asked me to succeeding' is wrong form and wrong verb. D) 'ordered success' changes the meaning; a prayer is not an order.
r: Same rule: She said, 'May God bless you' becomes She prayed that God might bless me. 'May' becomes 'might'.

q: Antonym of "frequent" is:
f: "Frequent" means happening often, so its antonym is "rare" (happening seldom). A) "common", B) "regular" and D) "repeated" all have meanings close to frequent, so they are synonyms, not opposites.
r: Other antonyms of frequent: infrequent, occasional, uncommon. Adverb pair: frequently versus rarely or seldom.

q: "Listen! Someone ___ at the door."
f: 'Listen!' shows the knocking is happening right now, so present continuous 'is knocking' is correct. A) 'knocks' is wrong: simple present is for habits. B) 'knocked' is wrong: it is past. D) 'has knocked' is wrong: it shows a completed action, not one in progress.
r: Clue words for present continuous: Look!, Listen!, now, at the moment. Example: Look! The children are playing.

q: "She is ___ best candidate in the group."
f: Superlative adjectives (best, tallest, most famous) take 'the', so 'the best candidate'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: a superlative points to one specific person, not any one. D) is wrong: a superlative normally needs 'the'.
r: Examples: the tallest boy, the most intelligent student, the highest peak. Also 'the' with ordinal numbers: the first, the second.

q: "Sustain" most nearly means:
f: A is right: 'sustain' means to keep something going or to maintain it. B) 'destroy' is the opposite. C) 'forget' is unrelated. D) 'interrupt' means to stop for a while, which is nearly the opposite.
r: Synonyms: maintain, uphold, support, continue. Related: 'sustainable development' means growth that can be kept going; 'sustain an injury' means to suffer an injury.

q: "He arrived ___ the airport on time."
f: We use 'arrive at' for a specific place or building like an airport, station or school. A) 'arrive in' is used for a city or country (arrive in Lahore). C) 'arrive on' is not used for places; 'on' is for days (arrive on Monday). D) 'arrive by' shows the means or a deadline (arrive by train, by 5 pm), not the place.
r: Remember: arrive at the station/office, arrive in Karachi/Pakistan. 'Reach' takes no preposition: He reached the airport.

q: "Adaptable" means:
f: A is right: 'adaptable' means able to adjust or change to fit new conditions. B) 'unable to change' is the opposite meaning. C) 'careless' means not paying attention, a different idea. D) 'slow only' has no link to the word.
r: Synonyms: flexible, versatile, adjustable. Antonyms: rigid, inflexible. Do not confuse adapt (adjust) with adopt (take as your own).

q: Choose the synonym of REASON.
f: As a verb, reason means to think and discuss logically, to argue a point; so Argue is the synonym. B) Ignore is wrong: it means to pay no attention. C) Accede is wrong: it means to agree to a demand. D) Obey is wrong: it means to follow orders.
r: Phrase: to reason with someone means to try to persuade them by argument. Other synonyms: deduce, infer, think.

q: Choose the antonym of MAJORITY.
f: Majority means the larger part or number; its opposite is Minority (the smaller part). A) Plurality, C) Bulk and D) Mass are wrong: they all refer to the larger part or a big amount.
r: Same pattern: major - minor, majority - minority. Majority means more than half.

q: Choose the antonym of ABILITY.
f: Ability means power or skill to do something; its opposite is Incapability (not being able). A) Capability, B) Skill and C) Talent are wrong: they all mean ability.
r: Other antonyms: inability, incapacity, incompetence. In sa-43, Capability is a synonym of ability.

q: In the same sentence, "omission" most nearly means:
f: A is right: an omission is something left out or forgotten. B) a reward is a prize, not related. C) an explanation is giving reasons. D) a prediction is a guess about the future.
r: Verb: omit (to leave out). Similar words: exclusion, oversight, gap. Opposite: inclusion, addition.

q: Which of the following is a conjunction?
f: 'Because' joins two clauses and gives a reason, so it is a (subordinating) conjunction. A) 'under' is wrong: it is a preposition of place. C) 'quickly' is wrong: it is an adverb of manner. D) 'brave' is wrong: it is an adjective.
r: Other subordinating conjunctions: since, as, although, though, unless, if, when, while. Example: He stayed home because he was ill.

q: "We crossed ___ Indus River."
f: Names of rivers take 'the', so it is 'the Indus River'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: a particular named river is not 'any one'. D) is wrong: river names are not used without 'the'.
r: Also with 'the': seas, oceans, canals and deserts - the Arabian Sea, the Pacific Ocean, the Suez Canal, the Thar Desert.

q: "He ___ for two hours before the rain stopped."
f: 'For two hours before the rain stopped' stresses how long an action continued before another past event, so past perfect continuous 'had been running' is correct. A) 'ran' is wrong: it does not show duration before another past event. C) 'has been running' is wrong: it links to the present, not the past. D) 'is running' is wrong: it is present.
r: Past perfect continuous: had been + verb-ing. Example: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.

q: Indirect: He said, "What a beautiful view!"
o: He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view.
He asked whether the view was beautiful.
He said what was a view?
f: An exclamation is reported with "exclaimed that" and changed into a statement: "He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view." The word "What" becomes "very". B) "asked whether" turns it into a question, which is wrong. C) "ordered" is for commands. D) "said what was a view?" keeps a question form and makes no sense.
r: Other exclamations: He said, "Hurrah! We won" becomes He exclaimed with joy that they had won. "Alas!" is reported with "exclaimed with sorrow".

q: "The train passed ___ the tunnel."
f: 'Through' is used for moving inside something from one end to the other, like a tunnel, pipe or forest. The train went in one end and came out the other. B) 'across' is for moving from one side of a flat surface to the other, like a road or river. C) 'over' means above, but a train goes inside a tunnel, not above it. D) 'beside' means next to, which is not movement inside.
r: Other examples: walk through the forest, look through the window, read through the book. Compare: walk across the road, fly over the city.

q: Passive of "They are building a bridge" is:
o: A bridge is being built by them.
A bridge was built by them.
A bridge has been built by them.
f: Present continuous active (are building) becomes 'is/are being + past participle' in passive: A bridge is being built by them. B) 'was built' is simple past, wrong tense. C) 'has been built' is present perfect, wrong tense. D) 'is built them' misses 'being' and the word 'by', and is the wrong tense.
r: Same rule: She is cooking food becomes Food is being cooked by her. Past continuous: was/were being + past participle.

q: "Concise" means:
f: A is right: concise means brief but complete, saying a lot in few words. B) 'very confusing' is wrong: that is muddled or obscure. C) 'lengthy' is wrong: it is the opposite (verbose, wordy). D) 'careless' is wrong: that is negligent, not about length.
r: Synonyms of concise: succinct, terse, brief, pithy, to the point. Antonyms: verbose, wordy, long-winded, prolix.

q: Passive of "You should follow the instructions" is:
f: With a modal verb, the passive is modal + be + past participle: "The instructions should be followed." B) "should followed" is missing "be". C) "are should follow" puts two verbs wrongly together; a modal never follows "are". D) "The instructions followed you" changes the meaning and is not passive.
r: Same rule with other modals: "You must finish the work" becomes "The work must be finished." "We can solve it" becomes "It can be solved."

q: Choose the synonym of RESCIND.
f: Rescind means to cancel a law, order or agreement; its synonym is Cancel. B) Enact, C) Approve and D) Confirm are wrong: they mean make or keep valid, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: revoke, repeal, annul, withdraw. Antonyms: enact, validate.

q: Neither Ali ___ Hamza was late.
f: C is right: 'neither' is always paired with 'nor': neither ... nor. A) 'and' is wrong: it pairs with 'both'. B) 'or' is wrong: it pairs with 'either'. D) 'but' is wrong: it is not a partner of 'neither'.
r: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were late.' Same for either ... or.

q: A writer says, "The plan is costly; nevertheless, it may be necessary." "Nevertheless" signals:
f: A is right: 'nevertheless' means 'in spite of that', so it shows contrast between 'costly' and 'necessary'. B) cause words are because or since. C) time words are then, later, after. D) addition words are also, moreover, furthermore.
r: Similar contrast words: however, nonetheless, still, even so, yet. Example: He was ill; nonetheless, he came to work.

q: Choose the antonym of "scarce".
f: 'Scarce' means not enough or hard to find, so the antonym is 'abundant' (more than enough). A) 'rare' is a synonym, not an antonym. B) 'limited' also means not much, a synonym. D) 'small' is about size and is close in meaning, not opposite.
r: Other antonyms: plentiful, ample. Noun: scarcity (shortage), abundance (plenty).

q: He is responsible ___ the equipment.
f: The fixed phrase is "responsible for" something or someone. A) "of" is wrong with responsible. B) "to" is used for the person you report to: "responsible to the manager", not for the equipment. D) "at" is not used with responsible.
r: Other adjectives with "for": famous for, ready for, eligible for, grateful for (something). Example: "Lahore is famous for its food."

q: "At 8 p.m. yesterday, we ___ for the test."
f: An action that was going on at a fixed past time (8 p.m. yesterday) uses past continuous 'were studying'. A) 'studied' is wrong: it shows a completed action, not one in progress at that moment. C) 'have studied' is wrong: present perfect cannot be used with 'yesterday'. D) 'study' is wrong: it is present tense.
r: Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing. Example: At 10 a.m. she was writing a letter. Also used for an interrupted action: I was reading when he came.

q: Synonym of "brave" is:
f: 'Brave' means not afraid of danger, so 'courageous' is the synonym. A) 'cowardly' is the opposite (antonym). C) 'weak' means lacking strength, not the same. D) 'silent' means quiet and has no link to bravery.
r: Other synonyms: bold, fearless, daring, valiant, gallant. Antonyms: cowardly, timid, fearful.

q: "Pakistan became independent ___ 1947."
f: Use 'in' for years: in 1947. B) 'on' is wrong: 'on' is for days and dates. C) 'at' is wrong: 'at' is for clock time. D) 'since' is wrong: it goes with perfect tenses (has been independent since 1947).
r: 'In' is used with months, years, seasons, centuries: in August, in 1947, in summer, in the 20th century. But 'on 14 August 1947' with a full date.

q: In reported questions, the word order is generally:
f: In reported questions we use statement order (subject + verb), not question order: He asked where she lived, not where did she live. A) question order is used only in direct speech. C) 'inverted twice' is not a grammar rule. D) 'verb only' is wrong; the clause needs a subject too.
r: Example: 'Is he coming?' becomes She asked if he was coming. 'Why are you sad?' becomes He asked why I was sad.

q: "The plane flew ___ the clouds."
f: 'Above' means at a higher level, so the plane flew above the clouds. B) 'between only' is wrong: 'between' needs two things and 'only' makes it ungrammatical. C) 'beside' is wrong: it means next to, at the side. D) 'since' is wrong: it is for time, not place.
r: Above vs over: above = higher than (the plane is above the clouds); over = covering or crossing (a bridge over the river). Opposite: below/under.

q: The team consists ___ ten members.
f: The fixed phrase is "consist of", meaning to be made up of. A) "consist in" is a different, formal phrase meaning "to have as the main part" and does not fit here. C) "on" and D) "at" are not used with consist.
r: Similar phrases: "be composed of" and "be made up of" mean the same: "Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen." Note: we never say "is consisted of".

q: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: Efficient readers vary their pace according to:
f: B is right: the passage says 'Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose.' A) 'page color' is wrong: not mentioned. C) 'handwriting' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'mood only' is wrong: not mentioned.
r: Pace means speed. Purpose decides the method: scan for facts, skim for the main idea, read slowly for dense reasoning.

q: Synonym of "robust" is:
f: "Robust" means strong and healthy, so its synonym is "strong". B) "fragile" means easily broken, which is the opposite. C) "silent" means quiet, not related. D) "rare" means not common, not related.
r: Other synonyms of robust: sturdy, tough, vigorous, hardy. Antonyms: weak, frail, delicate.

q: Choose the synonym of DETERMINATION.
f: Determination means firm decision to do something; its synonym is Resolution. A) Weakness, B) Hesitation and C) Doubt are wrong: they show lack of firmness, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: resolve, firmness, willpower. A New Year resolution is a firm decision to do something.

q: Choose the antonym of ATTRACT.
f: Attract means to pull towards; its opposite is Repel (push away). A) Charm, C) Allure and D) Draw are wrong: they all mean to attract or pull in.
r: In magnets, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Noun pair: attraction - repulsion (see sa-25).

q: Choose the antonym of WICKED.
f: Wicked means evil or very bad; its opposite is Virtuous (good, moral). A) Cruel, B) Evil and D) Sinful are wrong: they all mean bad, like wicked.
r: Other antonyms: righteous, noble, good. In sa-57, Evil is a synonym of wicked.

q: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: A conceptual misunderstanding may require:
f: B is right: the passage says a conceptual misunderstanding 'may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation'. A) 'more speed only' is wrong: speed is not mentioned as a fix. C) 'less attention' is wrong: careless mistakes need better (more) attention. D) 'memorizing the same answer' is wrong: it does not fix the concept.
r: Careless mistake = slip in attention; conceptual misunderstanding = wrong idea of the topic. Foundation means the basic level.

q: Passive of "They were watching the match" is:
o: The match was being watched by them.
f: Past continuous active (were watching) becomes 'was/were being + past participle': The match was being watched by them. A) 'was watched' is simple past, it loses 'being'. C) 'is being watched' is present continuous, wrong tense. D) 'has been watched' is present perfect, wrong tense.
r: Same rule: She was cooking food becomes Food was being cooked by her. Present continuous version: is/are being + past participle.

q: "Adverse" means:
f: B is right: adverse means harmful or unfavourable, e.g. adverse weather or adverse effects. A) 'favorable' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'equal' is wrong: that means the same. D) 'pleasant' is wrong: that is nice or agreeable.
r: Synonyms of adverse: unfavourable, harmful, hostile, detrimental. Do not confuse with 'averse' (unwilling): 'He is averse to risk.' Noun: adversity (hard times).

q: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The phrase "durable progress" most nearly means progress that is:
f: B is right: durable means long-lasting, so durable progress is progress that lasts. A) 'temporary' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'accidental' is wrong: the progress comes from a careful method. D) 'rapid only' is wrong: the passage says the method 'can feel slower'.
r: Synonyms of durable: lasting, enduring, permanent, long-lasting. Antonyms: temporary, fleeting, short-lived.

q: Antonym of "superior" is:
f: 'Superior' means higher in rank or better in quality, so the antonym is 'inferior' (lower or worse). A) 'higher' is a synonym. B) 'better' is a synonym. D) 'excellent' is close in meaning.
r: Both take 'to', not 'than': superior to, inferior to. Similar pair: senior to vs. junior to.

q: "This book belongs ___ me."
f: The verb 'belong' takes 'to': belongs to me. A) 'with', B) 'for' and D) 'at' are wrong: they do not go with 'belong' in this meaning of ownership.
r: Other verb + to: listen to, reply to, object to, refer to. 'Belong' is a stative verb, so not 'is belonging'.

q: Passive of "The committee may approve the plan" is:
o: The plan may be approved by the committee.
f: Modal passive is 'may + be + past participle': The plan may be approved by the committee. B) misses 'be'. C) 'is may approve' puts two helping verbs wrongly and is not passive. D) 'may been' is wrong; after a modal we use 'be', and 'been' needs 'have' (may have been).
r: Same rule: They can solve the problem becomes The problem can be solved. Past modal passive: may have been approved.

q: Passive of "The mechanic repaired the vehicle" is:
o: The vehicle was repaired by the mechanic.
f: The active is simple past, so the passive uses was/were + past participle: "The vehicle was repaired by the mechanic." A) "The vehicle repaired" has no "was", so it wrongly says the vehicle did the repairing. C) "is repair" uses the wrong tense and the base form instead of the past participle. D) "The mechanic was repaired" reverses the meaning.
r: Same rule: "She wrote a letter" becomes "A letter was written by her." Plural object uses were: "They built houses" becomes "Houses were built by them."

q: Choose the synonym of ABILITY.
f: Ability means power or skill to do something; its synonym is Capability. B) Weakness, C) Inability and D) Failure are wrong: they are opposite in meaning to ability.
r: Other synonyms: skill, talent, competence, capacity. Antonym: inability (see sa-29).

q: Choose the antonym of COMFORT.
f: Comfort means ease and relief from pain or worry; its opposite is Oppression (hard and cruel treatment, burden). A) Relief, B) Ease and C) Solace are wrong: they all mean comfort.
r: Other antonyms of comfort: distress, discomfort, misery. Solace means comfort in sadness.

q: Which is correct?
f: "Useful" starts with a "yu" sound, which is a consonant sound, so "a useful tool" is correct. A) "an useful" is wrong because "an" is only for vowel sounds. C) "the useful tool always" is not a correct phrase; "always" makes no sense here. D) "useful an tool" has the wrong word order: the article must come before the adjective.
r: Same rule: a university, a unit, a union. But "an umbrella" and "an uncle" take "an" because they start with an "uh" vowel sound.

q: Choose the synonym of DANGER.
f: Danger means the chance of harm; its synonym is Risk. A) Shelter, B) Safety and D) Security are wrong: they mean being protected, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: hazard, peril, threat. Antonym: safety (see sa-26).

q: A paragraph whose examples all support one claim has strong:
f: A is right: unity means every part of a paragraph supports one main idea or claim. B) ambiguity means unclear, with two possible meanings. C) contradiction means parts that go against each other. D) inversion means changing the normal word order.
r: Related writing ideas: coherence (ideas flow logically with good links) and topic sentence (the sentence that gives the main claim).

q: "She is interested ___ military history."
f: The fixed phrase is 'interested in' something. A) 'on', B) 'at' and D) 'for' are wrong: they do not go with 'interested'.
r: Similar collocations: keen on, fond of, good at, aware of, proud of. Example: He is fond of reading.

q: He apologized ___ being late.
f: The fixed phrase is "apologize for" something (the reason). B) "of" does not go with apologize. C) "with" does not go with apologize. D) "to" is used for the person: "apologize to someone", not for the reason.
r: Full pattern: "He apologized to the teacher for being late." Similar: thank someone for, blame someone for, forgive someone for.

q: If a passage states evidence first and a conclusion later, the reader should:
o: distinguish the supporting evidence from the conclusion
treat every sentence as identical in function
assume the first sentence is always the conclusion
f: A is right: a good reader separates the evidence (support) from the conclusion it leads to. B) wrong: sentences have different jobs, so they are not identical. C) wrong: connectors like 'therefore' and 'so' show where the conclusion starts. D) wrong: here the conclusion comes later, so the first sentence is not always the conclusion.
r: Conclusion signal words: therefore, thus, hence, so, consequently. Evidence signal words: because, since, for example, studies show.

q: Change to passive: "The officer signed the document."
o: The document was signed by the officer.
The document is signed by the officer yesterday.
The officer was signed by the document.
f: The active sentence is simple past, so the passive uses 'was/were + past participle': The document was signed by the officer. A) is wrong: without 'was' it means the document did the signing. C) is wrong: 'is signed' is present tense and does not match 'yesterday' or the past tense. D) is wrong: it swaps the doer and the object, so the meaning becomes nonsense.
r: Same rule: She wrote a poem becomes A poem was written by her. Plural object: He bought two books becomes Two books were bought by him.

q: Choose the synonym of LAUD.
f: Laud means to praise highly; its synonym is Praise. B) Blame, C) Condemn and D) Criticize are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: extol, acclaim, applaud. Laudable means worthy of praise.

q: Choose the antonym of WANT.
f: Here want means poverty or lack of things; its opposite is Prosperity (wealth, having plenty). A) Need, B) Shortage and D) Poverty are wrong: they all mean the same as want.
r: Other antonyms: plenty, wealth, abundance. Phrase: to live in want means to live in poverty.

q: The word "but" in "He was tired but continued" is a:
f: 'But' joins two parts of equal rank and shows contrast, so it is a coordinating conjunction. A) subordinating conjunction is wrong: those (although, because) start a dependent clause. C) preposition is wrong: here no noun object follows it. D) interjection is wrong: it shows no emotion.
r: Contrast words: but, yet (coordinating); although, though, whereas (subordinating); however (linking adverb). Example: He was tired, yet he continued.

q: "Deterrent" means something that:
f: A is right: a deterrent is something that discourages people or stops them from doing something, e.g. heavy fines are a deterrent to crime. B) a deterrent does not promise a reward; that is an incentive. C) it does not increase confusion. D) recording history is a record or archive, not a deterrent.
r: Verb: deter (to discourage). Opposite idea: incentive or motivation, which encourages an action. Example: Nuclear weapons are called a deterrent.

q: He is proud ___ his achievement.
f: A is right: the adjective 'proud' is followed by 'of'. B) 'from', C) 'with' and D) 'at' are wrong prepositions with 'proud'.
r: Other adjectives with 'of': afraid of, fond of, aware of, jealous of, capable of. Example: She is fond of reading.

q: Indirect questions use:
f: Indirect questions are not real questions, so they use statement word order: subject before verb, e.g. "He asked where I lived" (not "where did I live"). B) "question inversion" is used in direct questions only. C) An indirect question still has a verb. D) The tense depends on the reporting verb, not "only past perfect".
r: Same rule: Direct "Where is the bank?" becomes "Can you tell me where the bank is?" Yes/no questions use if or whether: "She asked if I was ready."

q: Choose the synonym of FERVOUR.
f: Fervour means strong, warm feeling or enthusiasm; its synonym is Zeal. A) Indifference, B) Coldness and D) Apathy are wrong: they mean lack of interest, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: passion, ardour, enthusiasm. Adjectives: fervent, zealous.

q: Antonym of "conceal" is:
f: 'Conceal' means to hide, so the antonym is 'reveal' (to show or make known). A) 'hide' is a synonym. B) 'cover' is close to hide. D) 'protect' means to keep safe, not the opposite.
r: Other antonyms: disclose, expose, show. Synonyms: hide, mask, cover up.

q: In "This is the man who helped us," "who" is a:
f: 'Who' refers back to 'the man' and starts the clause 'who helped us', so it is a relative pronoun. B) article is wrong: articles are only a, an, the. C) preposition is wrong: it shows no relation of place or time. D) interjection is wrong: it shows no feeling.
r: Relative pronouns: who (people), which (things), that (people or things), whom, whose. Example: The book which I bought is new.

q: Choose the antonym of SUPPORT.
f: Support means to help or hold up; its opposite is Abandon (leave and stop helping). A) Help, C) Assist and D) Uphold are wrong: they all mean the same as support.
r: Other antonyms of support: oppose, desert, undermine. Synonyms: back, aid, sustain.

q: Passive of "Who wrote this letter?" is:
o: By whom was this letter written?
This letter was wrote by whom?
f: A 'who' question in passive starts with 'By whom' + was + subject + past participle: By whom was this letter written? B) uses 'who' instead of 'whom' after 'by' and has no 'was'. C) 'Whom wrote' is wrong; 'whom' cannot be the subject. D) uses 'wrote' instead of the past participle 'written'.
r: Same rule: Who broke the glass? becomes By whom was the glass broken? Also: Who is calling you? becomes By whom are you being called?

q: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: The best title would be:
f: B is right: the whole passage explains what makes a team effective: coordination, trust, accountability and shared mission. A) is wrong: the passage says talent is not enough, not useless. C) is wrong: the passage supports accountability. D) is wrong: the passage is about cooperation, not individual competition.
r: A good title covers the main idea of the whole passage, not one detail, and avoids extreme words like 'useless' or 'only'.

q: "They ___ the task before the instructor arrived."
f: Two past actions: finishing the task came first, so it takes past perfect 'had completed'; the later one is simple past 'arrived'. A) 'complete' is wrong: it is present tense. C) 'have completed' is wrong: present perfect does not fit with a past time clause. D) 'were completing' is wrong: it shows the work was still going on, not finished before.
r: Past perfect pattern: had + past participle. Example: The train had left before we reached the station. 'Before' and 'after' are common clues.

q: "He went to ___ school to attend his class."
f: He went to school for its main purpose (to study), so no article is used: 'went to school'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: they would mean any one school building. C) 'the' is wrong: 'the' is used when we mean the building for another purpose.
r: Same rule: go to bed, go to hospital (as a patient), go to church, go to prison (as a prisoner), go to college.

q: Choose the antonym of OWN.
f: Here own means to admit or accept something; its opposite is Disclaim (refuse to accept or deny). A) Admit, B) Accept and D) Acknowledge are wrong: they all mean the same as own.
r: Other antonyms: deny, disown, reject. In sa-77, Acknowledge is a synonym of own.

q: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: Which distinction does the passage recommend?
f: B is right: the passage says learners 'distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding'. A) 'Easy and hard exams' is wrong: not mentioned. C) 'Teachers and students' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'Written and oral work' is wrong: not mentioned.
r: Distinguish means tell the difference between two things. Distinguish between A and B; distinguish A from B.

q: In "The very experienced instructor spoke calmly," "very" is a:
f: "Very" tells us how experienced the instructor is. It modifies the adjective "experienced", and a word that modifies an adjective is an adverb. A) It is not a noun: it does not name a person, place or thing. C) It is not an adjective: it does not describe the noun "instructor" directly. D) It is not a preposition: it does not join a noun to other words.
r: Other adverbs of degree: too, quite, extremely, so, rather. Example: "She is extremely clever" - "extremely" is an adverb modifying the adjective "clever".

q: Choose the antonym of MISLEAD.
