f: Mislead means to lead someone the wrong way or give a wrong idea; its opposite is Guide (show the right way). A) Confuse, B) Deceive and D) Misdirect are wrong: they all have the same meaning as mislead.
r: The prefix mis- means wrongly: misguide, misinform, misunderstand. Antonyms of mislead also include direct and inform correctly.

q: If you heat ice, it ___.
f: This is a general scientific fact, so we use the zero conditional: if + simple present, simple present. So "it melts". A) "melted" is past tense and does not fit a general truth. C) "will melted" is wrong: after "will" we use the base form (melt). D) "would melt always" is the second conditional form used for unreal situations, not facts.
r: More zero conditional examples: "If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils." "If it rains, the ground gets wet."

q: Choose the antonym of COMPLEX.
f: Complex means having many parts and hard to understand, so its opposite is Uncomplicated (simple, easy). A) Intricate, B) Complicated and D) Puzzling are wrong: they all mean the same as complex, so they are synonyms, not antonyms.
r: Other antonyms of complex: simple, easy, plain, straightforward. Synonyms: complicated, intricate, involved.

q: "Mitigate" means:
f: A is right: mitigate means to make something less severe or less harmful. B) 'make worse' is wrong: it is the opposite (aggravate, exacerbate). C) 'ignore entirely' is wrong: mitigate means acting to reduce harm. D) 'measure exactly' is wrong: that is to quantify.
r: Synonyms of mitigate: alleviate, lessen, ease, reduce, assuage. Antonyms: aggravate, worsen, intensify. Noun: mitigation.

q: Synonym of "diligent" is:
f: 'Diligent' means careful and hardworking, so 'hardworking' is the synonym. A) 'lazy' is the opposite. C) 'careless' is also opposite in meaning. D) 'reckless' means not caring about danger.
r: Other synonyms: industrious, sincere, painstaking. Antonyms: lazy, idle, negligent. Noun: diligence.

q: "The cat jumped ___ the wall."
f: 'Over' shows movement above something and to the other side, which is what a jump across a wall does. B) 'jump at' means to attack or grab something quickly, not to cross it. C) 'since' is about time (since Monday), not place. D) 'between' needs two things (between two walls), so it does not fit 'the wall'.
r: Similar: the horse jumped over the fence; the plane flew over the mountains. 'Above' shows position only, while 'over' can also show movement across.

q: Indirect: He said, "I must leave now." In ordinary backshift, "must" may become:
f: A is right: in reported speech 'must' (meaning need or duty) usually changes to 'had to': He said that he had to leave then. B) 'has to yesterday' is wrong tense and wrong time word. C) 'musted' does not exist; 'must' has no past form. D) 'would leaving' is wrong: 'would' needs a base verb.
r: Other backshifts: can to could, will to would, may to might, is to was. Also 'now' becomes 'then' and 'today' becomes 'that day'.

q: In "Courage inspires others," "Courage" is a:
f: "Courage" is a quality; we cannot see or touch it, so it is an abstract noun. A) It is not a proper noun: it is not the name of a particular person or place and is not written with a capital in normal use. C) It is not a verb: the verb in the sentence is "inspires". D) It is not an adverb: it is the subject of the sentence.
r: Other abstract nouns: honesty, love, freedom, wisdom, childhood. Many are made with endings like -ness, -dom, -hood, -ity (kindness, freedom, childhood, ability).

q: "The teacher distributed books ___ the students."
f: Use 'among' for more than two people: among the students. A) 'between' is wrong: it is mainly for two. C) 'through' is wrong: it means passing from one end to the other. D) 'onto' is wrong: it means movement to a surface.
r: Among the crowd, among friends, among the trees. 'Amongst' has the same meaning but is more formal.

q: Synonym of "terminate" is:
f: 'Terminate' means to bring to an end, so 'end' is the synonym. A) 'continue' is the opposite. C) 'begin' is the opposite. D) 'expand' means to grow bigger.
r: Other synonyms: finish, stop, conclude, cease. Antonyms: begin, start, commence. Noun: termination.

q: "Explicit" means:
f: A is right: 'explicit' means stated clearly and directly, with nothing left hidden. B) 'hidden' is the opposite. C) 'uncertain' means not sure, not clear. D) 'impossible' is unrelated.
r: Antonym: implicit (suggested but not said directly). Synonyms of explicit: clear, plain, direct, unambiguous.

q: Which sentence cannot normally be changed into passive voice?
f: Only verbs with an object (transitive verbs) can be made passive. 'Sleep' has no object, so 'The baby slept' cannot be changed. A) 'wrote a letter' has an object, so: A letter was written by him. B) 'repaired the road' has an object: The road was repaired. D) 'completed the form' has an object: The form was completed by her.
r: Other intransitive verbs with no passive: go, come, die, arrive, sleep, laugh (without 'at'). Example: He died cannot be passive.

q: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: Members can disagree about methods while still:
o: sharing commitment to the same mission
f: A is right: the last line says members may disagree about methods 'while still remaining committed to the same mission'. B) 'having no unity' is wrong: the passage says agreement and unity are different, and unity stays. C) 'rejecting all standards' is wrong: strong teams make standards clear. D) 'avoiding communication' is wrong: members must share information.
r: Unity means being together for one purpose; agreement means having the same opinion. You can disagree yet stay united.

q: "By the time the test started, I ___ my notes."
f: B is right: reviewing was finished before another past action (the test started), so we use the past perfect 'had reviewed'. A) 'reviewed already now' mixes past with 'now' and is wrong. C) 'have review' is wrong: present perfect needs 'reviewed', and the time is past. D) 'will reviewing' is wrong: future does not fit and 'will' needs a base verb.
r: 'By the time' + past simple usually goes with past perfect in the other clause. Example: By the time we reached the station, the train had left.

q: Choose the synonym of MOAT.
f: A moat is a deep ditch, usually filled with water, around a castle or fort; its synonym is Ditch. B) Hill and C) Mound are wrong: they are raised land, not dug land. D) Wall is wrong: a wall is built up, though a moat is often near one.
r: Other synonyms: trench, channel. Do not confuse moat with mote (a tiny particle of dust).

q: Antonym of "permanent" is:
f: 'Permanent' means lasting forever or for a long time, so the antonym is 'temporary' (for a short time only). A) 'lasting' is a synonym. B) 'fixed' is close to permanent. D) 'stable' is also close in meaning.
r: Other antonyms: transient, short-lived, momentary. Synonyms: everlasting, enduring, eternal.

q: Choose the synonym of APPROVAL.
f: Approval means agreeing or giving permission; its synonym is Consent. B) Rejection, C) Denial and D) Refusal are wrong: they mean saying no, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: assent, sanction, permission. Antonym: disapproval (see sa-19).

q: In "Honesty is essential for leadership," the word "Honesty" is a:
f: 'Honesty' is the name of a quality we cannot touch or see, so it is an abstract noun. A) verb is wrong: it shows no action. C) adjective is wrong: the adjective form is 'honest'. D) conjunction is wrong: it does not join words or clauses.
r: Other abstract nouns: bravery, loyalty, kindness, freedom, wisdom. Many are made with -ness, -ty, -dom, -ship (kind - kindness, friend - friendship).

q: Choose the synonym of WANT.
f: Want means lack or need of something; its synonym is Need. A) Wealth, B) Comfort and C) Excess are wrong: they mean having plenty, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: lack, poverty, shortage. Antonym: prosperity (see sa-32).

q: Which sentence contains an adverb of frequency?
f: 'Often' tells how many times the action happens, so it is an adverb of frequency. A) 'yesterday' is wrong: it is an adverb of time. C) 'here' is wrong: it is an adverb of place. D) 'softly' is wrong: it is an adverb of manner.
r: Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, seldom, rarely, never. They usually come before the main verb: He often exercises.

q: Choose the antonym of FREEDOM.
f: Freedom means being free; its opposite is Slavery (being owned or controlled). A) Liberty, C) Release and D) Independence are wrong: they all mean freedom.
r: Other antonyms of freedom: bondage, captivity, servitude. Synonyms: liberty, independence, autonomy.

q: In "The book is on the desk," "on" is a:
f: 'On' shows the position of the book in relation to the desk, so it is a preposition (it is followed by the noun 'the desk'). B) adverb is wrong: an adverb would have no noun object after it. C) interjection is wrong: it shows no feeling. D) pronoun is wrong: it does not replace a noun.
r: Prepositions of place: on, in, at, under, above, beside, between. A preposition is always followed by a noun or pronoun (its object).

q: "Divide the sweets ___ the two boys."
f: Use 'between' for two people or things: between the two boys. A) 'among' is wrong: it is for more than two. C) 'into' is wrong: it means movement inside or dividing into parts (divide into pieces). D) 'beside' is wrong: it means next to.
r: Between for two (between you and me); among for more than two (among the students). 'Divide into' is for parts: divide the cake into four pieces.

q: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The passage suggests that simply doing more questions can be inferior because it may:
o: fail to change the cause of error
f: B is right: the careful method is better 'because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure', so doing more questions may leave the cause unchanged. A) 'be illegal' is wrong: nothing in the passage. C) 'always lower confidence' is wrong: confidence is not mentioned. D) 'take no time' is wrong: the passage does not say this.
r: Inferior means worse or lower in quality; the opposite is superior. Both take 'to': inferior to, superior to.

q: "___ sun rises in the east."
f: There is only one sun, so it takes the definite article 'The'. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are wrong: indefinite articles mean 'any one', but there is only one sun. D) is wrong: unique objects need 'the'.
r: Other unique things with 'the': the moon, the earth, the sky, the world, the north pole.

q: Choose the synonym of LACK.
f: Lack means not having enough; its synonym is Deficiency. A) Abundance, C) Excess and D) Plenty are wrong: they mean a lot, the opposite of lack.
r: Other synonyms: shortage, want, dearth, scarcity. Antonym: abundance (see sa-3).

q: "He is ___ MBA graduate."
f: We go by sound: the letter M is said 'em', which starts with a vowel sound, so 'an MBA graduate'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' is for consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: no specific graduate is meant. D) is wrong: a singular countable noun needs an article.
r: Other letters starting with vowel sounds: an MA, an MP, an LLB, an X-ray, an SP. But: a BA, a PhD (pee), a UN officer (yoo).

q: "Obsolete" means:
f: B is right: obsolete means outdated and no longer in use. A) 'newly invented' is wrong: it is the opposite (novel, modern). C) 'expensive' is wrong: that is about price. D) 'dangerous' is wrong: that means risky.
r: Synonyms of obsolete: outdated, out of date, antiquated, defunct. Antonyms: modern, current, up-to-date. Example: typewriters are now obsolete.

q: Synonym of "commence" is:
f: 'Commence' is a formal word meaning to start, so 'begin' is the synonym. A) 'end' is the opposite. C) 'avoid' means to keep away from. D) 'reduce' means to make less.
r: Other synonyms: start, initiate, launch. Antonyms: end, conclude, terminate. Noun: commencement.

q: Which contains an auxiliary verb?
f: In "He has finished", "has" is a helping (auxiliary) verb used with the main verb "finished" to make the present perfect tense. A) "Birds fly" has only one main verb, "fly". C) "Tall trees grow" has only the main verb "grow". D) "Silence helps" has only the main verb "helps".
r: The main auxiliary verbs are be (is, am, are, was, were), have (has, have, had) and do (do, does, did). Modals like can, will, must and should are also auxiliaries: "She can swim."

q: "Plausible" means:
f: A is right: 'plausible' means something seems reasonable or believable. B) 'obviously impossible' is the opposite. C) 'very loud' is unrelated (that is 'loud' or 'deafening'). D) 'completely proven' is too strong; plausible only seems true, it is not proven.
r: Synonyms: believable, credible, likely. Antonyms: implausible, unlikely, far-fetched.

q: Antonym of "rigid" is:
f: 'Rigid' means stiff and not able to bend or change, so the antonym is 'flexible'. A) 'stiff' is a synonym. C) 'strict' is close to rigid (rigid rules). D) 'hard' is also close in meaning.
r: Other antonyms: elastic, pliable, adaptable. Synonyms: inflexible, firm, unbending.

q: She was absent ___ class yesterday.
f: The fixed phrase is "absent from" a place, class or duty. B) "of", C) "to" and D) "at" are not used with absent.
r: Opposite: "present at" or "present in": "She was present at the meeting." Similar "from" phrases: different from, free from, safe from.

q: Which option contains a possessive pronoun?
f: 'Mine' stands alone without a noun (The book is mine), so it is a possessive pronoun. A) 'my' is wrong: it must come before a noun (my book), so it is a possessive determiner/adjective. C) 'me' is wrong: it is an object pronoun. D) 'I' is wrong: it is a subject pronoun.
r: Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Their determiner pairs: my, your, his, her, our, their (used before nouns).

q: "Integrity" most nearly means:
f: B is right: integrity means honesty and strong moral principles, moral uprightness. A) 'dishonesty' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'physical speed' is wrong: not related to morals. D) 'anger' is wrong: that is rage or fury.
r: Synonyms of integrity: honesty, probity, rectitude, uprightness. Antonyms: dishonesty, corruption, deceit. Integrity can also mean wholeness, e.g. structural integrity.

q: Choose: "He studies at ___ university near his home."
f: We choose "a" or "an" by sound, not by letter. "University" starts with a "yu" sound, which is a consonant sound, so we use "a". B) "an" is only for vowel sounds. C) "the" is for a particular university already known; here it is just any one university near his home. D) A singular countable noun needs an article, so "no article" is wrong.
r: Similar words with "yu" or "w" sounds that take "a": a uniform, a European, a one-way street, a useful book.

q: Choose the antonym of DANGER.
f: Danger means the chance of harm; its opposite is Safety. A) Hazard, C) Risk and D) Peril are wrong: they all mean danger.
r: Other antonyms: security, protection, shelter. In sa-61, Risk is a synonym of danger.

q: "The cadets marched ___ the bridge."
f: 'Across' means from one side to the other side, so they marched across the bridge. B) 'between' is wrong: it needs two things (between the two posts). C) 'during' is wrong: it is used with time, not place. D) 'since' is wrong: it is used for a point of time.
r: Movement prepositions: across (side to side), through (inside, end to end), along (lengthwise), over (above), into (entering).

q: Choose the antonym of APPROVAL.
f: Approval means agreeing that something is good or allowed; its opposite is Disapproval. A) Sanction, B) Assent and C) Consent are wrong: they all mean approval or permission.
r: Other antonyms: rejection, refusal, disapprobation. In sa-64, Consent is a synonym of approval.

q: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: In timed tests, spending too long on one sentence can:
f: B is right: the passage says spending too long on one hard sentence 'can reduce the time available for easier questions'. A) is wrong: no automatic score increase is mentioned. C) is wrong: 'impossible forever' is extreme and not stated. D) is wrong: spending time does not guarantee understanding.
r: Exam tip: options with extreme words like 'always', 'forever', 'guarantee', 'all' are usually wrong in reading questions.

q: Ali said, "I will come tomorrow."
o: Ali said that he would come the next day.
Ali said that I will come tomorrow.
Ali says that he would come yesterday.
Ali told he would came next day.
f: 'Will' changes to 'would', 'I' to 'he', and 'tomorrow' to 'the next day': Ali said that he would come the next day. B) keeps 'I', 'will' and 'tomorrow'. C) uses 'says' and 'yesterday', which changes the meaning. D) 'told he' needs an object, and 'would came' is wrong; after 'would' use the base form 'come'.
r: Other time changes: today becomes that day, yesterday becomes the previous day, next week becomes the following week.

q: "We ___ dinner when the phone rang."
f: A longer action (having dinner) was going on when a short action (the phone rang) interrupted it, so past continuous 'were having' is right. A) 'had' is wrong: it suggests a complete action, not one in progress. C) 'have had' is wrong: present perfect does not fit a past story. D) 'will have' is wrong: it is future.
r: Pattern: past continuous + when + simple past. Example: I was sleeping when the alarm rang. 'While' often goes with the longer action.

q: "Ambiguous" means:
o: having more than one possible meaning
f: B is right: ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning, so it is not clear. A) 'clear' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'certain' is wrong: ambiguous suggests doubt, not certainty. D) 'short' is wrong: that is about length.
r: Synonyms of ambiguous: unclear, vague, equivocal, open to interpretation. Antonyms: clear, explicit, unambiguous. Noun: ambiguity.

q: Synonym of "evaluate" is:
f: "Evaluate" means to judge or measure the value or quality of something, so its synonym is "assess". B) "ignore" means to pay no attention, which is the opposite. C) "hide" means to keep out of sight. D) "destroy" means to ruin completely.
r: Other synonyms of evaluate: appraise, judge, rate, examine. Noun form: evaluation ("a performance evaluation").

q: Choose the synonym of LUCK.
f: Luck means what happens to a person by chance; Lot (fate, one's fortune in life) is the synonym. A) Effort, B) Plan and D) Labour are wrong: they mean things done on purpose by hard work, not chance.
r: Other synonyms: fortune, fate, destiny, chance. Phrase: to be content with one's lot.

q: She said, "Hurrah! We have won."
o: She exclaimed with joy that they had won.
She exclaimed with sorrow that they won.
She said hurrah we have won.
She ordered that they had won.
f: 'Hurrah' shows happiness, so we use 'exclaimed with joy', and 'we have won' becomes 'they had won': She exclaimed with joy that they had won. B) 'with sorrow' is the wrong feeling and 'won' should be 'had won'. C) keeps the exact words, which is direct, not indirect speech. D) 'ordered' is for commands, not exclamations.
r: Similar: He said, 'Bravo! Well done' becomes He applauded me, saying that I had done well. 'Alas' takes 'with sorrow'.

q: Choose the antonym of AGREE.
f: Agree means to have the same opinion; its opposite is Disagree. B) Consent, C) Approve and D) Accept are wrong: they all mean to agree.
r: Prefix dis- makes the opposite: agree - disagree, approve - disapprove, like - dislike.

q: "He has lived here ___ 2022."
f: Use 'since' with a point of time (2022) when the action continues to now. A) 'for' is wrong: 'for' is for a period (for three years). C) 'from only' is wrong: 'from' needs 'to/till' and does not suit present perfect. D) 'during' is wrong: it means within a period.
r: Since + point of time: since Monday, since morning, since 2010. For + period: for two days, for a week, for ten years.

q: Choose the antonym of PRAISE.
f: Praise means to say good things about someone; its opposite is Censure (strong criticism). B) Admire, C) Laud and D) Applaud are wrong: they all mean to praise or show approval.
r: Other antonyms: blame, condemn, criticize. In sa-86, Laud is a synonym of praise.

q: "Now" commonly changes to:
f: In reported speech, 'now' usually changes to 'then'. B) 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'; it is not a change for 'now'. C) 'there' is the change for 'here', a place word. D) 'before' is the change for 'ago', not for 'now'.
r: Other changes: ago becomes before, tonight becomes that night, here becomes there.

q: She is taller ___ her sister.
f: B is right: comparatives like 'taller' are followed by 'than'. A) 'then' is wrong: 'then' means 'after that' or 'at that time'. C) 'to' is wrong: 'to' is used only with Latin comparatives like senior to, superior to. D) 'from' is wrong: it is not used after comparatives in English.
r: Remember: than = comparison, then = time. Example: 'He is older than me. We ate, then we left.' Latin words: senior to, junior to, prefer to.

q: Indirect: She said to him, "Please sit down."
o: She requested him to sit down.
She asked that he sat down.
f: A polite request with "please" is reported with "requested" + object + to-infinitive, and "please" is dropped: "She requested him to sit down." B) "said him" is wrong ("said" takes "to": said to him) and it keeps "please". C) "asked that he sat down" is not the right pattern for a command. D) "ordered" is too strong for a polite request, and "sitting" should be "to sit".
r: For orders use ordered or commanded: He said, "Close the door" becomes He ordered me to close the door. For negative requests: requested him not to go.

q: "She ___ already ___ the form."
f: Present perfect is has/have + past participle, and 'already' comes between them: 'has already submitted'. B) 'had submit' is wrong: 'submit' is not a past participle. C) 'is submitted' is wrong: it is passive and does not fit 'She ... the form'. D) 'was submit' is wrong: 'was' with a base verb is not correct grammar.
r: Words like already, just, never, ever, yet go with present perfect: He has just arrived. Have you ever seen snow? I haven't finished yet.

q: Passive of "They have postponed the match" is:
f: The active is present perfect, so the passive is has/have been + past participle: "The match has been postponed." B) "had postpone" uses the wrong tense and the base form. C) "is postponing" is active present continuous. D) "was postponing" is active past continuous, not passive.
r: Same rule: "She has written the report" becomes "The report has been written by her." The doer "by them" is often dropped when it is general.

q: Choose the antonym of WILD.
f: Wild means not tamed, savage; its opposite is Civilized. A) Fierce, B) Untamed and C) Savage are wrong: they all mean the same as wild.
r: Other antonyms of wild: tame, gentle, domesticated. In sa-58, Savage is a synonym of wild.

q: Passive of "Open the door" is best expressed as:
o: Let open the door by you.
f: Imperative sentences (orders) become passive with 'Let + object + be + past participle': Let the door be opened. B) 'The door open' has no 'be' and no passive form. C) 'Door is opened you' is broken grammar with no 'by'. D) 'Let open the door by you' has wrong word order and no 'be'.
r: Same rule: Close the window becomes Let the window be closed. For requests you can also say: You are requested to close the window.

q: I ___ him yesterday at the library.
f: "Yesterday" is a finished past time, so we use the simple past "met". A) "meet" is present tense and does not fit a past time. B) "have met" is present perfect, which is not used with a definite past time like yesterday. D) "am meeting" is present continuous and shows now or the future, not yesterday.
r: Other definite past time words that need simple past: last week, ago, in 2010, last night. Example: "I saw him two days ago" (not "have seen").

q: Choose the synonym of WILD.
f: Wild means untamed and fierce; its synonym is Savage. B) Gentle, C) Civilized and D) Tame are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: untamed, fierce, ferocious. Antonym: civilized (see sa-23).

q: Take an umbrella ___ it rains.
f: A is right: 'in case' shows a precaution against something that may happen. B) 'although' is wrong: it shows contrast. C) 'because of' is wrong: it must be followed by a noun, not a clause. D) 'despite' is wrong: it shows contrast and also needs a noun.
r: In case is followed by present tense for the future: 'Take a map in case you get lost.' Compare 'if': 'Take an umbrella if it rains' means only take it when it rains.

q: Choose the antonym of JUSTICE.
f: Justice means fairness; its opposite is Inequity (unfairness). A) Honesty, C) Equity and D) Fairness are wrong: they are close in meaning to justice.
r: Do not confuse inequity (unfairness) with iniquity (wickedness). Other antonyms of justice: injustice, unfairness.

q: The word "resilient" most nearly means:
f: A is right: resilient means able to recover quickly from difficulty or shock. B) 'easily broken' is wrong: that is fragile, the opposite. C) 'unwilling to learn' is wrong: that is stubborn or obstinate. D) 'extremely noisy' is wrong: that is boisterous or deafening.
r: Synonyms of resilient: tough, hardy, buoyant, adaptable. Antonyms: fragile, vulnerable. Noun: resilience.

q: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The passage argues that errors become useful when learners:
f: B is right: the passage says effective learners 'identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction'. A) 'ignore them' is wrong: the passage says to analyse errors. C) 'repeat more questions immediately' is wrong: 'Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement.' D) 'avoid difficult topics' is wrong: it is not suggested.
r: Analyse means study carefully to find causes. Key idea: learning comes from understanding mistakes, not just practising more.

q: Synonym of "allocate" is:
f: A is right: 'allocate' means to give or assign something for a purpose, e.g. allocate funds for schools. B) 'remove' is almost the opposite. C) 'hide' is unrelated. D) 'oppose' means to be against.
r: Synonyms: assign, distribute, allot, earmark. Noun: allocation (budget allocation).

q: "She bought ___ umbrella and ___ raincoat."
f: 'Umbrella' starts with a vowel sound, so 'an umbrella'; 'raincoat' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a raincoat'. A) 'a / a' is wrong: 'a umbrella' is incorrect. C) 'the / an' is wrong: 'an raincoat' is incorrect and no specific umbrella is meant. D) 'an / an' is wrong for the same reason.
r: Quick check: an apple, an egg, an idea, an orange, an umbrella; a bag, a pen, a raincoat.

q: Choose the synonym of DISCLOSE.
f: Disclose means to make known a secret; its synonym is Reveal. B) Hide, C) Cover and D) Conceal are wrong: they mean keep secret, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: expose, divulge, uncover. Antonyms: conceal, hide.

q: "Coherent" means:
f: A is right: coherent means logical and well connected, easy to follow. B) 'broken physically' is wrong: coherent is about ideas, not physical damage. C) 'secret' is wrong: that is covert or confidential. D) 'angry' is wrong: that is irate.
r: Synonyms of coherent: logical, consistent, lucid, clear. Antonyms: incoherent, confused, disjointed. Related: cohesion, cohesive (sticking together).

q: She said, "Where are you going?"
o: She asked where was I going.
She asked where I was going.
She said where I am going.
She asked that where I went.
f: A wh-question keeps the wh-word but uses statement order (subject before verb): She asked where I was going. A) keeps question order 'was I'. C) uses 'said' and present 'am', with no tense change. D) 'asked that where' is wrong; do not add 'that', and 'went' changes the tense wrongly.
r: Same rule: He said, 'What is your name?' becomes He asked what my name was. Subject comes before the verb in reported questions.

q: Choose the synonym of TROTH.
f: Troth is an old word meaning faith, loyalty or a promise; so Faith is the synonym. A) Doubt, B) Betrayal and D) Treachery are wrong: they mean distrust or disloyalty, the opposite.
r: Betroth (to promise in marriage) comes from troth. Other synonyms: fidelity, loyalty, pledge.

q: Choose the antonym of ACCUSATION.
f: An accusation is a charge that someone did wrong; its opposite is Defence (speaking to protect oneself against the charge). B) Allegation, C) Charge and D) Blame are wrong: they all mean the same as accusation.
r: Accuse (verb) - defend (verb). Other related words: vindication, exoneration (being cleared of blame).

q: Active of "English is spoken in many countries" is:
o: People speak English in many countries.
People spoke English in many countries only.
Many countries are speaking English people.
f: 'Is spoken' is simple present passive with no agent, so the active uses a general subject in simple present: People speak English in many countries. B) 'spoke' is past tense and 'only' adds a new meaning. C) 'English speaks people' reverses the meaning. D) is wrong tense (continuous) and broken word order.
r: When no agent is given, use people, someone or they as subject. Example: Rice is grown in Punjab becomes People grow rice in Punjab.

q: She ___ for the interview when I called.
f: When one past action was in progress and another past action happened in the middle of it, the longer action takes the past continuous: "was preparing". A) "prepared" is simple past and shows a completed action, not one in progress. C) "has prepared" is present perfect and does not match the past clause "when I called". D) "will prepare" is future and does not fit a past event.
r: Same pattern: "I was reading when the lights went out." The longer action uses was/were + verb-ing; the short action that interrupts uses simple past.

q: In "He is extremely careful," "extremely" modifies:
f: 'Extremely' is an intensifier that tells how careful he is, so it modifies the adjective 'careful'. A) 'He' is wrong: adverbs do not modify pronouns. B) 'is' is wrong: it does not tell how he 'is'; it grades the quality. D) is wrong: it modifies one word, not the whole sentence.
r: Adverbs can modify adjectives (very tall), other adverbs (very quickly) and verbs (ran quickly). Other intensifiers: very, too, quite, highly, fairly.

q: Choose the antonym of SIN.
f: Sin means a wrong or evil act; its opposite is Virtue (goodness). A) Crime, C) Evil and D) Wrongdoing are wrong: they all mean the same as sin.
r: Other antonyms: goodness, merit, righteousness. In sa-48, Crime is a synonym of sin.

q: Choose the antonym of FLEXIBLE.
f: Flexible means easy to bend or change; its opposite is Rigid (stiff, cannot bend). A) Pliable, B) Supple and D) Elastic are wrong: they all mean bendable, so they are synonyms.
r: Other antonyms of flexible: stiff, inflexible, unbending. Synonyms: pliant, bendable.

q: Choose the antonym of QUESTIONABLE.
f: Questionable means doubtful, not certain; its opposite is Unquestionable (certain, beyond doubt). A) Doubtful, C) Dubious and D) Uncertain are wrong: they all mean the same as questionable.
r: Other antonyms: certain, sure, undeniable, indisputable. Prefix un- makes the opposite: questionable - unquestionable.

q: "Meticulous" means:
f: B is right: meticulous means very careful about every small detail. A) 'careless' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'lazy' is wrong: that is idle or indolent. D) 'fearful' is wrong: that means afraid.
r: Synonyms of meticulous: painstaking, scrupulous, thorough, punctilious. Antonyms: careless, sloppy, negligent.

q: "Contingency" most nearly means:
o: a possible future event or emergency
f: A is right: a contingency is a possible future event or emergency that you prepare for. B) 'a fixed certainty' is wrong: contingency means something that may or may not happen. C) 'a celebration' is wrong: that is a festivity. D) 'a routine fact only' is wrong: a contingency is unplanned, not routine.
r: Related: contingency plan (a backup plan), contingent on (depending on): 'Promotion is contingent on results.' Synonyms: eventuality, possibility, emergency.

q: He studied hard; ___, he passed the test.
f: B is right: passing the test is the result of studying hard, so 'therefore' fits. A) 'however' is wrong: it shows contrast. C) 'otherwise' is wrong: it means 'if not', giving a bad result. D) 'nevertheless' is wrong: it shows contrast, but here there is cause and effect.
r: Other result linkers: thus, hence, consequently, as a result, so. Contrast linkers: however, nevertheless, nonetheless, yet.

q: Which is an adverb of manner?
f: A is right: an adverb of manner tells HOW something is done, and 'carefully' tells how. B) 'yesterday' is an adverb of time (when). C) 'often' is an adverb of frequency (how often). D) 'outside' is an adverb of place (where).
r: Many adverbs of manner end in -ly: quickly, slowly, loudly. Some do not: fast, hard, well (She sings well).

q: Antonym of "ancient" is:
f: 'Ancient' means very old, from long ago, so the antonym is 'modern' (new, of present times). A) 'old' is a synonym. B) 'historic' is about the past, close in meaning. D) 'former' means earlier, also close in meaning, not opposite.
r: Other antonyms: new, recent, contemporary. Synonyms of ancient: antique, archaic, primeval.

q: "She wants to become ___ engineer."
f: 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' comes before consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: she wants to be any one engineer, not a specific one. D) is wrong: a singular countable noun of profession needs an article.
r: Professions take a/an: She is a doctor. He is an officer. He wants to be an architect.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is capable to do it.
He is capable of doing it.
He is capable for do it.
f: The correct pattern is "capable of" + verb-ing: "He is capable of doing it." A) "capable to do" is a common mistake; capable does not take a to-infinitive. C) "capable for do" uses the wrong preposition and the base verb. D) "He capable of do it" has no verb "is" and uses "do" instead of "doing".
r: Compare: "able to do" uses to-infinitive (He is able to do it), but "capable of doing" uses -ing. Similar: fond of reading, good at swimming.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: "Police" is a plural noun even without "s", so it takes the plural verb: "The police are investigating." A) "is" is singular, so it is wrong. C) "are investigates" is wrong grammar: after "are" we use the -ing form. D) "A police" is wrong: we cannot use "a" with police; we say "a police officer".
r: Other nouns that are always plural: cattle, people, clothes, scissors, trousers. Example: "The cattle are grazing."

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
I look forward for meet you.
I am look forward to meeting you.
f: In "look forward to", the word "to" is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so it is followed by verb-ing: "I look forward to meeting you." A) "to meet" wrongly treats "to" as an infinitive. C) "for meet" uses the wrong preposition and the base verb. D) "am look" is wrong grammar; it should be "I am looking forward".
r: Other phrases where "to" is a preposition and takes -ing: be used to, object to, be committed to, get used to. Example: "I am used to waking up early."

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She has less books than me.
She has fewer books than I do.
She has lesser books than I.
f: B is right: 'books' can be counted, so we use 'fewer', and 'than I do' is correct (I have books). A) 'less' is for uncountable nouns like water or sugar, not books. C) 'lesser' means lower in importance, not smaller in number. D) 'She have' is wrong: with 'she' we use 'has'.
r: Fewer time, less water: fewer is for things you count (fewer chairs), less is for things you cannot count (less money). Compare: 'He is taller than I am' or 'taller than me' in informal English.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He denied to take the money.
f: B is right: the verb 'deny' is followed by a gerund (verb + ing), so 'denied taking'. A) 'deny to take' is wrong: 'deny' does not take 'to' + verb. C) 'denied take' is wrong: a bare verb cannot follow 'deny'. D) 'denied that taking' is wrong: 'that' needs a full clause like 'that he took'.
r: Other verbs followed by -ing: admit, avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, suggest (He admitted stealing). You can also say 'He denied that he had taken the money.'

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She is one of the best player.
She is one of the best players.
She is one of best players is.
She one of the best player.
f: B is right: 'one of the' + superlative is followed by a plural noun: 'one of the best players'. A) 'player' is singular, which is wrong after 'one of the'. C) extra 'is' at the end and missing 'the' make it wrong. D) it has no verb ('is') and uses a singular noun.
r: Same rule: one of my friends, one of the tallest buildings. The verb stays singular: One of the boys is absent.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: 'candidates' is a plural countable noun, so we use 'are fewer'. A) 'less' is for uncountable nouns, not candidates. C) 'is' does not agree with plural 'candidates'. D) 'lesser' is wrong here and 'candidate' should be plural.
r: Fewer students, less homework. Also: 'a number of' (countable) versus 'an amount of' (uncountable).

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: With 'does not', the main verb stays in the base form: He does not know me. A) 'He do not' is wrong; 'he' takes 'does', not 'do'. B) 'does not knows' is wrong; after 'does' do not add -s. D) 'not does know' has wrong word order.
r: Same rule: She does not like tea. Did not also takes base form: He did not go (not 'did not went').

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: She is more senior than me always.
f: Latin comparatives like senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior take 'to', not 'than': She is senior to me. A) 'senior than' is a common mistake. C) 'senior from' is wrong. D) 'more senior than' is wrong here, and 'always' adds extra meaning.
r: Similar: He is junior to me. This is superior to that. Also: prefer to, prior to.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Neither of the boys are absent.
Neither of the boys is absent.
f: 'Neither of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: Neither of the boys is absent. A) 'are' is the plural verb, wrong here. C) 'Neither boys' is wrong; without 'of', neither takes a singular noun (neither boy). D) misses 'the' and uses plural 'are'.
r: Same rule with either, each, every one: Either of the answers is correct. Each of them is ready.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: Each of the players have a kit.
Each of the players has a kit.
Each of players have a kit.
f: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: Each of the players has a kit. A) 'have' is plural, wrong here. C) 'Each players' is wrong; without 'of', 'each' takes a singular noun, and 'a' is missing. D) misses 'the' and uses plural 'have'.
r: Same rule: Every student has a book. Each of the girls is talented.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He has been living here since five years.
He has been living here for five years.
He is living here for five years ago.
He lived here since five years.
f: Use 'for' with a period of time (five years) and 'since' with a point of time (2020): He has been living here for five years. A) 'since five years' is a common mistake. C) mixes present 'is living' with 'ago'. D) simple past 'lived' does not go with 'since'.
r: Examples: since Monday, since 2019, since morning; for two hours, for a week, for ten years.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I prefer tea over than coffee.
f: 'Prefer' takes 'to', not 'than': I prefer tea to coffee. A) 'prefer than' is a common mistake. C) 'over than' mixes two forms and is wrong. D) 'prefer from' is wrong.
r: With verbs: I prefer walking to driving. With 'would rather' we use 'than': I would rather walk than drive.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: One of my friend is here.
One of my friends is here.
One of my friends are here.
f: 'One of' is followed by a plural noun, and the verb is singular because the subject is 'one': One of my friends is here. A) 'friend' must be plural after 'one of'. C) 'are' is wrong; the subject 'one' is singular. D) misses 'of'.
r: Same rule: One of the students is absent. One of the best players has left.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: 'News' looks plural but is uncountable and takes a singular verb: The news is good. A) 'are' is plural, wrong. C) 'were' is plural, and 'always' adds extra meaning. D) 'are a good' is broken grammar.
r: Other singular words ending in s: mathematics, physics, economics. Example: Mathematics is my favourite subject.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: The fixed phrase is 'good at' a subject or skill: He is good at English. A) 'good in' is a common mistake in Pakistani English. C) 'good on' is wrong. D) 'good for' means helpful to (Milk is good for health), a different meaning.
r: Similar: bad at, clever at, expert at; but we say weak in a subject. Example: She is good at drawing.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object with no preposition: She discussed the issue. A) 'discussed about' is a common mistake. C) 'discussed on' is also wrong. D) 'was discussed' is passive and makes no sense with 'the issue' after it.
r: Other verbs with no preposition: reach (not reach at), enter (not enter into a room), describe (not describe about). But the noun takes 'about': a discussion about the issue.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: 'return' already means 'go back', so 'returned home' is enough. A) 'returned back' is wrong: 'back' repeats the meaning (redundant). C) 'back returned' is wrong word order and still redundant. D) 'returned to back home' is wrong: 'to back' makes no sense and is redundant.
r: Other redundant phrases to avoid: 'repeat again', 'revert back', 'reply back', 'return back'. Just say 'repeat', 'revert', 'reply', 'return'.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: I am used to wake early.
I am used to waking early.
I used to waking early now.
I am use to wake early.
f: B is right: 'be used to' means 'be in the habit of', and here 'to' is a preposition, so it takes the -ing form: 'am used to waking'. A) 'used to wake' is wrong: after 'be used to' we need -ing, not the base verb. C) 'I used to waking' is wrong: 'am' is missing, and 'used to' alone (past habit) takes a base verb. D) 'am use to wake' is wrong: it must be 'used', and the verb must be 'waking'.
r: Compare: 'I used to play cricket' (past habit, base verb) and 'I am used to playing cricket' (present habit, -ing). Same rule: 'look forward to meeting', 'get used to living'.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: If I was you, I would apply.
If I were you, I would apply.
If I am you, I would apply.
If I were you, I will applied.
f: B is right: for an imaginary or unreal condition we use 'were' for all subjects, then 'would + base verb': 'If I were you, I would apply.' A) 'If I was you' is wrong in formal and exam English: the subjunctive 'were' is needed. C) 'If I am you' is wrong: present tense cannot express an impossible situation. D) 'will applied' is wrong: second conditional needs 'would', and 'will' never takes a past form.
r: Second conditional pattern: If + past simple, would + base verb. Example: 'If he were rich, he would buy a car.' Same 'were' is used in 'I wish I were taller.'

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He is married with a doctor.
He is married to a doctor.
He is married by a doctor.
He married to with a doctor.
f: B is right: the correct preposition is 'married to' someone. A) 'married with' is wrong: 'with' is not used for the spouse (it can be used for children: married with two kids). C) 'married by' is wrong: 'by' shows the person who performs the ceremony, not the spouse. D) 'married to with' is wrong: two prepositions together, and 'is' is missing.
r: Similar fixed prepositions: 'engaged to', 'divorced from', 'similar to', 'different from'. But we say 'He married a doctor' with no preposition.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: after 'did not' (did/does/do) we use the base form of the verb: 'did not go'. A) 'did not went' is wrong: the past is already shown by 'did', so 'went' is double past. C) 'not did go' is wrong word order: 'not' comes after 'did'. D) 'did not gone' is wrong: 'gone' is a past participle, used with have/has/had.
r: Same rule for questions: 'Did she go?' not 'Did she went?'. Also 'He does not know' not 'He does not knows'.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: 'furniture' is an uncountable noun, so it takes a singular verb: 'The furniture is expensive.' A) 'furniture are' is wrong: uncountable nouns take singular verbs. C) 'furnitures' is wrong: 'furniture' has no plural form. D) 'Furniture are an expensive' is wrong: plural verb, and 'an' cannot come before an adjective with no noun.
r: Other uncountable nouns with no plural: information, advice, luggage, baggage, equipment, news, scenery. To count them say 'a piece of furniture' or 'two pieces of advice'.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: He asked that where I lived.
He asked where did I live.
He asked where I did lived.
f: B is right: in reported (indirect) questions we use statement word order and no 'that': 'He asked where I lived.' A) 'asked that where' is wrong: 'that' is not used before a question word. C) 'where did I live' is wrong: this is direct question order, not reported speech. D) 'where I did lived' is wrong: 'did' plus 'lived' is a double past and wrong order.
r: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether': He asked, 'Are you ready?' becomes He asked if I was ready. Another example: She asked what time it was (not what time was it).

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: 'reasons' is plural, so we use 'There are' and 'many'. A) 'There is' is wrong: 'is' is singular but 'reasons' is plural. C) 'There have' is wrong: we use 'there is/are' to show existence, not 'there have'. D) 'much reasons' is wrong: 'much' is for uncountable nouns; 'reasons' is countable.
r: many + countable (many books, many people); much + uncountable (much water, much time). Similarly: few/fewer with countable, little/less with uncountable.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: My brother is elder than me.
My brother is older than I am.
My brother is more elder than me.
f: B is right: to compare age with 'than' we use 'older': 'older than I am'. A) 'elder than' is wrong: 'elder' is not used with 'than'. C) 'more elder' is wrong: double comparative, and 'elder' still cannot take 'than'. D) 'older to me' is wrong: the verb 'is' is missing and comparatives take 'than', not 'to'.
r: 'Elder' and 'eldest' are used before a noun for family members: 'my elder brother', 'the eldest son'. Words like senior, junior, superior, inferior take 'to': 'He is senior to me.'

q: Choose the correct sentence.
f: B is right: 'hardly' is already negative, so we pair it with 'ever': 'hardly ever complains' (almost never). A) 'hardly never' is wrong: it is a double negative. C) 'ever hardly never' is wrong: wrong order and double negative. D) 'hardly complains never' is wrong: double negative and 'never' is in the wrong place.
r: Other negative words that should not take another negative: scarcely, barely, seldom, rarely. Say 'I can hardly hear', not 'I can't hardly hear'.

q: "Feasible" means:
f: A is right: feasible means possible and practical to do. B) 'illegal' is wrong: that means against the law. C) 'dangerous only' is wrong: that means risky, not about possibility. D) 'impossible' is wrong: it is the opposite.
r: Synonyms of feasible: viable, practicable, workable, achievable. Antonyms: impossible, impractical, unworkable. Noun: feasibility (a feasibility study).

q: Choose the antonym of TROUBLE.
f: Here trouble is a verb meaning to disturb or worry someone; its opposite is Appease (calm or soothe). A) Disturb, B) Annoy and C) Worry are wrong: they all mean the same as trouble.
r: Other antonyms of trouble: calm, soothe, comfort, pacify. Appease means to calm someone by giving what they want.

q: Choose the antonym of EXCESS.
f: Excess means more than needed; its opposite is Scarcity (too little). A) Surplus, B) Abundance and D) Plenty are wrong: they all mean a large amount, like excess.
r: Other antonyms of excess: shortage, deficiency, lack. Synonyms: surplus, glut.

q: Choose the correct article: "He is ___ honest man."
f: The h in 'honest' is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound (on-est) and takes 'an'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' is for consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: the man is not a specific one already known. D) is wrong: a singular countable noun needs an article.
r: Silent h words that take 'an': an hour, an heir, an honour, an honest man. But 'a house', 'a hotel' because h is pronounced.

q: Which sentence is correct?
f: Games and sports used in general take no article, so 'He plays cricket' is correct. A) is wrong: 'the cricket' is not used for the game. C) is wrong: 'a cricket' means an insect. D) is wrong: 'an' is used only before vowel sounds, and no article is needed anyway.
r: No article with games: play hockey, play football, play chess. But musical instruments take 'the': play the guitar, play the piano.

q: "___ Himalayas lie north of Pakistan."
f: Names of mountain ranges (plural) take 'the', so 'The Himalayas'. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are wrong: these are for one non-specific thing. D) is wrong: plural names of ranges are not used without 'the'.
r: Also: the Alps, the Andes, the Karakoram, the Hindu Kush. Plural country names also take 'the': the Netherlands, the Philippines.

q: Active form of "The gate was opened by the guard" is:
o: The guard was opening by the gate.
f: In the passive, 'was opened' is simple past, so the active is simple past: The guard opened the gate. B) 'opens' is present tense, wrong tense. C) swaps doer and object, so the gate opens the guard, which is nonsense. D) is wrong: 'was opening by' is not a correct active form and the meaning is reversed.
r: Rule: the 'by' person becomes the subject in active. The letter was written by Sara becomes Sara wrote the letter.

q: Mother said, "Do not waste time."
o: Mother advised me not to waste time.
Mother said me do not waste time.
Mother told that not waste time.
f: Advice or a negative imperative is reported with 'advised' + object + 'not to' + verb: Mother advised me not to waste time. B) 'said me' is wrong and keeps 'do not'. C) 'told that' needs an object and 'that' is wrong for imperatives. D) 'advised not wasting me' has wrong word order and form.
r: Same rule: Teacher said, 'Do not talk' becomes Teacher told us not to talk. Use 'not to', never 'to not' or 'do not'.

q: Synonym of "obstacle" is:
f: 'Obstacle' means something that blocks your way, so 'hindrance' is the synonym. B) 'benefit' means an advantage, the opposite idea. C) 'reward' is something given for good work. D) 'solution' is the answer to a problem.
r: Other synonyms: barrier, hurdle, impediment, obstruction. Antonyms: help, aid, advantage.

q: "When I was a child, I ___ cricket every evening."
f: 'When I was a child' places the habit in the finished past, so simple past 'played' is correct. A) 'play' is wrong: it is present. C) 'have played' is wrong: present perfect does not go with a finished past time. D) 'am playing' is wrong: it shows action happening now.
r: Past habits can also be shown with 'used to' or 'would': When I was a child, I used to play cricket every evening.

q: The correct collocation is:
f: B is right: the verb 'depend' is always followed by 'on'. A) 'depend of' is a common mistake. C) 'depend at' is wrong. D) 'depend to' is wrong.
r: Also 'rely on', 'insist on', 'count on'. The adjective too: dependent on (but independent of).

q: Choose the antonym of NERVOUS.
f: Nervous means worried and afraid; its opposite is Bold (brave, confident). A) Anxious and B) Restless are wrong: they mean worried or uneasy, like nervous. C) Timid is wrong: it means shy and fearful, also close to nervous.
r: Other antonyms of nervous: calm, confident, composed. In sa-74, Timorous is a synonym of nervous.

q: Complete: "___ he was inexperienced, he learned quickly."
f: A is right: 'although' joins two clauses that show contrast: he was inexperienced, but he learned quickly. B) 'because of' needs a noun (because of his inexperience) and shows reason, not contrast. C) 'unless' means 'if not' and gives no sense. D) 'therefore' shows result and cannot start the first clause like this.
r: Other contrast words: though, even though, despite (+ noun or -ing), in spite of. Example: Despite being inexperienced, he learned quickly.

q: Read the passage: Pressure narrows attention. This can be useful when a task demands immediate focus, but it can also make a person overlook information that would normally be considered. Good decision makers therefore use simple structures under stress: they identify the objective, separate facts from assumptions, compare the most realistic options, and consider the likely consequences of each. They also know when time is too limited for perfect information. In such cases, the goal is not certainty but a reasonable decision based on the best available evidence. Afterward, reviewing the outcome helps improve future judgment.  QUESTION: The tone of the passage is primarily:
f: A is right: the passage calmly explains steps for making decisions, so its tone is instructional and analytical. B) 'comic' is wrong: there is no humour. C) 'angry' is wrong: there is no strong emotion. D) 'nostalgic' is wrong: it does not long for the past.
r: Common tone words: objective, didactic (teaching), critical, optimistic, sarcastic, nostalgic (missing the past). Explanatory texts are usually instructional or analytical.

q: Choose the antonym of TENDENCY.
f: Tendency means a natural leaning to do something; its opposite is Disinclination (unwillingness). B) Habit, C) Leaning and D) Inclination are wrong: they are all close in meaning to tendency.
r: Other antonyms: aversion, reluctance, unwillingness. Inclination and disinclination are an opposite pair made with dis-.

q: "She ___ the report before the meeting began."
f: A is right: the reading finished before the meeting began (both in the past), so we use the past perfect 'had read'. B) 'has read tomorrow' mixes present perfect with a future word. C) 'reads yesterday' mixes present tense with a past word. D) 'is read' is a present passive and gives the wrong meaning.
r: Pattern: had + past participle for the earlier past action. Example: The guests had left before we arrived.

q: The cadet trained daily ___ he wanted to improve his endurance.
f: A is right: the second part gives the reason for training, so 'because' fits. B) 'although' is wrong: it shows contrast, but there is no contrast here. C) 'unless' is wrong: it means 'if not', which makes no sense. D) 'whereas' is wrong: it compares two opposite facts.
r: Other reason words: since, as, for. 'Because of' is followed by a noun: 'He trained because of his weak stamina.'

q: No sooner had the bell rung ___ the candidates entered.
f: B is right: 'No sooner' is always followed by 'than': No sooner had ... than. A) 'when' is wrong: 'when' goes with 'hardly' or 'scarcely'. C) 'then' is wrong: it is about time, not this fixed pair. D) 'that' is wrong: it is not part of this pattern.
r: Note the inversion: 'No sooner had the bell rung than...'. Similar pattern: 'Hardly had I arrived when...' and 'Scarcely had he left when...'.

q: "If he studies hard, he ___ the test."
f: This is a first conditional (a real, possible future): if + simple present, then will + base verb, so 'will pass'. A) 'passes' is wrong: the result clause needs 'will'. B) 'passed' is wrong: past does not fit a present-tense condition. D) 'would pass' is wrong: it is used in the second conditional (If he studied, he would pass).
r: Conditionals: 1st - If it rains, we will stay home. 2nd - If I were rich, I would travel. 3rd - If he had studied, he would have passed.

q: Choose the antonym of PUNCTUAL.
f: Punctual means arriving on time; its opposite is Unpunctual (late, not on time). A) Regular and D) Careful are wrong: they are not opposites of punctual. B) Prompt is wrong: it is a synonym (on time).
r: Other antonyms: late, tardy, delayed. Synonyms of punctual: prompt, timely.

q: Choose the antonym of ACHIEVEMENT.
f: Achievement means success in doing something; its opposite is Failure. A) Accomplishment, B) Attainment and C) Success are wrong: they all mean achievement.
r: Other antonyms: defeat, loss. In sa-60, Accomplishment is a synonym of achievement.

q: "This is ___ same book that I borrowed."
f: 'Same' is always used with 'the': 'the same book'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: 'a same' or 'an same' is incorrect English. D) is wrong: 'same' cannot be used without 'the' before it.
r: Other fixed uses of 'the': the same, the only, the whole, the first, the last. Example: He is the only person who came.

q: Choose the synonym of URGE.
f: Urge means to push or strongly encourage; its synonym is Incite (stir up, provoke to action). A) Discourage, B) Deter and C) Restrain are wrong: they mean to stop or hold back, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: prompt, spur, press, impel. Antonyms: deter, dissuade.

q: In "Ali and Hamza trained together," "and" is a:
f: 'And' joins two words of equal rank (Ali and Hamza), so it is a coordinating conjunction. B) preposition is wrong: it does not show relation of place or time. C) adjective is wrong: it describes nothing. D) adverb is wrong: it does not modify a verb.
r: The seven coordinating conjunctions can be remembered as FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.

q: Choose the antonym of ATTRACTION.
f: Attraction means a pull towards something; its opposite is Repulsion (pushing away, strong dislike). B) Appeal, C) Allure and D) Charm are wrong: they all mean attraction.
r: Verb pair: attract - repel (see sa-13). Other antonyms: aversion, revulsion.

q: Choose the antonym of EFFICIENCY.
f: Efficiency means doing work well without waste; its opposite is Inefficiency. A) Skill, B) Competence and C) Capability are wrong: they are close in meaning to efficiency.
r: Prefix in- makes the opposite: efficient - inefficient, capable - incapable, competent - incompetent.

q: Choose the synonym of NERVOUS.
f: Nervous means fearful and worried; its synonym is Timorous (full of fear). A) Bold, B) Calm and D) Brave are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: anxious, timid, uneasy. Antonym: bold (see sa-11).

q: If I had known, I ___ you.
f: B is right: third conditional: If + had + past participle, would have + past participle: 'would have told'. A) 'would tell' is wrong: that is second conditional, for present unreal. C) 'will tell' is wrong: that is first conditional, for real future. D) 'told' is wrong: the result part needs 'would have'.
r: Third conditional talks about the unreal past. Another example: 'If she had studied, she would have passed.' Inverted form: 'Had I known, I would have told you.'

q: "Vigilant" means:
f: A is right: vigilant means alert and watchful, especially for danger. B) 'sleepy' is wrong: it is almost the opposite (drowsy). C) 'careless' is wrong: it is the opposite of watchful. D) 'weak' is wrong: that means feeble.
r: Synonyms of vigilant: alert, watchful, attentive, wary, on guard. Antonyms: careless, negligent, inattentive. Noun: vigilance.

q: Choose the synonym of SCOLD.
f: Scold means to speak angrily to someone for doing wrong; its synonym is Reprove. A) Praise, B) Commend and D) Flatter are wrong: they all mean saying good things, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: rebuke, reprimand, chide, admonish. Antonyms: praise, commend.

q: Antonym of "hostile" is:
f: 'Hostile' means unfriendly and showing enmity, so the antonym is 'friendly'. A) 'unfriendly' is a synonym. B) 'aggressive' is close to hostile, not opposite. D) 'angry' is also close, not opposite.
r: Other antonyms: kind, amiable, cordial. Synonyms: inimical, antagonistic. Noun: hostility.

q: Choose the synonym of GODLY.
f: Godly means religious and devoted to God; its synonym is Pious. B) Wicked, C) Irreligious and D) Sinful are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
r: Other synonyms: devout, religious, saintly. Antonyms: ungodly, impious.

q: She said, "I can swim."
o: She said that she could swim.
She said that she can swam.
She told that I could swim.
f: 'Can' changes to 'could', and 'I' changes to 'she': She said that she could swim. B) keeps 'can' and uses 'swam'; after a modal use the base form 'swim'. C) 'told that' needs an object and keeps 'I'. D) 'could swam' is wrong; after 'could' use 'swim'.
r: Other modal changes: may becomes might, shall becomes should, will becomes would. Must often stays must or becomes had to.

q: "He was accused ___ theft."
f: The fixed phrase is 'accused of' a crime. A) 'for' is wrong: 'accused for' is a common mistake. C) 'with' is wrong: we say 'charged with' theft, not 'accused with'. D) 'by' is wrong: 'by' shows who accused him (accused by the police).
r: Similar: guilty of, suspected of, convicted of, charged with, blamed for.

q: "He ___ to Lahore last week."
f: 'Last week' is a finished past time, so simple past 'went' is correct. A) 'has gone' is wrong: present perfect cannot be used with a definite past time. B) 'goes' is wrong: it is present. D) 'had go' is wrong: the past participle is 'gone', and past perfect is not needed.
r: Irregular verb forms: go - went - gone, see - saw - seen, take - took - taken. Never say 'I have seen him yesterday'; say 'I saw him yesterday'.

q: Passive of "They had finished the work" is:
f: Past perfect active (had finished) becomes 'had been + past participle': The work had been finished. B) 'has been finished' is present perfect, wrong tense. C) 'was finishing' is past continuous active. D) 'had finished them' is active and reverses the meaning.
r: Same rule: She had cooked dinner becomes Dinner had been cooked by her. Tense must stay the same when changing voice.

q: Choose the antonym of PROGRESS.
f: Progress means moving forward; its opposite is Retrogress (go backward). A) Develop, C) Proceed and D) Advance are wrong: they all mean moving forward, like progress.
r: Other antonyms: regress, decline, deteriorate. In sa-71, Advance is a synonym of progress.

q: In "She worked despite the rain," "despite" is a:
f: "Despite" comes before the noun phrase "the rain" and shows its relation to the verb "worked", so it is a preposition. B) It is not a pronoun: it does not stand in place of a noun. C) It is not an interjection: it shows no sudden emotion. D) It is not an adverb of manner: it does not tell how she worked (like "quickly").
r: "Despite" and "in spite of" mean the same and are followed by a noun or verb-ing: "despite the rain" or "in spite of being tired". "Although" is a conjunction and needs a full clause: "although it was raining".

q: Indirect: "Do not touch the switch," he said to us.
o: He warned us not to touch the switch.
He said us do not touch.
He asked that we not touched.
f: A is right: a negative command in reported speech uses 'not to' + verb, and 'warned' suits a caution: He warned us not to touch the switch. B) 'said us' is wrong ('said to us') and the command form is not changed. C) 'asked that we not touched' is wrong grammar. D) 'told not touch us' has wrong word order and no 'to'.
r: Positive commands use 'to' + verb: 'Open the door' becomes He told me to open the door. Reporting verbs for commands: told, ordered, advised, requested.

q: Choose the synonym of EMPTY.
f: Empty means containing nothing; its synonym is Vacant. A) Crowded, B) Full and C) Occupied are wrong: they mean filled, the opposite.
r: Other synonyms: void, blank, unoccupied, hollow. Antonyms: full, occupied.

q: In "He can swim well," "can" is a:
f: 'Can' helps the main verb 'swim' and shows ability, so it is a modal auxiliary. A) main verb is wrong: the main verb is 'swim'. C) noun is wrong: here 'can' is not a tin container. D) preposition is wrong: it shows no relation of place or time.
r: Other modals: could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must. A modal is always followed by the base form: can swim, must go, should study.

q: In which Surah does Bismillah occur twice?
f: A) is right: In Surah An-Naml, Bismillah comes at the start and also inside, in the letter of Hazrat Sulaiman (AS) to Queen Bilqees. B) Al-Baqarah has Bismillah only at the start. C) Surah At-Tauba has no Bismillah at its start. D) Al-Fatiha has Bismillah only once.
r: Surah Tauba is the only Surah without Bismillah at its start.

q: In which year of Hijri did the Holy Prophet PBUH send letters to kings inviting them to Islam?
f: D) 7 AH is right. The letters to kings were sent at the end of 6 AH and in 7 AH. A) 2 AH is wrong: that is the year of Badr. B) 4 AH is wrong: that is the year of Rajih. C) 10 AH is wrong: that is the year of Hajjat-ul-Wida.
r: Najashi, the king of Habsha, was one of the kings who received a letter.

q: What was the religion of Najashi, the king of Habsha, before Islam?
f: D) Christianity is right. Najashi was a Christian king who gave shelter to the Muslims. A) Judaism is wrong: he was not a Jew. B) Fire worship (Majoosi) is wrong: that was the religion of Persia. C) Idol worship is wrong: that was the religion of the Quraish.
r: The Muslims migrated to Habsha in 615 and 616 AD.

q: Which companion of the Holy Prophet PBUH is mentioned by name in the Holy Quran?
f: D) is right: Hazrat Zaid (RA) is the only companion named in the Quran (Surah Al-Ahzab). A) Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) is referred to (companion in the cave) but not by name. B) Hazrat Umar (RA) is not named in the Quran. C) Hazrat Ali (RA) is not named in the Quran.
r: Hazrat Maryam is the only woman named in the Quran.

q: Hazrat Saleh (AS) was sent to which nation?
f: D) Samood is right. Hazrat Saleh (AS) was sent to the nation of Samood. A) Aad is wrong: Hazrat Hood (AS) was sent to Aad. B) Bani Israel is wrong: Hazrat Moosa (AS) was sent to Bani Israel. C) Ahl-e-Madyan is wrong: Hazrat Shoaib (AS) was sent to Madyan.
r: The miracle of Hazrat Saleh (AS) was a she-camel.

q: The first revelation came to the Holy Prophet PBUH in which cave?
f: A) is right: The first revelation came in Cave Hira on Jabal-e-Noor. B) There is no such revelation cave; Uhud is a mountain of a battle. C) Cave Saur is where the Holy Prophet PBUH hid during Hijrat. D) That is the cave of the sleepers in Surah Al-Kahf.
r: The first revelation was Surah Al-Alaq.

q: Hajj was made compulsory in which year?
f: B) is right: Hajj was made Farz in 9 AH. A) 2 AH is the year of fasting and Zakat. C) 10 AH is the year of Hajjat-ul-Wida (Last Hajj). D) 8 AH is the year of Conquest of Makkah.
r: The order of Hajj is in Surah Al-Imran (Ayat 97).

q: Ghazwa Hunain was fought in which year of Hijri?
f: D) 8 AH is right. Ghazwa Hunain was fought in 8 AH, soon after the Conquest of Makkah. A) 3 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Uhud. B) 5 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Khandaq. C) 9 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Tabuk.
r: The siege of Taif was also in 8 AH.

q: Which prophet is called Abu-al-Arab (father of the Arabs)?
f: B) Hazrat Ismail (AS) is right. Hazrat Ismail (AS) is called Abu-al-Arab. A) Hazrat Ishaq (AS) is wrong: he is the ancestor of Bani Israel. C) Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) is wrong: he is called Abu-al-Anbiya (father of prophets). D) Hazrat Hood (AS) is wrong: he was sent to Aad.
r: The mother of Hazrat Ismail (AS) was Hazrat Hajra.

q: Masjid Zarrar was demolished in which year of Hijri?
f: A) 9 AH is right. Masjid Zarrar, built by the hypocrites, was demolished in 9 AH after Tabuk. B) 3 AH is wrong: that is the year of Uhud. C) 6 AH is wrong: that is the year of Hudaibiya. D) 11 AH is wrong: the Holy Prophet PBUH passed away in this year.
r: Ghazwa Tabuk was also in 9 AH.

q: Hazrat Khalid bin Waleed (RA) accepted Islam in which year of Hijri?
f: C) 8 AH is right. Hazrat Khalid bin Waleed (RA) accepted Islam in 8 AH, before the Conquest of Makkah. A) 6 AH is wrong: that is the year of Sulah Hudaibiya. B) 5 AH is wrong: that is the year of Ghazwa Khandaq. D) 3 AH is wrong: in 3 AH he fought against the Muslims at Uhud.
r: Hazrat Amr bin Aas (RA) accepted Islam at about the same time.

q: The Nikah of Hazrat Fatima (RA) with Hazrat Ali (RA) took place in which year of Hijri?
f: D) 2 AH is right. The Nikah of Hazrat Fatima (RA) and Hazrat Ali (RA) took place in 2 AH. A) 5 AH is wrong: that is the year of the Nikah of Hazrat Zainab bint Jahsh (RA). B) 7 AH is wrong: that is the year of Khaibar. C) 9 AH is wrong: that is the year of Tabuk.
r: Ghazwa Badr was also in 2 AH.

q: How many Surahs are there in the Holy Quran?
f: A) is right: The Holy Quran has 114 Surahs. B) 120 is wrong; there are only 114 Surahs. C) 110 is not the count; Surah An-Nasr is the 110th Surah. D) 124 is wrong; there are only 114 Surahs.
r: The Quran has 30 Paras (Juz) and 6236 Ayats.

q: The second migration to Habsha (Abyssinia) took place in:
f: C) 616 AD is right. The second migration to Habsha took place in 616 AD. A) 615 AD is wrong: this is the year of the first migration. B) 610 AD is wrong: this is the year of the first revelation. D) 622 AD is wrong: this is the year of Hijrat to Madina.
r: Najashi, the Christian king of Habsha, gave them shelter.

q: Masjid Qiblatain (mosque of two Qiblas) is located in:
f: C) Madina is right. Masjid Qiblatain is in Madina, where the order to change the Qibla came. A) Makkah is wrong: it is not in Makkah. B) Taif is wrong: it is not in Taif. D) Bait-ul-Muqaddas is wrong: that was the first Qibla, not this mosque.
r: The Qibla was changed in 2 AH.

q: Ghazwa Tabuk was against which power?
f: B) The Romans (Byzantine Empire) is right. Ghazwa Tabuk (9 AH) was against the Romans (Byzantine Empire). A) The Egyptians is wrong: Egypt was not the enemy at Tabuk. C) The Persians is wrong: the Persians were not the enemy at Tabuk. D) The Quraish of Makkah is wrong: Makkah had already been conquered in 8 AH.
r: The Battle of Mutah (8 AH) was also against the Romans.

q: How many Ayats (verses) are there in the Holy Quran?
f: C) is right: The commonly accepted count of Ayats in the Holy Quran is 6236. A) 6348 is wrong; it is not the accepted count. B) 6666 is a popular but wrong number. D) 6000 is wrong; it is only a round figure.
r: Longest Surah Al-Baqarah has 286 Ayats; shortest Surah Al-Kausar has 3 Ayats.

q: When does the pilgrim stop reciting Talbiyah?
o: At the first Rami (10th Zil Hajj)
f: B) is right: Talbiyah stops when the pilgrim starts the first Rami of Jamrat-ul-Aqabah on 10th Zil Hajj. A) Talbiyah continues during Arafat. C) Talbiyah starts on entering Ihram; it does not stop then. D) Talbiyah has already stopped long before Tawaf-e-Wida.
r: Rami is done at Mina.

q: What was the real name of Iblees?
f: D) Azazeel is right. The real name of Iblees was Azazeel. A) Haroot is wrong: Haroot and Maroot were two angels in Babylon. B) Qabeel is wrong: he was a son of Adam (AS). C) Samri is wrong: he made the calf in the time of Moosa (AS).
r: Iblees was called the teacher of the angels before he disobeyed.

q: Ghazwa Uhud was fought in which year of Hijri?
f: A) 3 AH is right. Ghazwa Uhud was fought in 3 AH, in Shawwal. B) 2 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Badr. C) 5 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Khandaq. D) 7 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Khaibar.
r: Uhud came one year after Badr (2 AH).

q: Which of the following Surahs is NOT named after a Prophet?
f: A) is right: Hazrat Maryam was a pious lady, not a Prophet, so Surah Maryam is not named after a Prophet. B) Surah Younis is named after Hazrat Younis (AS), a Prophet. C) Surah Hood is named after Hazrat Hood (AS), a Prophet. D) Surah Ibrahim is named after Hazrat Ibrahim (AS), a Prophet.
r: The 6 Surahs named after Prophets: Yousaf, Hood, Younis, Ibrahim, Nooh, Muhammad.

q: The tragedy of Karbala took place in which year of Hijri?
f: C) 61 AH is right. The tragedy of Karbala took place in 61 AH. A) 11 AH is wrong: that is the year the Holy Prophet PBUH passed away. B) 40 AH is wrong: that is the year Hazrat Ali (RA) was martyred. D) 35 AH is wrong: that is the year Hazrat Usman (RA) was martyred.
r: Karbala happened on 10th Muharram (Ashura).

q: The event of Mubahila with the Christians of Najran took place in which year of Hijri?
f: D) 10 AH is right. The Mubahila with the Christians of Najran is placed in 10 AH. A) 3 AH is wrong: that is the year of Uhud. B) 5 AH is wrong: that is the year of Khandaq. C) 7 AH is wrong: that is the year of Khaibar.
r: Hajjat-ul-Wida was also in 10 AH.

q: Which angel is in charge of rain and sustenance (Rizq)?
f: B) is right: Hazrat Mikail (AS) is in charge of rain and sustenance. A) Izrail (AS) takes the souls. C) Israfeel (AS) blows the trumpet. D) Jibrail (AS) brought revelation.
r: Izrail (AS) is the angel of death.

q: In which year of Hijri was Ghazwa Waddan (Abwa), the first Ghazwa, fought?
f: C) 2 AH is right. Ghazwa Waddan (Abwa) was fought in Safar 2 AH. A) 3 AH is wrong: that is the year of Ghazwa Uhud. B) 4 AH is wrong: that is the year of the Rajih incident. D) 5 AH is wrong: that is the year of Ghazwa Khandaq.
r: Ghazwa Badr was also in 2 AH, in Ramadan.

q: The siege of Taif took place in which year of Hijri?
f: C) 8 AH is right. The siege of Taif came right after Ghazwa Hunain in 8 AH. A) 2 AH is wrong: that is Ghazwa Badr. B) 4 AH is wrong: that is the Rajih incident. D) 6 AH is wrong: that is Sulah Hudaibiya.
r: Fath Makkah and Hunain were in the same year, 8 AH.

q: On which date was Ghazwa Badr fought?
f: B) 17th Ramadan is right. Ghazwa Badr was fought on 17th Ramadan, 2 AH. A) 7th Shawwal is wrong: this is the date of Ghazwa Uhud (3 AH). C) 10th Muharram is wrong: this is the day of Ashura and Karbala. D) 9th Zil Hajj is wrong: this is the day of Arafat in Hajj.
r: Fasting in Ramadan was made Farz in the same year, 2 AH.

q: Ghazwa Khandaq is also known as:
f: B) Ghazwa Ahzab is right. Ghazwa Khandaq is also called Ghazwa Ahzab (the Battle of the Confederates). A) Ghazwa Hunain is wrong: Hunain was a separate battle in 8 AH. C) Ghazwa Tabuk is wrong: Tabuk was a separate expedition in 9 AH. D) Ghazwa Mutah is wrong: Mutah was a separate battle in 8 AH.
r: Khandaq means trench; a trench was dug around Madina.

q: Which was the first revelation (Wahi) of the Holy Quran?
f: B) is right: The first revelation was the first five Ayats of Surah Al-Alaq (Iqra). A) Al-Fatiha is the first Surah in order of the Mushaf, not the first revealed. C) Al-Baqarah is a Madani Surah revealed much later. D) Al-Muddassir came after the gap in revelation, not first.
r: It was revealed in Cave Hira on Jabal-e-Noor near Makkah.

q: Which event is called Fath-e-Mubeen (a clear victory) in the Quran?
f: B) Sulah Hudaibiya is right. Sulah Hudaibiya (6 AH) is called Fath-e-Mubeen in Surah Al-Fath. A) Ghazwa Badr is wrong: Badr is called Yaum-ul-Furqan. C) Ghazwa Khaibar is wrong: Khaibar is not given this title. D) Ghazwa Hunain is wrong: Hunain is not given this title.
r: Bait-e-Rizwan was also taken at Hudaibiya in 6 AH.

q: Fasting in Ramadan was made Farz in which year of Hijri?
f: D) 2 AH is right. Fasting in Ramadan became Farz in 2 AH. A) 1 AH is wrong: that is the year of the first Azan. B) 3 AH is wrong: that is the year of Uhud. C) 5 AH is wrong: that is the year of Khandaq.
r: Zakat was also made Farz and the first Eid-ul-Fitr was celebrated in 2 AH.

q: King Namrood was killed by:
f: C) A mosquito is right. A mosquito entered the nose of Namrood and caused his death. A) Drowning in the sea is wrong: that was the end of Firaun. B) Birds with stones is wrong: that was the end of Abraha's army. D) A windstorm is wrong: that was the end of the nation of Aad.
r: Namrood had thrown Hazrat Ibrahim (AS) into the fire.

q: Hajjat-ul-Wida (the Farewell Hajj) was performed in which year of Hijri?
f: C) 10 AH is right. The Holy Prophet PBUH performed Hajjat-ul-Wida in 10 AH. A) 8 AH is wrong: that is the Conquest of Makkah. B) 9 AH is wrong: in 9 AH Hazrat Abu Bakar (RA) led the Hajj. D) 11 AH is wrong: the Holy Prophet PBUH passed away in this year.
r: The Holy Prophet PBUH passed away in 11 AH.

q: Banu Quraiza were punished for their treachery in which year of Hijri?
f: A) 5 AH is right. Banu Quraiza were dealt with in 5 AH, right after Ghazwa Khandaq. B) 2 AH is wrong: that is the year of Badr. C) 7 AH is wrong: that is the year of Khaibar. D) 9 AH is wrong: that is the year of Tabuk.
r: Ghazwa Khandaq was also in 5 AH.

q: In Hajj, stoning the devil (Shaitan) is called:
f: B) Rami is right. Stoning the devil is called Rami. A) Istilam is wrong: it is touching the Black Stone. C) Saee is wrong: it is walking between Safa and Marwa. D) Tawaf is wrong: it is going around the Kaaba.
r: Istilam is touching the Black Stone.

q: Which was the first Ghazwa of the Holy Prophet PBUH?
f: A) Ghazwa Waddan (Abwa) is right. Ghazwa Waddan (also called Abwa) was the first Ghazwa, in Safar 2 AH. B) Ghazwa Badr is wrong: it came later, in Ramadan 2 AH, and was the first big battle. C) Ghazwa Uhud is wrong: it was fought in 3 AH. D) Ghazwa Khandaq is wrong: it was fought in 5 AH.
r: Ghazwa Badr (2 AH) was the first major battle of Islam.

q: Which of the following is one of the 3 Farz of Hajj?
f: C) is right: The 3 Farz of Hajj are Ihram, Wuquf-e-Arafat and Tawaf-e-Ziarat. A) Rami is Wajib, not Farz. B) Saee is Wajib, not Farz. D) Tawaf-e-Wida (farewell) is Wajib, not Farz.
